Mid-infrared illumination redistributes Nd3+ emission pathways, and the resulting optical-state change is read electrically through a silicon Schottky junction. At room temperature and zero bias, it reaches 103 µA/W modulation responsivity and distinguishes three current states corresponding to combined gate and mid-infrared inputs.
main_result: The system electrically detects 6.8 µm radiation at zero bias with 103 µA/W modulation responsivity and resolves three optically programmed current states.
application_angle: This transduction scheme could support silicon-integrated infrared sensors, programmable photonic circuits, and optical signal-processing elements.

title: Kinetic Slush in Dissipative Rydberg Arrays
abstract: We investigate the nonequilibrium dynamics of a kinetic slush state realized via facilitated excitations in a two-dimensional dissipative Rydberg atom array. Utilizing kinetic Monte Carlo simulations in the strong dephasing regime, we show that tuning the laser detuning to compensate for nearest-neighbor interactions enables facilitated dynamics, while residual next-nearest-neighbor interactions induce kinetic frustration. This competition gives rise to an emergent slush phase characterized by pronounced dynamical heterogeneity and the coexistence of liquid- and solid-like configurations. By probing its nonequilibrium real-time evolution, we uncover a dynamical crossover from isotropic spreading to one-dimensional constrained growth, which can be continuously tuned by the frustration strength. Within this crossover regime, the slush dynamics generate fractal cluster geometries and generalized Ornstein-Zernike spatial correlations. Finite-size scaling analysis supports the system's proximity to criticality. Our findings establish driven-dissipative Rydberg systems as a highly controllable platform for engineering complex nonequilibrium soft-matter phenomena.
one_liner: Simulations predict a tunable kinetic-slush regime with heterogeneous, frustrated growth and fractal clusters in dissipative 2D Rydberg arrays.
why_it_matters: It positions programmable Rydberg hardware as a controllable simulator of nonequilibrium criticality, kinetic frustration, and soft-matter-like dynamics.
detailed_summary: Kinetic Monte Carlo simulations examine facilitated excitation dynamics in a strongly dephased two-dimensional Rydberg array. Compensation of nearest-neighbor interactions enables facilitation, while residual next-nearest-neighbor interactions create frustration and coexistence of liquid- and solid-like configurations. Increasing frustration tunes a crossover from isotropic spreading to constrained one-dimensional growth, with fractal clusters, generalized Ornstein–Zernike correlations, and finite-size behavior consistent with proximity to criticality.
main_result: The study identifies a tunable kinetic-slush phase and a frustration-controlled crossover producing heterogeneous dynamics and fractal excitation clusters.
application_angle: Programmable dissipative Rydberg arrays could emulate complex nonequilibrium materials and test theories of constrained dynamics and critical behavior.

title: Controlled Dark-State Energy Storage and Work Extraction in V-Type Quantum Batteries
abstract: The performance of a quantum battery depends not only on its ability to retain stored energy against unwanted discharge but also on the amount of useful work that can be extracted from it. Here, we investigate these complementary aspects in an ensemble of V-type qutrits coupled to a lossy cavity. By applying a finite splitting pulse to the two excited states of each qutrit, cavity-bright excitations are converted into atomic dark states, whose populations remain protected upon restoring degeneracy, even while the light-matter coupling remains active. Simulations with finite-duration pulses reveal a capture window governed by the competition among energy transfer, bright-to-dark conversion, and photon leakage. We further show that if the energy is stored in the fully symmetric atomic subspace, the passive energy is bounded by twice the transition energy for number of atoms $N\geq2$. Consequently, if the stored energy scales extensively with $N$, the ratio of extractable work to stored energy approaches unity in the thermodynamic limit. Comparing different initial preparations at equal mean input energy, we find that coherent-state can yield greater finite-time ergotropy despite capturing less energy, whereas Fock-state favors greater extractable work in the stationary component. Our results demonstrate how controlled dark-state population trapping in an atom-cavity coupled system can protect stored energy while providing a conditional route toward high extractable work.
one_liner: Finite splitting pulses transfer cavity-bright excitations into protected atomic dark states in a V-type qutrit quantum battery.
why_it_matters: The proposal links robust energy trapping to high ergotropy, clarifying how atom–cavity quantum batteries can preserve energy without sacrificing useful work.
detailed_summary: An ensemble of V-type qutrits is coupled to a lossy cavity, and a finite excited-state splitting pulse converts bright excitations into atomic dark states. Simulations identify a capture window set by energy transfer, bright-to-dark conversion, and photon leakage. For storage in the fully symmetric atomic subspace, passive energy is bounded by twice the transition energy for N≥2, so extensively stored energy becomes almost entirely extractable as N grows.
platform_or_system: V-type qutrit ensemble coupled to a lossy cavity
main_result: Controlled splitting pulses trap excitation in protected dark states, while extensive symmetric storage yields an extractable-work fraction approaching unity at large atom number.
application_angle: The protocol provides a hardware-oriented strategy for cavity-based quantum energy storage with controlled capture, suppressed discharge, and high useful-work recovery.

title: The Disordered Universe 2025: Open Effective Field Theories
abstract: Effective field theories (EFTs) offer a powerful method to unify diverse models under a small set of control parameters, allowing systematic expansions around well-established theories. While these techniques were traditionally developed for particle physics experiments with clean, isolated initial states, realistic macroscopic environments are often noisy and dissipative. Recognising the limitations of traditional EFTs has recently sparked intense progress at the interface of high-energy physics and condensed matter. These developments motivate a new approach to gravitation and cosmology, one that models the gravitational sector as evolving in the presence of an unobservable medium. Open Effective Field Theories provide a systematic, controllable framework for this endeavour. This chapter presents this versatile framework and illustrates how the Schwinger-Keldysh formalism captures the influence of unknown environments, manifesting as dissipation and noise, on observational probes. These notes are based on a series of lectures held during the La Ricotta Summer School "The Disordered Universe 2025" from 21 July to 1 August 2025.
one_liner: These lecture notes formulate open effective field theories for observational probes influenced by inaccessible, noisy, and dissipative environments.
why_it_matters: The framework offers systematic tools for separating environmental noise and dissipation from underlying dynamics in gravitation, cosmology, and quantum probes.
detailed_summary: This pedagogical chapter develops open effective field theories for systems whose observable sector interacts with an unobserved environment. It uses the Schwinger–Keldysh formalism to organize environmental effects as controlled dissipative and stochastic terms. The treatment targets gravitation and cosmology but emphasizes methods applicable to noisy observational probes more broadly.
platform_or_system: Open-system observational probes modeled by Schwinger–Keldysh EFT
main_result: The work presents a systematic effective-field-theory framework for incorporating unknown-environment-induced noise and dissipation into observable dynamics.
application_angle: The formalism can guide inference and model construction for precision measurements where uncontrolled environments alter signals or introduce correlated noise.

title: Qubit-environment entanglement in pure dephasing dynamics for mixed initial states
abstract: Decoherence of qubits is one main limitation in quantum information processing, where the qubits themselves can be mixed because of decoherence and additional decoherence may generated through interactions with a bath. Here, we present a complete study of qubit-environment entanglement in the case of interactions that lead to pure dephasing of the qubit by allowing the initial state of the qubit to be mixed, exceeding previous restrictions. We find that the criteria for separability that hold for pure initial states of the qubit are reduced to witness status. Yet, the evolution of the witnesses reflects the array of features that entanglement can exhibit in the mixed case but are forbidden in the pure-qubit case. Most notably, this includes sudden birth of entanglement as the initial phase of the evolution is typically separable. Moreover, there is a stark numerical advantage to the study of entanglement for large environments when using the witness rather than the traditional measures available. We include the study of entanglement generated between a spin qubit and a sparse spin environment to illustrate the peculiarities of the evolution of entanglement in this case, as well as to emphasize the level of reliability of the entanglement witness.
one_liner: A scalable witness reveals sudden-birth and other mixed-state qubit–environment entanglement features during pure dephasing.
why_it_matters: Efficiently diagnosing bath entanglement can improve interpretation of decoherence and validation of noise models in solid-state qubit hardware.
detailed_summary: The analysis extends qubit–environment entanglement studies under pure dephasing to initially mixed qubit states. Separability criteria valid for pure qubits become witnesses, yet still capture mixed-state phenomena such as an initially separable interval followed by sudden entanglement birth. A spin qubit coupled to a sparse spin environment illustrates both the richer dynamics and the witness’s numerical advantage for large baths.
platform_or_system: Spin qubit undergoing pure dephasing in a sparse spin bath
main_result: The study establishes a computationally efficient witness for detecting mixed-state qubit–bath entanglement and identifies generic sudden-birth behavior.
application_angle: The witness could help characterize environment-induced errors and assess microscopic decoherence models without computing costly full entanglement measures.

title: Correlation-sensitive magic-state distillation from spin-squeezed neutral atoms
abstract: We show that interblock correlations can reverse magic-state distillation even when every input exceeds the threshold for independent states. For the five-to-one Bravyi-Kitaev protocol with independent local Clifford twirls, we express the output in terms of measurable target-axis moments. Fourth-order correlations determine acceptance, while third- and fifth-order correlations determine the output polarization. This relation yields a direct sign test for distillation gain and opposite gains for inputs with identical single-qubit and two-qubit reduced states. We connect this mechanism to neutral-atom resource preparation through finite-range Ising dynamics. Block separation suppresses detrimental interblock coupling, and locally addressed Clifford phases release interaction-generated magic from a spin-squeezed precursor by changing the symmetry selected by code projection. A protocol that retains accepted source outputs achieves positive gain above a source-contrast threshold set by circuit errors and storage dephasing. The same moments specify a finite-sample experimental diagnostic. These results connect the correlation structure of a resource state to its preparation, acceptance, and distillation gain.
one_liner: Higher-order interblock correlations can reverse five-to-one magic-state distillation gain in spin-squeezed neutral-atom resources.
why_it_matters: The results expose a failure mode invisible to low-order state metrics and provide experimentally measurable tests for neutral-atom fault-tolerance resources.
detailed_summary: For five-to-one Bravyi–Kitaev distillation with independent local Clifford twirls, acceptance depends on fourth-order target-axis moments, while output polarization depends on third- and fifth-order moments. Consequently, states with identical one- and two-qubit reduced density matrices can exhibit opposite distillation gains. Finite-range Ising preparation, block separation, and locally addressed Clifford phases are analyzed as controls for suppressing harmful coupling and releasing interaction-generated magic from a spin-squeezed precursor.
platform_or_system: Spin-squeezed neutral-atom arrays with finite-range Ising interactions
main_result: The paper derives a moment-based sign test for distillation gain and shows how preparation geometry and local Clifford phases can restore positive gain.
application_angle: The measurable correlation diagnostics can qualify neutral-atom magic-state sources and guide their layout, control phases, and error-budget requirements.

title: Quantum and Classical Memory for Storage and Retrieval of Quantum Measurements
abstract: We study the persistent quantum and classical memory required for exact heralded storage and retrieval of quantum measurements. Given only black-box access to the measurement channel, we construct an exact compression of the port-based program into an outcome-type record and a quantum register, with total dimension polynomial in the query count. For every universal retrieval processor we prove the bounds $Q+C\ge\log_2 n$ and $2Q+C\ge\log_2\bigl((n-1)d^2+1\bigr)$ on the numbers $Q$ of qubits and $C$ of bits of the program, for $n$-outcome POVMs on $\mathbb{C}^d$ with $d\ge2$. For $n\ge2$, no finite classical memory removes the need for quantum memory: any such processor requires a quantum program of dimension at least $d$, at that dimension its classical alphabet must have at least $n$ symbols, and both minima are attained by a single-query protocol with success $1/d^2$. Combining direct-program compression with a converse from approximate measurement programming gives logarithmic total-memory scaling in $1/(1-p)$ as the uniform success probability $p$ approaches one, at fixed $d,n\ge2$. At fixed input dimension and target success below one, the optimal total-memory scaling is logarithmic in $n$. We also construct self-contained programs under branch-decomposition access and compare the quantum and classical costs of all constructions, including where the outcome-type record is kept: for POVMs with $n$ nonzero rank-one effects the direct program admits a purely quantum allocation whose register is never larger than that of the minimal-Naimark unitary program and which succeeds more often whenever $n>d$.
one_liner: Exact heralded measurement storage requires irreducible quantum memory, with tight quantum-classical trade-offs for universal retrieval.
why_it_matters: The bounds clarify the minimum persistent resources needed to store programmable measurements in distributed quantum processors and communication nodes.
detailed_summary: The authors compress a port-based measurement program into an outcome-type classical record and a quantum register whose total dimension is polynomial in the query count. For universal retrieval of n-outcome POVMs on dimension d, they prove Q+C≥log2 n and 2Q+C≥log2((n−1)d²+1). They further show that finite classical storage cannot eliminate a quantum register of dimension at least d, while logarithmic total-memory scaling is achievable as success approaches unity.
main_result: The work establishes achievable protocols and lower bounds showing that exact universal measurement retrieval intrinsically requires quantum memory.
application_angle: These resource limits inform the design of measurement-program storage for modular processors, repeaters, and networked quantum devices.

title: The TEMPO network can be made independent of the system size
abstract: The time-evolving matrix product operator (TEMPO) method efficiently simulates non-Markovian open quantum system dynamics by contracting a two-dimensional tensor network representing the time-discretized Feynman-Vernon influence functional. The standard form of this network has an unfavorable scaling with the size of the system. We show that, within the usual second-order time-step error, the dimensions of all internal network bonds can be reduced to $(2m+1)(m+1)$, where $m$ is the number of independent coupling channels. This dimension does not depend on the number of distinct eigenvalues of the coupling operators. The system size only enters in the final boundary layer of the network, making large system sizes accessible to TEMPO methods. This structure was discovered by Claude Opus 5.5 during guided algorithm development.
one_liner: A compressed TEMPO tensor network makes its internal bond dimensions depend on bath-coupling channels rather than quantum-system size.
why_it_matters: The result could extend accurate non-Markovian simulations to much larger sensing and quantum-device models without enlarging the network bulk.
detailed_summary: Within the standard second-order time-step error, the authors reduce every internal TEMPO bond dimension to (2m+1)(m+1), where m is the number of independent coupling channels. This bound is independent of the number of distinct eigenvalues of the system coupling operators. System-size dependence is confined to the final boundary layer, potentially making large multilevel or composite systems accessible.
main_result: The TEMPO network bulk is compressed to a bond dimension controlled only by the number of environmental coupling channels.
application_angle: The compression enables more tractable modeling of non-Markovian decoherence in large sensors and quantum hardware.

title: Exact decoherence dynamics of a detector coupled to vacuum fluctuations in bounded geometries
abstract: The properties of quantum vacuum are highly sensitive to the underlying spacetime geometry and boundary conditions. We investigate in this paper the decoherence dynamics of a two-level system (detector) coupled to a vacuum scalar field through the $\hatσ_z$-coupling scheme under various boundary environments. By rigorously evaluating the reduced density matrix of the detector, we derive an exact general expression for the detector's decoherence function, $γ(Δt)$, and use it to characterize the dynamical decoherence of a detector in three scenarios: free space, a perfectly reflecting boundary, and a cavity formed by two parallel reflecting boundaries. We find that in free space the detector's coherence decays monotonically with time, indicating that vacuum fluctuations alone inevitably lead to a complete loss of coherence. In the single-boundary case, by contrast, the detector's coherence displays non-monotonic time evolution: $γ(Δt)$ increases with time up to a maximum and then settles to a steady value, indicating that the initial coherence can be partially preserved due to the presence of the boundary. When the detector is placed inside a cavity, its coherence evolution exhibits oscillatory behavior, and a significant fraction of the initial coherence survives. Moreover, for the same detector-boundary distance, more coherence is preserved in the cavity case than in the single-boundary case. These results provide a viable route for engineering quantum coherence via boundary conditions.
one_liner: Exact detector dynamics show that reflecting boundaries and cavities can preserve coherence otherwise lost to vacuum fluctuations.
why_it_matters: It identifies boundary geometry as a passive control knob for suppressing vacuum-induced decoherence in confined quantum systems.
detailed_summary: The paper derives an exact decoherence function for a two-level detector coupled through σz to a vacuum scalar field. Coherence decays completely and monotonically in free space, but a single reflecting boundary leaves a nonzero steady fraction after non-monotonic evolution. Between two parallel boundaries, coherence oscillates and a larger fraction survives than in the corresponding single-boundary geometry.
main_result: Exact solutions predict partial coherence preservation near one reflecting boundary and stronger oscillatory preservation inside a cavity.
application_angle: Engineered boundaries could passively extend coherence in cavity-based quantum nodes and confined communication hardware.

title: Generative quantum extreme learning machines
abstract: Training the circuit of a quantum generative model is hampered by barren plateaus, where gradients vanish exponentially with the number of qubits. In the present work we propose a generative protocol based on the paradigm of quantum extreme learning machines, in which the circuit is never trained. A random latent vector is encoded into a quantum state, evolved with a fixed unitary and measured, and only a linear output layer is trained. The encoding of the latent variable determines the functions available to the model, while the unitary decides which combinations of them are seen by the trained layer. With the help of Pauli propagation we show that for a Clifford unitary each feature is a single product of sines and cosines of the encoded angles, so that a Clifford circuit, even a strongly entangling one, does not create new functions. Doping the circuit with $T$ gates mixes these products and changes the nonstabilizerness of the state, but the space of functions remains the one fixed by the encoding. For brickworks of Haar-random two-qubit gates the features are no longer single products, and their variation with the latent variable decreases with the depth of the circuit. For the proposed encoding and for one- and two-dimensional distributions, generated both from expectation values and from single measurements, neither the entanglement produced by a Clifford reservoir nor the additional nonstabilizerness of Haar-random brickworks systematically improves the generator, and a reservoir with no gates at all is competitive with entangling circuits.
one_liner: Fixed quantum reservoirs avoid barren-plateau training, but simple ungated encodings can rival entangling Clifford and random circuits.
why_it_matters: The negative hardware-complexity result suggests that useful quantum generative models may not require deep, entangling, or nonstabilizer reservoirs.
detailed_summary: The protocol encodes random latent variables, applies a fixed unitary, measures quantum features, and trains only a linear classical output layer. Pauli propagation shows that Clifford reservoirs merely select products of encoding-derived sine and cosine functions, while T gates mix those products without expanding the encoding-defined function space. Across tested one- and two-dimensional distributions, neither Clifford entanglement nor Haar-random brickworks consistently improves generation over an ungated reservoir.
main_result: A trainable linear readout with no reservoir gates performs competitively with entangling Clifford and Haar-random quantum circuits on the studied generators.
application_angle: The approach could reduce circuit depth, calibration burden, and training instability for near-term generative quantum-learning experiments.

title: QNETSIM for memory assisted design of satellite and hybrid quantum networks
abstract: Space-based quantum information networks require simulation tools that capture orbital dynamics, probabilistic quantum operations, and classical coordination. We introduce QNETSIM, a modular discrete-event simulator for the design and performance evaluation of satellite and hybrid space-ground quantum networks. The framework integrates orbital geometry, free-space optical and fiber channels, quantum memories, entanglement generation, and Bell-state measurements within a common event-driven architecture. Physical models account for optical loss, atmospheric turbulence, detector imperfections, finite memory capacity, and storage-induced decoherence. Space-time routing and segmented nesting support entanglement distribution across changing topologies, while a software-defined control plane coordinates generation, storage, and swapping. Configurable scenarios encompass onboard repeaters, satellite constellations, ground-based repeaters, and direct satellite distribution. Through explicit interfaces between physical models, network protocols, and orchestration, QNETSIM links component characteristics and operational policies to entanglement fidelity, throughput, latency, availability, and memory utilization, enabling systematic exploration of architectural and resource-management trade-offs in future space-based quantum information networks.
one_liner: QNETSIM combines orbital motion, lossy quantum channels, finite memories, routing, and control for satellite-network design.
why_it_matters: It connects device specifications and scheduling policies directly to fidelity, throughput, latency, availability, and memory use in space-ground networks.
detailed_summary: QNETSIM is a modular discrete-event framework integrating orbital geometry, free-space and fiber links, quantum memories, entanglement generation, and Bell-state measurements. Its physical models include atmospheric turbulence, optical loss, imperfect detectors, finite memory capacity, and storage decoherence. Space-time routing, segmented nesting, and a software-defined control plane support onboard repeaters, constellations, hybrid terrestrial repeaters, and direct satellite links.
main_result: The simulator evaluates memory-assisted entanglement distribution across time-varying space-ground topologies using coupled physical, protocol, and control models.
application_angle: It enables architecture and resource-policy studies before costly deployment of satellite repeaters and hybrid quantum-network infrastructure.

title: Quantum circuits of elastic wave equations via Schrödingerisation
abstract: We construct explicit quantum circuits for the velocity-stress formulation of elastic wave equations in homogeneous media using Schrödingerisation. After rewriting the equations in symmetric matrix form(SMF), we use Fourier spectral discretization for source-driven periodic problems and staggered-grid finite differences for Dirichlet, Neumann, and impedance boundary conditions. The Schrödingerisation method transforms any linear PDEs into a system of Schrödinger-type PDEs -with unitary evolution- using the warped phase transformation that maps the equations in one higher dimension. For periodic problems, we develop circuits by combining controlled Fourier-mode rotations. For physical boundaries, interleaved encoding swaps the spatial and field-component registers, enabling a more efficient circuit construction using shift operators. We analyze $p$th-order Trotter-Suzuki formulas and derive splitting-error and CNOT-gate estimates, under the assumptions of smooth auxiliary initialization and solution-state recovery. Comparison with classical partitioned splitting methods identifies a polynomial improvement in spatial-resolution dependence for the quantum state-evolution subroutine. Noiseless circuit simulations of a forced periodic problem and an impedance problem illustrate the constructions and quantify their errors against exact solutions and classical reference computations.
one_liner: Schrödingerisation yields explicit unitary circuits for elastic-wave propagation with periodic and physical boundary conditions.
why_it_matters: The construction advances quantum wave simulation toward realistic source-driven geometries while quantifying discretization, splitting, and gate costs.
detailed_summary: The authors map velocity-stress elastic-wave equations to unitary Schrödinger-type evolution in one auxiliary dimension. Fourier spectral circuits treat source-driven periodic problems, while staggered-grid finite differences and interleaved register swaps handle Dirichlet, Neumann, and impedance boundaries. They derive Trotter-Suzuki error and CNOT estimates and validate forced-periodic and impedance examples using noiseless simulations against exact or classical references.
main_result: Explicit circuits reproduce representative elastic-wave solutions and offer polynomially improved spatial-resolution dependence for the state-evolution subroutine under stated assumptions.
application_angle: The method could support future quantum simulation of acoustic, elastic, and wave-based sensing structures with realistic boundaries.

title: Wavefunction-templated metamaterials
abstract: Metamaterials, which store, guide and emit waves through their eigenmodes, have enabled the development of devices with unprecedented functionalities. Yet the spatial profiles of conventional metamaterials' eigenmodes are typically determined by their pre-determined structures (Hamiltonians). In this work, we introduce `wavefunction-templated metamaterials', a class of physically realizable metamaterials hosting diverse prescribed, spectrally isolated eigenstates. The resulting Hamiltonian geometries obey a boundary law, with the required nonlocality determined solely by single-contact boundary sites, independent of the state interior or lattice size. The sparse Hamiltonians are then Hermitianized, followed by spectral reshaping to open a protective gap around the target eigenstate. We validate our approach in discrete lattices and acoustic metamaterials. Although demonstrated in acoustics, the principle can be applied to thermal, electrical-circuit and photonic metamaterials.
one_liner: A design method creates metamaterials whose spectrally isolated eigenmodes reproduce prescribed spatial wavefunctions.
why_it_matters: Programmable eigenmode profiles could enable tailored wave storage, transport, emission, and sensing across acoustic, photonic, thermal, and electrical platforms.
detailed_summary: The authors construct physically realizable sparse Hamiltonians that host a prescribed eigenstate, with required nonlocality determined only by single-contact boundary sites. They Hermitianize the resulting Hamiltonians and reshape their spectra to open a protective gap around the target mode. The method is validated in discrete lattices and acoustic metamaterials, with proposed extension to photonic, thermal, and electrical systems.
main_result: The work demonstrates metamaterials supporting user-prescribed, spectrally protected eigenmodes through a boundary-law-based Hamiltonian construction.
application_angle: The approach offers a route to devices with custom field profiles for wave localization, routing, emission control, and spatially selective sensing.

title: HTM: A Hybrid Classical-Quantum Computation Model
abstract: Classical and quantum computers have achieved collaborative computation and completed applications across numerous fields. Nevertheless, the absence of a unified hybrid computation model has led to issues such as non-standardized engineering architecture design, ambiguous task partitioning criteria and so on. To address these issues, this research proposes a hybrid classical-quantum computation model (HTM). By constructing unified state sets and transition function representations, HTM clarifies hybrid control logic and implements a control-sharing mechanism. Simultaneously, a comprehensive complexity calculation method based on entanglement and superposition was proposed, supporting computation task partitioning and resource scheduling. The HTM fills a theoretical gap in the classical-quantum hybrid computation area and implements the joint promotion and development of computing models and hardware.
one_liner: HTM formalizes hybrid classical-quantum computation through unified states, transitions, shared control, and complexity metrics.
why_it_matters: A common abstraction for control and resource accounting could help engineers partition workloads and schedule heterogeneous classical-quantum hardware.
detailed_summary: HTM represents classical and quantum execution using unified state sets and transition functions intended to clarify hybrid control flow. It introduces a control-sharing mechanism and a complexity calculation incorporating entanglement and superposition. The contribution is a theoretical computation model rather than an experimental hardware demonstration.
main_result: The paper proposes a unified formal model for hybrid control, task partitioning, complexity estimation, and resource scheduling.
application_angle: The framework could support more standardized orchestration of quantum accelerators within classical computing systems.

title: Deployed entanglement-based BBM92 quantum key distribution using frequency-converted photons emitted by a quantum dot
abstract: Establishing secure communication is an important requirement in existing and future networks. Although current solutions rely on classical approaches, quantum mechanics offers the possibility of moving from computational to information-theoretic security. Quantum key distribution (QKD) has been extensively studied as a means of achieving such security. Recently, epitaxial quantum dots started to be studied and employed in quantum cryptography, because of their rapid development that made them one of the brightest sources of quantum light to date. In particular, they are known to be excellent sources of polarization-entangled photon pairs, especially droplet-etched dots operating at $\sim$780 nm. Here, we employ such a quantum dot to generate entangled photon pairs under 1 GHz excitation rate. Using quantum frequency conversion, we interface the emitted photons with the telecommunication wavelength range while preserving their polarization entanglement. This enables quantum key distribution over a 1.59 km field-deployed fibre link across the University of Stuttgart - campus Vaihingen, using the BBM92 protocol: we achieve a secure key rate of 206 Hz over 19 h of stable operation, resulting in a total secure key length of 14.2 Mbit. This key enables the safe encryption and decryption of a colour image with further implementation of error correction and privacy amplification. These results demonstrate important steps towards hybrid quantum networks by combining high-quality entangled-photon sources operated at high excitation rates, efficient frequency conversion module, and picosecond-level time synchronization in a realistic deployed network.
one_liner: A frequency-converted quantum-dot source delivers entanglement-based BBM92 QKD over 1.59 km of deployed campus fiber.
why_it_matters: The 19-hour field trial combines a bright solid-state entangled-photon source, telecom conversion, and precise synchronization in a realistic network.
detailed_summary: A droplet-etched quantum dot, excited at 1 GHz, generates polarization-entangled photon pairs near 780 nm that are converted to telecom wavelengths while retaining entanglement. The system runs BBM92 over a 1.59 km field-deployed fiber link with picosecond-level synchronization. It produces a 206 Hz secure key rate during 19 hours of stable operation, accumulating 14.2 Mbit after error correction and privacy amplification.
main_result: The deployed system generated 14.2 Mbit of secure key at 206 Hz over 19 hours and used it to encrypt and decrypt a color image.
application_angle: The demonstration advances hybrid quantum networks that connect high-rate solid-state photon sources to existing telecom fiber infrastructure.

title: Rubidium-Referenced Frequency-Doubled Pockels Laser with High-Speed Electro-Optic Tuning
abstract: Narrow-linewidth lasers with rapid frequency control are essential for atomic physics and quantum technologies, yet combining these capabilities in chip-integrated sources at visible wavelengths remains challenging. Here we demonstrate a hybrid integrated InP/thin-film lithium niobate Pockels laser that emits at 780 nm through intracavity second-harmonic generation and supports gigahertz-bandwidth frequency tuning. A periodically poled lithium niobate waveguide is embedded in a laser cavity terminated by an extended distributed Bragg reflector, which provides electro-optically tunable feedback only at the 1560 nm fundamental wavelength. This design yields a singly resonant cavity that enhances frequency conversion while allowing the second-harmonic output to follow rapid tuning without resonance alignment. The laser achieves intrinsic linewidths of 2.7 kHz at 1560 nm and 9.0 kHz at 780 nm, with electro-optic tuning bandwidths beyond 1 GHz at both wavelengths. A mode-hop-free tuning range of 6.48 GHz at 780 nm enables direct spectroscopy of the rubidium D2 transition. Locking the second-harmonic output to this transition reduces the standard deviation of its frequency fluctuations from 135 MHz to 8 MHz and transfers the atomic frequency reference to the fundamental. These results establish integrated frequency-doubled Pockels lasers as compact, rapidly tunable sources that could simplify the optical architectures for future atomic and quantum photonic systems.
one_liner: An integrated frequency-doubled Pockels laser delivers kilohertz linewidths and gigahertz-speed tuning at 780 nm.
why_it_matters: The source combines visible output, rapid electro-optic control, and rubidium referencing in a compact architecture suited to atomic and quantum systems.
detailed_summary: The hybrid InP/thin-film lithium-niobate laser uses intracavity second-harmonic generation to produce 780 nm light from a 1560 nm fundamental. It reaches intrinsic linewidths of 2.7 kHz and 9.0 kHz at the fundamental and harmonic, respectively, with tuning bandwidths above 1 GHz. A 6.48 GHz mode-hop-free range enables rubidium D2 spectroscopy, while atomic locking reduces frequency-fluctuation standard deviation from 135 MHz to 8 MHz.
main_result: The device combines narrow-linewidth 780 nm generation, greater-than-1 GHz tuning bandwidth, and rubidium-referenced stabilization on an integrated platform.
application_angle: It could simplify compact laser systems for atomic clocks, quantum memories, neutral-atom hardware, spectroscopy, and precision sensing.

title: Prepare-and-measure quantum key distribution from a bound on information leakage
abstract: Every quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol must limit the information available outside the users' laboratories. In device-independent QKD this is essentially the only assumption made on the devices. In a prepare-and-measure setting it cannot be imposed strictly, since the sender's device must emit a signal that depends on her private input. The natural replacement, and a minimal one, is a leakage bound: a bound on how much information about the input leaves the sender's laboratory, through the intended signal or through any side channel. We ask how far this unavoidable requirement can replace a detailed model of the source. We show that this single bound, quantified by the probability of guessing the input from everything the source emits, suffices to prove security against collective attacks. In our analysis, nothing is assumed about the precise form of the emitted states, their dimension, energy or purity, nor about the receiver's measurement device, beyond the standard requirement that it does not leak Bob's data. The standard B92 and BB84 protocols do not certify any key under this minimal leakage bound assumption. But closely related protocols can and, in the ideal limit, achieve one secret bit per key round. For noisy implementations, we compute key rates using semidefinite programming relaxations. Our best protocols tolerate visibilities down to 0.84, corresponding to an 8% quantum bit error rate, compared with the 11% threshold of standard device-dependent BB84.
one_liner: Prepare-and-measure QKD security is derived from a single operational bound on information leaking from the sender.
why_it_matters: The framework reduces reliance on detailed source models and accommodates arbitrary emitted-state dimension, energy, purity, and receiver measurements.
detailed_summary: The security proof assumes only a bound on the probability of guessing the sender's input from everything emitted by the source, plus no leakage of Bob's data. It makes no detailed assumptions about emitted-state dimension, energy, purity, or Bob's measurement device. Standard B92 and BB84 fail under this minimal model, but modified protocols can approach one secret bit per key round and tolerate visibility down to 0.84, equivalent to 8% QBER.
main_result: A single leakage bound suffices for collective-attack security, with optimized protocols retaining positive key rates down to 0.84 visibility.
application_angle: The result may enable QKD implementations with weaker source-characterization requirements and explicit protection against unintended side-channel emissions.

title: Security Analysis of Ekert-type QKD Protocol Coming Under Cloning Attacks
abstract: We analyze the security of an Ekert type bipartite key distribution protocol coming under cloning attacks by an untrusted observer. Precisely, an eavesdropper is assumed to intercept and apply an asymmetric, phase-variant cloner on one or both qubits which are transmitted over public channel from an authenticated source to the trusted parties. We partially characterize two-qubit states from the perspective of designing a QKD protocol that can generate a distillable secret key among the trusted users even under such cloning attacks. We rely upon Devetak Winter framework for computing key rate so as to identify states, which when used in the protocol, secret-key can be distilled. Utility of an entangled state, for designing a successful QKD protocol, changes from single-qubit to double-qubits cloning attacks. Interestingly, we can distinguish some useful families of two-qubit entangled states when only one of the transmitted qubits is cloned by a malicious third party.
one_liner: The study evaluates Ekert-type QKD key generation when asymmetric phase-variant cloning attacks target one or both transmitted qubits.
why_it_matters: It identifies how the usefulness of two-qubit entangled states changes with the location and extent of cloning attacks.
detailed_summary: The authors model an eavesdropper applying an asymmetric, phase-variant cloner to one or both qubits distributed from an authenticated source. Secret-key rates are assessed using the Devetak–Winter framework to partially classify useful two-qubit input states. The analysis finds that state utility differs between single-qubit and double-qubit cloning, and identifies entangled-state families useful when only one qubit is cloned.
main_result: The paper partially characterizes two-qubit states that retain distillable secret key under specified asymmetric cloning attacks.
application_angle: The findings can inform entangled-state selection and threat modeling for QKD links exposed to interception and cloning strategies.

title: Measurement incompatibility and noiseless quantum codes
abstract: We construct a rank-one minimal informationally complete measurement (MIC) with an invertible dual operator and prove that, for arbitrary finite input and output dimensions, a channel universally preserves measurement incompatibility if and only if its input space contains a noiseless code subspace of the full output dimension. Preserving the compatibility threshold of a finite family of binary measurements already guarantees such a code. Furthermore, for every $d\ge2$, there exists a family of binary measurements that is incompatible on the full space but compatible after compression to any proper subspace. These results resolve the conjecture of Chitambar and Zhang and the existence question posed by Uola and coauthors. We also give an explicit construction of exact encodings and show that, for a sufficiently small shift in the compatibility threshold, the transmission error of an approximate encoding is bounded by a constant times the square of the shift. These results establish a connection between measurement compatibility, quantum steering, and quantum error correction.
one_liner: Universal preservation of measurement incompatibility is shown to be equivalent to hosting a full-output-dimension noiseless quantum code.
why_it_matters: It links operational measurement tests to exact and approximate quantum error correction, offering a route to certify protected encodings through incompatibility.
detailed_summary: The authors construct a rank-one minimal informationally complete measurement with an invertible dual and characterize channels that universally preserve measurement incompatibility. Such preservation occurs exactly when the input contains a noiseless code subspace whose dimension equals the full output dimension. A finite family of binary measurements suffices for certification, and a small compatibility-threshold shift yields a quadratic bound on approximate-encoding error.
main_result: Measurement-incompatibility preservation exactly certifies a noiseless code, with quantitative robustness bounds for approximate encodings.
application_angle: The result could support measurement-based verification of protected logical subspaces in quantum processors and communication hardware.

title: Homodyne Unravelling and Parameter Estimation in Squeezed Thermal Baths
abstract: We derive an alternative formulation of the stochastic master equation describing the evolution of quantum systems continuously measured via homodyne detection in a squeezed-thermal environment. This formulation allows us to identify two distinct collapse operators, corresponding respectively to the monitored and unmonitored channels, and to express the quantum state evolution directly in terms of Kraus-like operators. As a consequence, it facilitates the application of advanced numerical methods that account for higher-order corrections and discrete-time monitoring, and it also enables the efficient numerical evaluation of Cramér-Rao bounds in parameter estimation problems. To demonstrate the latter, we evaluate the Fisher information of the continuous homodyne monitoring for qubit frequency estimation in the presence of a squeezed-thermal bath. Our results show that exponential scaling of the steady-state Fisher information rate with squeezing is retained even at non-zero temperature.
one_liner: A homodyne stochastic model enables efficient metrology calculations in squeezed thermal baths while retaining squeezing-enhanced sensitivity.
why_it_matters: The formulation makes realistic continuous-monitoring simulations easier and shows that thermal noise need not erase exponential metrological gains from squeezing.
detailed_summary: The work reformulates homodyne stochastic evolution in a squeezed thermal environment using separate monitored and unmonitored collapse operators and Kraus-like updates. This structure supports higher-order numerical integration, discrete-time monitoring, and efficient Cramér–Rao-bound evaluation. For qubit-frequency estimation, the steady-state Fisher-information rate retains exponential scaling with squeezing even at nonzero temperature.
platform_or_system: homodyne-monitored qubit in a squeezed thermal bath
main_result: The derived unravelling preserves exponential squeezing enhancement of the steady-state Fisher-information rate at finite temperature.
application_angle: It provides practical modeling tools for continuous optical readout and parameter estimation in noisy squeezed-reservoir experiments.

title: Dynamical quantum simulations as laboratories for quantum information
abstract: Dynamical quantum simulations are commonly designed to access a particular response function or correlation function. Yet the underlying protocol prepares a family of many-body states that contains information well beyond the observable for which the simulation was originally designed. In this work, we explore the idea of using these states as laboratories for quantum information. As a case study, we consider the local-pulse protocols used to compute Green functions in finite XX and XXX spin chains, and we interpret opposite source rotations as encoding a classical bit into the many-body system. This allows us to follow how the resulting record propagates, how it is encoded across local subsystems, and how readily it can be accessed with different measurements. We also find a clear separation between representation and readout. While fermionic covariance data exactly reconstruct the signed response in the XX chain, simple spin measurements recover a larger fraction of the locally available information in the XXX chain. This reversed ordering persists when we move from finite-pulse discrimination to local source-angle estimation. Going beyond the source record, the same reduced states also allow us to reinterpret results in terms of Bell state recovery and quantum communication rates, as well as providing direct access to the evolving bipartite and genuine multipartite entanglement of the system. Our results show that dynamical quantum simulations developed for response calculations can naturally be used to ask a much broader set of quantum-information questions about the many-body states they already prepare.
one_liner: Spin-chain response simulations are repurposed to quantify information transport, readout, entanglement, and communication rates.
why_it_matters: It extracts quantum-information capabilities from states already prepared for many-body response measurements, expanding the value of existing simulators.
detailed_summary: Local-pulse protocols for Green-function calculations in finite XX and XXX chains are reinterpreted as encoding a classical bit through opposite source rotations. Reduced states reveal how the record propagates, distributes across subsystems, and depends on the measurement used for readout. The same data yield Bell-state recovery, communication-rate, and multipartite-entanglement diagnostics, with contrasting optimal readouts in XX and XXX models.
platform_or_system: finite XX and XXX spin-chain simulators
main_result: Standard dynamical-response protocols can simultaneously characterize information transfer, accessible records, communication performance, and evolving entanglement.
application_angle: Existing quantum simulators could assess communication channels and information scrambling without requiring entirely new state-preparation protocols.

title: Optimal quantum discrimination at Liouvillian exceptional points
abstract: Central to non-Hermitian sensing is the question of whether exceptional points (EPs) can make weak perturbations easier to detect. We show that despite enhanced spectral response, in finite-dimensional Lindblad systems with a unique stationary state and a nonzero relaxation gap, EPs offer no fundamental advantage in how the observation time required for reliable detection of a weak perturbation scales with the perturbation strength. We nevertheless demonstrate that by selectively choosing perturbations that enhance the quantum Fisher information rate, EPs can shorten the observation time needed to reach a predefined detection accuracy relative to a comparable non-EP reference at the same decay rate. As an illustration, we show using an optomechanical model at an EP that we can detect a weak force through the cavity output at the same reliability in less time than a non-EP reference. Our results establish fundamental limits on perturbation detection at EPs and can guide the design of faster non-Hermitian sensors based on optomechanical resonators, superconducting qubits, and trapped ions.
one_liner: Liouvillian exceptional points cannot improve asymptotic detection scaling but can reduce the time needed for fixed-accuracy sensing.
why_it_matters: It separates genuine speed gains from spectral-response hype and gives actionable criteria for designing faster non-Hermitian quantum sensors.
detailed_summary: For finite-dimensional Lindblad systems with a unique stationary state and finite relaxation gap, exceptional points do not improve the fundamental scaling of observation time with perturbation strength. Carefully selected perturbations can nevertheless increase the quantum Fisher-information rate and reduce the prefactor for a fixed detection target. An optomechanical example demonstrates faster weak-force discrimination through cavity-output monitoring than a decay-matched non-EP reference.
main_result: An exceptional-point sensor detects a weak force in less time at fixed reliability, despite having no advantage in asymptotic perturbation scaling.
application_angle: The bounds and design rule can guide faster force and perturbation sensors using optomechanical resonators, superconducting qubits, or trapped ions.

title: Defining 2-group symmetries on lattices and extracting their anomalies
abstract: Ordinary $0$-form symmetries $G$ can mix with $1$-form symmetries $Π_2$ to form a $2$-group $\mathcal{G}$. We give a concrete lattice definition for a class of finite $2$-group symmetries in terms of local relations among symmetry operators. These relations identify the Postnikov class $[ρ]\in H^3(BG,Π_2)$ that characterizes the mixing. We develop a method to extract anomalies of these symmetries in one spatial dimension by restricting symmetry operations to an interval and comparing their composition near its endpoints. We also construct explicit qubit symmetry actions in $d=1,2,3$ spatial dimensions for a $2$-group with $G=Π_2=\mathbb{Z}_2$. These actions share the same nontrivial Postnikov class but include both anomaly-free and anomalous realizations. Their cohomological anomalies are classified by $H^{d+2}(B\mathcal G,U(1))$, which is $\mathbb{Z}_2$ for $d=1,2$ and $\mathbb{Z}_2\times\mathbb{Z}_2$ for $d=3$, and our constructions realize every class in these dimensions. Our results connect higher-group symmetry and its anomalies to concrete lattice operations, providing a microscopic framework for studying anomalous symmetries.
one_liner: Concrete qubit-lattice constructions realize and diagnose every classified anomaly of a finite 2-group symmetry in one to three dimensions.
why_it_matters: It turns abstract higher-group symmetry data into microscopic lattice operations that can be implemented and tested in programmable quantum simulators.
detailed_summary: The authors define finite 2-group symmetries through local relations among lattice symmetry operators, exposing the Postnikov class that mixes zero-form and one-form sectors. They extract one-dimensional anomalies by restricting symmetry operations to intervals and comparing endpoint composition laws. Explicit qubit actions in one, two, and three dimensions realize all cohomologically classified anomaly classes for a Z2–Z2 2-group.
main_result: Explicit local qubit symmetry actions realize every anomaly class of the studied finite 2-group across one, two, and three spatial dimensions.
application_angle: The constructions provide implementable targets for probing anomalous higher symmetries and topological phases on quantum-simulation hardware.

title: Long-Range Toric Code: Finite-Temperature Topological Order in Two Dimensions
abstract: We introduce two-dimensional toric code models with additional long-range loop interactions. Our models preserve the topologically ordered ground states of the ordinary toric code, while confining anyons at zero temperature. For sufficiently long-ranged interactions, we argue that this confinement persists at finite temperatures, strongly constraining anyon mobility and giving rise to finite-temperature topological order. This topological phase acts as a self-correcting quantum memory and exhibits long-range entanglement. For shorter-ranged interactions, signatures of topological order survive only up to an exponentially large length scale at finite temperature, yielding a partially self-correcting quantum memory.
one_liner: Long-range loop interactions can stabilize two-dimensional toric-code order at finite temperature and produce self-correcting quantum memory.
why_it_matters: A finite-temperature self-correcting memory in two dimensions would directly address passive protection of quantum information against thermal errors.
detailed_summary: The proposed toric-code variants add long-range loop interactions while preserving the conventional topologically ordered ground-state manifold. Sufficiently long-ranged interactions confine anyons even at finite temperature, suppressing their mobility and sustaining long-range entanglement. Shorter-range interactions instead provide topological protection only up to an exponentially large finite length scale, producing partial self-correction.
main_result: Long-range loop interactions yield finite-temperature topological order and self-correcting quantum-memory behavior in a two-dimensional toric code.
application_angle: The model suggests a route to passive quantum memories with reduced active error-correction overhead, provided suitable long-range interactions can be engineered.

title: A photonic-integrated optomechanical mid-infrared detector
abstract: Tracking the resonance frequency of a mechanical oscillator is the basis of atomic force microscopy, mass sensing and thermometry. Nanomechanical thermal detectors exploit this principle to sense absorbed radiation, most effectively with tensile-stressed resonators, whose tension converts thermal expansion into a large frequency shift and dilutes dissipation. Approaching their fundamental sensitivity limit, however, has required free-space or fibre-coupled interferometers, hindering compact deployment and scaling to arrays. Here we remove this bottleneck by monolithically integrating a high-Q nanomechanical resonator with a silicon nitride photonic integrated circuit. A tensile-stressed silicon nitride trampoline with an impedance-matched platinum absorber is dispersively coupled to a photonic integrated microresonator beneath it. At room temperature and with microwatt-level optical power, the detector reaches a noise-equivalent power of 3.4 pW/$\sqrt{\rm Hz}$ for broadband thermal radiation (3-12 $μ$m), referred to incident power. Referred to absorbed power, this is within a factor of 1.5 of its fundamental thermal fluctuation limit. Using our detector in a state-of-the-art commercial Fourier-transform infrared spectrometer, we resolve the vibrational fingerprint of a polymer film across 2-20 $μ$m and reach the precision of the built-in pyroelectric detector with about an order of magnitude lower incident power. This architecture opens a route to multiplexed optomechanical focal-plane arrays.
one_liner: A monolithic SiN optomechanical detector achieves near-thermal-limit broadband mid-infrared sensing with integrated photonic readout.
why_it_matters: It replaces bulky interferometric readout with a scalable photonic circuit while retaining sensitivity suitable for practical infrared spectroscopy and detector arrays.
detailed_summary: A tensile-stressed silicon nitride trampoline with an impedance-matched platinum absorber is dispersively coupled to an underlying integrated microresonator. At room temperature and microwatt optical readout power, it reaches an incident-power NEP of 3.4 pW/√Hz over 3–12 μm and an absorbed-power sensitivity within 1.5× of the thermal fluctuation limit. In a commercial FTIR spectrometer, it resolves a polymer fingerprint across 2–20 μm with pyroelectric-class precision using roughly tenfold lower incident power.
main_result: The integrated detector combines 3.4 pW/√Hz broadband NEP with practical 2–20 μm FTIR spectroscopy at room temperature.
application_angle: The monolithic architecture could enable compact spectrometers and multiplexed optomechanical focal-plane arrays for chemical and thermal imaging.

title: Parity-Resolved Many-Body Kinetics of a Topological Qubit under Nonequilibrium Phonon Pulses
abstract: Phonon bursts from ionizing radiation cause correlated errors in superconducting quantum processors. We study prescribed nonequilibrium phonon pulses in a Majorana qubit formed by two $2\,μ\mathrm{m}$ proximitized nanowires. Combining the lattice Lutchyn--Oreg model, microscopic electron--phonon coupling, and parity-resolved many-body dynamics, we track excitation, relaxation, and logical coherence. Without quasiparticle escape, recombination restores the initial Majorana occupations in about 130 ns, while phonons exchanged during excitation and recovery can retain logical-state information, leaving permanent coherence loss. For mirror-symmetric wires, the fractional coherence loss per wire is 0.75--1.0 times the excitation probability averaged over the two logical states, even at zero Majorana splitting; breaking mirror symmetry can suppress dephasing at small splitting. Factorized Boltzmann kinetics neglects quasiparticle correlations and overestimates residual parity flips. At equal deposited energy density, phonon spectra yield different excitation probabilities and coherence losses. Comparisons with Kitaev chains matched to the wire's gap and Majorana decay length reveal that low electron density suppresses excitation by energetic phonons, whereas hard-wall boundaries in a high-density control increase excitation efficiency by a factor of $5\times10^4$ relative to the wire for pulses centered at 1 meV. Magnetic-field and chemical-potential tuning yield different phonon sensitivities at the same bulk gap through changes in spin and electron--hole structure. Including hybrid states' semiconductor weights reduces near-threshold excitation rates fourfold when the tunnel coupling equals the parent superconducting gap. Our framework connects phonon spectra to leakage, poisoning, and coherence loss to guide Majorana-device design.
one_liner: Parity-resolved simulations quantify how nonequilibrium phonon pulses cause leakage, poisoning, and irreversible dephasing in Majorana qubits.
why_it_matters: The model exposes device-dependent phonon vulnerabilities that simpler Boltzmann kinetics miss, informing radiation-hard topological-qubit engineering.
detailed_summary: The study combines a lattice Lutchyn–Oreg model, microscopic electron–phonon coupling, and parity-resolved many-body dynamics for two 2 μm proximitized nanowires. Recombination restores Majorana occupations in about 130 ns without quasiparticle escape, but phonons retain logical-state information and leave permanent coherence loss. Excitation varies strongly with phonon spectrum, symmetry, carrier density, boundaries, tuning parameters, and semiconductor weight; factorized Boltzmann kinetics overestimates residual parity flips.
main_result: The framework maps phonon spectra and device structure to correlated excitation, parity errors, and persistent logical-coherence loss.
application_angle: It provides quantitative design guidance for suppressing radiation-induced errors in Majorana-based quantum processors.

title: Complex Langevin kernels for real-time SU(N) lattice gauge theory in 3+1 dimensions
abstract: We investigate complex Langevin (CL) dynamics for real-time SU($N$) gauge theories in 3+1 dimensions and introduce new kernel modifications tailored for lattice gauge theory (LGT). Using the anisotropic kernel as a baseline, we demonstrate that on a rectangular regularized Schwinger-Keldysh time contour, stable simulations are possible for pure SU(2) gauge theory up to a real-time extent of $2β$ at a bare coupling $g=0.5$, where $β$ denotes the inverse temperature. We show that a contour-dependent phase kernel extends this reach to $3β$, while a local, field-dependent kernel based on traced plaquettes achieves $3.5β$. These constructions represent the first application of such kernels to LGTs, especially in 3+1 dimensions. To validate the approach, we generalize the CL correctness criterion based on the drift magnitude to kernelled dynamics, providing a practical tool to assess correct convergence. Our results substantially advance the applicability of CL to real-time simulations in Minkowski space, establishing a framework for controlled studies of non-Abelian gauge theories at unprecedented time scales. A forthcoming paper applies these developments to the computation of unequal-time correlation functions.
one_liner: New complex-Langevin kernels extend stable real-time 3+1D SU(2) lattice-gauge simulations from 2β to 3.5β.
why_it_matters: Longer controlled Minkowski-time evolution enables more credible calculations of nonequilibrium non-Abelian dynamics and future unequal-time observables.
detailed_summary: The authors formulate contour-phase and local plaquette-dependent kernels for complex Langevin evolution of pure SU(2) gauge theory on a rectangular Schwinger–Keldysh contour. At bare coupling g=0.5, the anisotropic baseline remains stable to 2β, the phase kernel to 3β, and the field-dependent kernel to 3.5β. They also generalize the drift-magnitude correctness criterion to kernelled dynamics for practical convergence assessment.
main_result: A local field-dependent kernel enables controlled complex-Langevin evolution to a real-time extent of 3.5β.
application_angle: The method supports longer nonequilibrium simulations relevant to extracting real-time correlations and transport observables in non-Abelian quantum systems.

title: Shor's algorithm compiled on cat qubits: 22 593 qubits for RSA-2048 in 3.14 days
abstract: We present an end-to-end resource estimation of Shor's algorithm on superconducting cat qubits, from its mathematical description to the allocation and scheduling of physical qubits on a chip layout. We review modern versions of Shor's algorithm for RSA, ECDLP and FFDLP, and make their logical circuits and trade-offs explicit. We compile the dominant subroutines down to physical-qubit operations on two architectures: one based on repetition cat codes and one on LDPC cat codes. We design a parity-Cnot gate for cat qubits, extend a multi-target Cnot gate to the LDPC-cat architecture, and adapt an active injection procedure to cat qubits. Building on these primitives, we adapt to cat qubits the adder from Gidney's 2025 resource estimate for factoring RSA-2048. We combine our adder compilation and a coarser estimate for the phaseup with the factory designs and lookup compilation from the FeMoco resource estimation of Kroell et al. Together, these lead to chip layouts and schedules for factoring RSA-2048. Assuming a 1$μ$s error-correction cycle time, a 10$μ$s reaction time, circuit-level phase-flip noise with probability $p_Z = 5 \times 10^{-4}$ and no bit-flips, factoring RSA-2048, the configuration we compile in full, requires about 23 000 cat qubits and 3.14 days. Reusing the compiled operations, solving ECDLP on secp256k1 requires at most 30 000 cat qubits and 1 hour, and FFDLP-512, which we propose as an intermediate benchmark, about 6 700 cat qubits and 21 minutes. Trading space for time, RSA-2048 runs in 1.25 hours on about 611 000 cat qubits. The no-bit-flip requirement (a bit-flip time of about 100 years) can be relaxed to a bit-flip time of about one hour by adding a concatenation layer with a distance-3 bit-flip code, in which case RSA-2048 needs about 45 000 cat qubits.
one_liner: An end-to-end cat-qubit compilation estimates RSA-2048 factoring at 22,593 qubits and 3.14 days under strongly biased noise.
why_it_matters: It connects Shor circuits to physical layouts and schedules, giving concrete hardware targets and exposing the decisive role of cat-qubit bit-flip suppression.
detailed_summary: The work compiles arithmetic, parity-CNOT, multi-target CNOT, state injection, lookup, and factory operations onto repetition-cat and LDPC-cat architectures with explicit layouts and schedules. Assuming 1 μs correction cycles, 10 μs reaction time, pZ=5×10⁻⁴, and negligible bit flips, RSA-2048 requires 22,593 cat qubits and 3.14 days. It also estimates secp256k1 ECDLP at up to 30,000 qubits for one hour and shows how added bit-flip coding changes the RSA requirement.
main_result: The fully compiled RSA-2048 configuration uses 22,593 cat qubits for a projected 3.14-day runtime under the stated noise assumptions.
application_angle: The estimates translate cryptanalytic workloads into chip-scale engineering requirements for cat-qubit control, routing, factories, and error correction.

title: Ground-state energy estimation compiled on cat qubits: 7 164 qubits for FeMoco-54 in 23.5 hours
abstract: We provide a detailed resource estimate of the state-of-the-art sum-of-squares block encoding algorithm for electronic structure Hamiltonians of Low et al. on superconducting cat qubits. To achieve this, we present compilations with closed-form costs of the dominant subroutines such as skew-tree Qrom, a Swap network and a Phaseup for both a repetition-cat and an LDPC-cat architecture. Our compilation represents algorithmic qubits in the $X$ basis, taking advantage of the asymmetric cost of $X$ and $Z$ access that the concatenation of cat qubits with phase-flip classical code brings. Additionally, we provide a protocol for $\vert i \rangle$-state distillation and a two-level Toffoli-like $\vert \text{C}_X\text{C}_X X \rangle$ magic state distillation protocol, including three factory layouts. To minimize the cost of Clifford corrections induced by magic state injections we tailor injection gadgets to each subroutine. Combining our compilation work with the adder compilation from the companion work Pappalardo et al., we provide global layouts for the block encoding in both architectures which we use to obtain resource estimates for ground-state energy estimation for the benchmarks of FeMoco-54 and FeMoco-76. Assuming a cycle time of 1$μ$s, a reaction time of 10$\mathrmμ$s, a phase estimation precision of 1 mHa and circuit-level phase-flip noise with probability $p_Z = 5 \times 10^{-4}$ with negligible bit-flip error, FeMoco-54 requires fewer than $7\,500$ cat qubits with an expected runtime of under one day for a single phase estimation run using an LDPC-cat architecture. Relaxing the bit-flip requirement to $p_X = 10^{-11}$ with an additional layer of elevator codes raises this to an estimated $13\,000$ cat qubits.
one_liner: A cat-qubit compilation projects 1 mHa FeMoco-54 ground-state estimation with 7,164 qubits in 23.5 hours.
why_it_matters: It supplies a hardware-level path from modern electronic-structure algorithms to a chemically relevant fault-tolerant quantum-computing benchmark.
detailed_summary: The authors compile sum-of-squares block encoding onto repetition-cat and LDPC-cat architectures, exploiting asymmetric X- and Z-access costs through X-basis logical encoding. Closed-form constructions cover skew-tree QROM, swap networks, Phaseup, tailored injection gadgets, and magic-state factories. With 1 μs cycles, 10 μs reaction time, 1 mHa precision, pZ=5×10⁻⁴, and negligible bit flips, FeMoco-54 uses 7,164 cat qubits and 23.5 hours; additional bit-flip protection raises the estimate to about 13,000 qubits.
main_result: A single FeMoco-54 phase-estimation run is projected to finish in 23.5 hours using 7,164 cat qubits under the baseline assumptions.
application_angle: The compilation defines concrete processor, factory, and scheduling targets for fault-tolerant quantum simulation of challenging molecular systems.

title: An Eigenmode Expansion Framework for Bi-Directional Multimode Nonlinear Mixing Processes
abstract: An approach to simulating complex photonic systems is the eigenmode expansion method, in which scattering matrices are used to model and track the electric field in layered media. In this work, we formulate parametric nonlinear processes within the eigenmode expansion framework, enabling the simulation of nonlinear generation in varying photonic systems. This new simulation method includes both classical nonlinear processes and their quantum counterparts, including spontaneous parametric down-conversion and spontaneous four-wave mixing.
one_liner: An eigenmode-expansion framework models bidirectional multimode nonlinear mixing, including classical generation, SPDC, and SFWM.
why_it_matters: It brings quantum and classical nonlinear-source modeling into a scattering-matrix framework suited to complex layered and integrated photonic structures.
detailed_summary: The paper extends eigenmode expansion, traditionally used to propagate fields through layered structures via scattering matrices, to parametric nonlinear interactions. The formulation accommodates bidirectional and multimode mixing in spatially varying photonic systems. It treats both classical nonlinear generation and quantum processes such as spontaneous parametric down-conversion and spontaneous four-wave mixing.
main_result: The framework enables unified eigenmode-expansion simulation of bidirectional classical and spontaneous quantum nonlinear mixing.
application_angle: It can aid the design and optimization of integrated photon-pair sources, wavelength converters, and other nonlinear photonic circuits.

title: Quantum Foundations Beyond Bell's Theorem: A Topical Review
abstract: We review a series of recent no-go theorems that extend the methodological and conceptual framework introduced by Bell's theorem to more sophisticated operational scenarios involving independent sources, quantum networks, joint measurements, and multiple observers. Many of these results were originally developed within quantum information science and are scattered across the literature, where their technical and application-driven success has partly obscured their broader foundational significance. We organize them around a common Bell-inspired methodology that extends beyond quantum nonlocality, and emphasize how increasingly rich operational structures change which physical assumptions can be tested.
one_liner: A topical review unifies Bell-inspired no-go theorems for networks, independent sources, joint measurements, and multiple observers.
why_it_matters: It clarifies which physical assumptions can be experimentally tested as quantum communication networks gain more complex sources, measurements, and observer structures.
detailed_summary: The review organizes recent no-go theorems using a common methodology derived from Bell's theorem. It covers operational scenarios with independent sources, quantum networks, joint measurements, and multiple observers. The central theme is how richer network structures alter the physical assumptions accessible to experimental tests.
main_result: The article provides a unified framework for understanding Bell-inspired tests beyond conventional bipartite nonlocality.
application_angle: The framework can guide the design and interpretation of foundational tests in increasingly complex quantum networks and communication systems.

title: The Geometry of Quantum Teleportation in Phase Space
abstract: We formulate the standard quantum teleportation protocol within the framework of deformation quantization, employing the Stratonovich--Weyl (SW) correspondence and the associated star product on the coadjoint orbits of $SU(2)$. Each qubit is represented by a spherical phase space $S^2$ endowed with the Kirillov--Kostant--Souriau (KKS) symplectic structure. Within this setting, we explicitly construct the phase space representations of the entangled Bell resource, the controlled-NOT and Hadamard operators, the projective measurements, and the conditional Pauli corrections. We demonstrate how the quantum information initially encoded in the Wigner function for the input qubit is redistributed through bipartite and tripartite phase space correlations. Upon consideration of a conditional unitary transformation, the measurement outcome produces a Wigner function on the receiver's coadjoint orbit that is related to the input by an outcome-dependent rotation, which can subsequently be inverted through the implementation of an appropriate Pauli correction. The covariance of the SW correspondence provides a geometric interpretation of this process, in which quantum information is redistributed and reconstructed without transferring the underlying symplectic geometry. Our formulation can also be extended to study quantum teleportation in more general phase space geometries equipped with suitable star products.
one_liner: Qubit teleportation is reconstructed geometrically through Wigner functions, star products, and rotations on SU(2) spherical phase spaces.
why_it_matters: The formulation exposes how teleportation redistributes and reconstructs quantum information, offering tools for analyzing protocols on more general phase-space geometries.
detailed_summary: The authors formulate standard qubit teleportation using deformation quantization and the Stratonovich–Weyl correspondence on SU(2) coadjoint orbits. They explicitly represent the Bell resource, gates, projective measurements, and conditional Pauli corrections in spherical phase space. Teleportation appears as redistribution into multipartite correlations followed by an outcome-dependent rotation of the receiver's Wigner function.
main_result: The work shows that the receiver's conditional Wigner function is a rotated version of the input and is restored by the corresponding Pauli correction.
application_angle: This geometric toolkit may support analysis and extension of teleportation protocols to systems with nonstandard phase spaces and star products.

title: Continuous variable quantum key distribution through a fading channel with minimal information leakage
abstract: Continuous variable quantum key distribution enables two parties to extract provably secure keys for cryptography by exploiting aspects of quantum mechanics. A central challenge in achieving QKD over long distances is overcoming optical loss, which limits the secret key rates and achievable transmission distances. Recent work has illustrated how to perform continuous variable quantum key distribution while eliminating information leakage to an eavesdropper in a pure-loss channel and minimizing information leakage in a noisy channel. In this work, we analyse this protocol under conditions where the quantum channel linking the sender and receiver is a fading channel, which can be used to model free-space links. We find that the protocol maintains strong performance over fading channels and outperforms comparable protocols.
one_liner: A low-leakage continuous-variable QKD protocol retains strong performance over fading channels that model free-space optical links.
why_it_matters: Accounting for time-varying transmission is essential for translating low-leakage CV-QKD concepts into atmospheric, airborne, and satellite communication links.
detailed_summary: The paper analyzes a continuous-variable QKD protocol designed to eliminate leakage in pure-loss channels and minimize it under noise. The analysis extends the protocol to fading transmission, a key feature of free-space optical channels. The reported results indicate robust performance and an advantage over comparable protocols under the modeled fading conditions.
main_result: The low-leakage CV-QKD protocol maintains strong performance over fading channels and outperforms the compared alternatives.
application_angle: The result supports secure key distribution over realistic atmospheric links where turbulence and pointing variations cause fluctuating optical loss.

title: Perspective on AI and quantum open-source software
