abstract: Quantum open-source software provides essential infrastructure for quantum science, and artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping its capabilities and transforming its development. However, verifying quantum software at scale remains difficult, and AI-generated contributions can increase the workload of maintainers. In this Perspective, we examine verification as a central requirement for reliable AI-assisted quantum software development and research. We analyze public repositories, records covering 110 repositories from five annual quantum open-source hackathons that we organize, and responses from more than 1600 participants in a community survey. Our analysis connects limitations in automated verification with the review burden on quantum software maintainers. We propose verification practices and contribution standards that require contributors to support their changes with reproducible evidence for maintainer review. We also examine how quantum open-source software can provide infrastructure for AI-driven research whose results the community can independently verify and build upon. We maintain an open-source companion repository to support reproducibility and help projects adopt and refine these proposals. Together, these contributions help the quantum open-source software community translate advances in AI into reliable quantum research through reproducible verification.
one_liner: A data-backed perspective proposes reproducible verification standards for AI-assisted development of open-source quantum software.
why_it_matters: Reliable verification is critical when AI-generated code affects software used to control experiments, analyze measurements, and reproduce quantum research.
detailed_summary: The authors examine verification challenges in AI-assisted quantum software using records from 110 repositories across five hackathons and survey responses from more than 1,600 participants. They connect limited automated verification with increased maintainer review burden. The paper proposes evidence-based contribution standards and supplies an open-source companion repository to support adoption and reproducibility.
main_result: The study develops reproducible verification practices for AI-generated quantum-software contributions, grounded in repository and community data.
application_angle: The proposed standards can improve trust in software pipelines used for quantum experiments, sensing workflows, data analysis, and hardware control.

title: Coherent control and high purity single-photon emission from telecom quantum dots on metamorphic InGaAs
abstract: Semiconductor quantum dots emitting in the telecommunication O- and C-bands are promising candidates as single-photon sources for fiber-based quantum communication. In this work, we show how coherent quasi-resonant and phonon-assisted excitation help reveal the intrinsic optical properties of InAs quantum dots embedded in relaxed InGaAs matrices on top of metamorphic InGaAs layers for achieving emission in the telecom bands. By systematically comparing excitation schemes, we separate excitation-induced effects from intrinsic emitter properties. This allows us to observe linewidths as narrow as 21 $μ$eV, the disappearance of slow decay channels, and single-photon purity reaching second-order autocorrelation values in the order of $10^{-2}$. Photoluminescence excitation reveals higher excited states, enabling coherent control of trion transitions and the observation of Rabi-like oscillations in both telecom bands. These results confirm the promising potential of these quantum dots for applications in quantum technologies.
one_liner: Telecom-band InAs quantum dots deliver coherent trion control, 21 μeV linewidths, and single-photon purity with g²(0) on the order of 10⁻².
why_it_matters: The combination of fiber-compatible emission, high purity, narrow lines, and coherent control addresses core requirements for practical quantum-network photon sources.
detailed_summary: InAs quantum dots embedded in relaxed InGaAs matrices on metamorphic InGaAs layers are studied under coherent quasi-resonant and phonon-assisted excitation. Comparing excitation schemes separates excitation-induced artifacts from intrinsic emitter behavior, revealing linewidths down to 21 μeV, suppression of slow decay channels, and g²(0) values on the order of 10⁻². Photoluminescence excitation identifies higher states and enables coherent trion control with Rabi-like oscillations in both telecom O- and C-bands.
main_result: The devices combine high-purity telecom single-photon emission with coherent trion control in both O- and C-band emitters.
application_angle: These quantum dots are promising chip-compatible photon sources for fiber-based quantum communication and distributed photonic quantum technologies.

title: A Coherent Neutron-Nucleus Hybrid System Mediated by the Strong Interaction
abstract: A coherent ensemble of polarized helium-3 nuclei and free neutrons are coupled, forming a neutron-nucleus hybrid system. The nuclei are prepared in a spin superposition, while a magnetic field induces Zeeman splitting. The resulting nuclear energy phase is coherently transferred to the neutron, producing an intensity beat at the nuclear Zeeman frequency. Finally, the incident neutron is prepared in a spin-energy superposition state. The nuclear and neutron phases then heterodyne coherently, producing a signal at the sum or difference frequency depending on their relative helicity.
one_liner: Polarized helium-3 nuclei coherently transfer their Zeeman phase to free neutrons, enabling strong-interaction-mediated beats and heterodyne signals.
why_it_matters: The experiment introduces a coherent neutron–nuclear interface and a phase-sensitive method for probing spin dynamics through the strong interaction.
detailed_summary: A polarized helium-3 nuclear ensemble is prepared in a spin superposition whose phase evolves under Zeeman splitting. Strong-interaction coupling transfers this nuclear phase to free neutrons, producing an intensity beat at the nuclear Zeeman frequency. Preparing the neutron in a spin-energy superposition further enables coherent heterodyne signals at the sum or difference frequency, selected by relative helicity.
main_result: The work demonstrates coherent phase transfer and helicity-dependent heterodyne mixing between a nuclear ensemble and free neutrons.
application_angle: The hybrid interaction could enable phase-sensitive neutron probes of nuclear spin dynamics and new sensing or spectroscopy modalities.

title: Experimental Observation of Error-Resilience Phase Transition on Superconducting Quantum Processor
abstract: Random unitaries scramble quantum information into highly nonlocal degrees of freedom, thereby providing protection from local noise. However, as demonstrated by Turkeshi and Sierant (Phys. Rev. Lett. 132, 140401, 2024 and arXiv:2603.00235), this protection may fail once local noise grows sufficiently strong. These works describe a phase transition in a noisy random encoding-decoding circuit model between an error-protecting phase, in which encoded information is recoverable, and an error-vulnerable phase, in which encoded information is lost, with the transition occurring at a critical coherent noise angle $α_c \approx 1.14$. Here, we present the first experimental observation of this transition, conducted on IBM's ibm_pittsburgh Heron r3 device for system sizes of up to $N = 26$ qubits. We detect this transition via three order parameters: fidelity, Rényi-2 entanglement entropy, and stabilizer Rényi-2 entropy. For the latter two, we employ randomized measurement protocols to construct estimators, and for all three, we rely on zero-noise extrapolation and M3 SPAM error mitigation. We then jointly model the finite-size scaling collapse across all three order parameters with a Gaussian process regression, yielding a critical angle $α_c \approx 1.01$, well below the theoretical value. Inputting noiseless simulated data into the same model yields $α_c \approx 1.05$, implying that the discrepancy between experiment and theory is due to our encoding circuits, which are not deep enough to be truly Haar-random. Finally, we observe that the same model cannot adequately identify critical behavior in unmitigated, raw experimental data. This indicates that error mitigation techniques are crucial for detecting the transition on hardware.
one_liner: A 26-qubit superconducting processor reveals a noise-driven transition between recoverable and lost encoded quantum information.
why_it_matters: The experiment shows that phase-transition diagnostics can quantify error resilience on real processors, but only with substantial error mitigation.
detailed_summary: Experiments on IBM’s 26-qubit ibm_pittsburgh Heron r3 processor probe a noisy random encoding-decoding circuit through fidelity, Rényi-2 entanglement entropy, and stabilizer Rényi-2 entropy. Randomized measurements, zero-noise extrapolation, and M3 SPAM mitigation enable a joint Gaussian-process finite-size-scaling analysis that estimates a critical coherent-noise angle of about 1.01. Noiseless simulations of the implemented circuits give about 1.05, indicating that their limited depth, rather than hardware noise alone, explains the offset from the theoretical Haar-random value near 1.14.
main_result: The study experimentally observes an error-resilience phase transition up to 26 qubits and finds that raw, unmitigated data cannot reliably expose the critical behavior.
application_angle: The protocol offers a hardware-level benchmark for testing whether scrambling circuits protect quantum information under realistic coherent noise.

title: Converting a superseded Raith electron beam pattern generator into an unattended Critical Dimension SEM
abstract: Design-based metrology of academic electron beam lithography (EBL) is bottlenecked by low-throughput imaging. For integrated photonics, where nanometre-scale structural variation can significantly limit device performance, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) is the standard tool for critical dimension (CD) metrology, revealing the structure of devices that is not available from optical measurements. Manual SEM imaging on a wafer-scale is time-intensive, can feature operator-dependent distortions, and yields too few data to reliably close the nanofabrication calibration loop. The following details a methodology that utilises existing hardware in an academic cleanroom: a GDSII-to-SEM software workflow that converts a facility's superseded pattern generator into a CD-SEM for unattended image acquisition and efficient CD and line edge roughness (LER) extraction. This is shown for a Raith eLine Plus, and is expected to be applicable to other pattern generators running Raith's NanoSuite. Presented are results demonstrating its three use cases within a facility: accelerated calibration of two photoresists' process windows; chip-scale metrology of integrated photonic devices to track CD variation; and mass dataset acquisition for convolutional neural network training to predict process distortion. This methodology enables foundry-style, metrology-driven process calibration in academic cleanrooms, generalisable beyond photonics to any EBL nanofabrication that requires nanometre-scale CD control.
one_liner: A retired Raith electron-beam writer is repurposed for unattended, design-linked SEM metrology of nanofabricated photonic devices.
why_it_matters: The workflow brings higher-throughput, foundry-style dimensional feedback to academic cleanrooms using existing equipment.
detailed_summary: The authors develop a GDSII-to-SEM workflow that converts a superseded Raith eLine Plus pattern generator into an unattended critical-dimension SEM. Automated acquisition supports critical-dimension and line-edge-roughness extraction while reducing operator-dependent imaging variation. Demonstrations cover photoresist process-window calibration, chip-scale photonic-device metrology, and large image datasets for convolutional-network prediction of process distortion.
main_result: The repurposed tool performs unattended wafer- and chip-scale imaging for automated critical-dimension and roughness analysis across multiple fabrication use cases.
application_angle: Academic nanofabrication facilities can close process-calibration loops faster without purchasing a dedicated industrial CD-SEM.

title: Active Approach to Fast Quantum State Preparation and Reset in Atomic Arrays
abstract: Rapid preparation of a target quantum state and reset to the many-body ground state are essential for quantum information processing. Here, we investigate both processes in a waveguide-coupled emitter array in the low-excitation regime. By decomposing the effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian into biorthogonal eigenmodes, we show that relaxation depends on the initial overlap with the more subradiant modes, providing a modal explanation of the Mpemba effect. Guided by this insight, we design a reset protocol in which a finite-duration local drive activelysuppresses the relatively slow-decaying components. For the parameters studied, this reduces the time to reach a fixed residual-excitation threshold by up to approximately 25% compared with free decay. To prepare a target Dicke state, we introduce a two-step protocol that initially leaves one emitter undriven before restoring the full drive that stabilizes the target. This local control redistributes spectral weight into the more subradiant modes, driving them closer to their target amplitudes, which reduces the preparation time by up to approximately 45% while consuming less driving energy than continuous driving. Finally, we show how directional waveguide coupling shifts collective modes toward a preferred boundary through the non-Hermitian skin effect, providing guidance for selecting the preferred site for local operations. We term this fundamental dependence of the relaxation dynamics on the system's chirality the ``non-Hermitian Skin-Mpemba effect.'' These results demonstrate how selective local control can accelerate state preparation and reset in open quantum systems.
one_liner: Selective local driving accelerates Dicke-state preparation and many-body reset in waveguide-coupled atomic arrays.
why_it_matters: The protocols reduce quantum-operation latency and drive energy by deliberately redistributing population among collective radiative modes.
detailed_summary: A biorthogonal-mode analysis connects slow relaxation in a waveguide-coupled emitter array to initial overlap with subradiant collective modes. A finite-duration local drive suppresses slow components and shortens reset time by up to about 25% at a fixed residual-excitation threshold. A two-step drive protocol prepares a target Dicke state up to about 45% faster than continuous driving while using less energy, and directional coupling identifies favorable control sites through the non-Hermitian skin effect.
main_result: Local control yields up to roughly 25% faster reset and 45% faster Dicke-state preparation while reducing drive-energy consumption.
application_angle: The approach could increase repetition rates and reduce control overhead in waveguide-QED quantum processors and collective-emitter memories.

title: Maximally-Matched Mixture Decoding for Correlated Atom Loss in Quantum LDPC Codes
abstract: Heralded atom loss is a dominant noise channel in neutral atom quantum computing platforms, and losses at a two-qubit gate are strongly correlated: when one atom is lost, its gate partner is often lost too. This work shows how to exploit this correlation to construct a better decoder, focusing on [[144,12,12]] Gross code syndrome extraction circuits. Given a loss readout, the possible pairings of the lost qubits according to shared gates form a graph whose maximum matchings carry almost all of the conditional probability mass. Our maximal-matching-mixture (MMM) decoder builds a per-readout decoding hypergraph as a weighted mixture over exactly these loss scenarios. This decoding hypergraph can be used by an ordinary belief-propagation decoder. On the [[144,12,12]] Gross code, MMM lowers the logical error rate by as much as ~25x relative to a loss-unaware decoder and ~2x relative to a loss-aware uniform-mixture baseline from Baranes et al. (2026).
one_liner: A correlation-aware decoder exploits paired atom-loss patterns to improve logical performance of a neutral-atom quantum LDPC code.
why_it_matters: Using physical loss correlations delivers large logical-error reductions without requiring a specialized replacement for standard belief propagation.
detailed_summary: The work targets correlated, heralded atom loss during two-qubit gates in [[144,12,12]] Gross-code syndrome-extraction circuits. For each loss readout, maximum matchings of a shared-gate graph capture nearly all conditional probability mass. The maximal-matching-mixture decoder converts these likely scenarios into a weighted decoding hypergraph that can be processed by an ordinary belief-propagation decoder.
main_result: The decoder lowers logical error rates by up to about 25× versus loss-unaware decoding and about 2× versus a uniform loss-aware mixture.
application_angle: Correlation-aware decoding can improve neutral-atom fault-tolerance using heralded loss information already available from the hardware.

title: Einstein Metrics and Quantum Control on Symmetric Tensor Product Quotients
abstract: Let $M_n=(\mathrm{PU}(2)^n\rtimes S_n)\backslash\mathrm{PU}(2^n)$ be the space of projective $n$-qubit unitaries modulo local unitaries and permutations of the qubits. We prove that for all sufficiently large $n$ the manifold $M_n$ carries exactly two $\mathrm{PU}(2^n)$-invariant Einstein metrics up to scaling. Both Einstein metrics have uniformly bounded diameter after normalizing two-qubit costs, although approximating a Haar-random unitary requires exponentially many two-qubit gates. In contrast, we construct non-Einstein metrics with nonnegative Ricci curvature and exponentially growing typical control distances, and determine the sharp curvature threshold for this family.
one_liner: The geometry of nonlocal n-qubit control admits two invariant Einstein metrics but does not make geometric distance track gate complexity.
why_it_matters: The result clarifies which geometric cost models can—or cannot—faithfully represent the exponential difficulty of synthesizing generic quantum unitaries.
detailed_summary: The paper studies projective n-qubit unitaries modulo local operations and qubit permutations as a symmetric quotient manifold. For sufficiently large n, it proves that exactly two invariant Einstein metrics exist up to scale, yet both retain bounded diameter after normalizing two-qubit costs despite exponential Haar-random circuit complexity. A separate non-Einstein family with nonnegative Ricci curvature exhibits exponentially growing typical control distances, with its sharp curvature threshold characterized.
main_result: Invariant Einstein geometry is shown to miss exponential generic-unitary complexity, whereas constructed non-Einstein metrics recover exponentially growing typical distances.
application_angle: The findings guide the design of geometric cost functions for realistic quantum-control optimization and circuit-complexity analysis.

title: Drift-induced nonreciprocity in image-polariton-mediated dipole emission
abstract: Electrical current bias offers a magnet-free route to nonreciprocal light propagation at the nanoscale. Here, we theoretically explore drift-induced nonreciprocity in graphene heterostructures containing hexagonal boron nitride (hBN), where graphene plasmons interact with hBN phonon polaritons in the infrared. Both the random-phase approximation and the Boltzmann transport equation are used to characterize the nonlocal optical response of drift-biased graphene. We compare graphene on hBN with an image-polaritonic structure comprising graphene, a thin hBN spacer, and a gold substrate. Carrier drift produces pronounced directional shifts of the polariton dispersion, while coupling to hBN phonon polaritons strongly modifies the nonreciprocal response. In the image-polaritonic structure, the graphene polaritons become up to twice as confined while retaining a comparable Fizeau shift. The nonreciprocal polariton dispersion produces directional near-field emission and nonreciprocal dipole-dipole interactions, the latter quantified through the cross density of optical states, reaching a left-right dissymmetry of up to ~40%. Our results identify image polaritons in drift-biased graphene as a compact, electrically tunable platform for directional coupling between quantum emitters at the nanoscale.
one_liner: Current-biased graphene–hBN image polaritons enable strongly confined, electrically tunable directional coupling between nanoscale emitters.
why_it_matters: The proposed magnet-free platform combines deep confinement with substantial nonreciprocity for compact directional quantum-optical interfaces.
detailed_summary: Random-phase and Boltzmann-transport models quantify the nonlocal response of drift-biased graphene coupled to hBN phonon polaritons. Adding a thin hBN spacer and gold substrate produces image polaritons with up to twice the confinement while preserving a comparable drift-induced Fizeau shift. The resulting directional dispersion generates asymmetric near-field emission and dipole-dipole coupling with left-right cross-density-of-states dissymmetry reaching about 40%.
main_result: The image-polaritonic geometry doubles confinement while retaining drift nonreciprocity and producing up to approximately 40% directional interaction dissymmetry.
application_angle: Electrical tuning without magnetic bias could support compact directional emitter coupling, on-chip routing, and nonreciprocal infrared quantum photonics.

title: Coherent errors, syndrome extraction and the Robustness of Magic in stabiliser codes
abstract: Coherent errors leave stabiliser-code-encoded magic states in superpositions of syndrome sectors. We ask how much magic these coherent errors add, and whether syndrome extraction depletes logical magic. Using Robustness of Magic, we show that, for a unitary error U on a correctable region which supports no stabiliser, the encoded state has the same robustness as the logical state plus one copy of the Choi state of U , in every stabiliser code encoding. Syndrome extraction removes this copy, returning the logical robustness. The removed magic is positive for every non-Clifford error: adding a non-stabiliser state to any state multiplies one plus the robustness by a (tightly- bounded) factor above one. The magic capacity of two-qubit gates Clifford-equivalent to diagonal or single-qubit gates is equal to their Choi-state robustness. We give a linear-algebraic test for when a Clifford error makes syndrome extraction measure a logical operator, and give magic lifetimes of stored single-qubit magic states under Pauli noise. Choosing the plane of the stored state extends these lifetimes about 1.5x on rotated surface codes under low code-capacity depolarising noise. We identify states and channels in odd-prime dimension for which Wigner negativity and robustness show equal lifetimes.
one_liner: Syndrome extraction removes error-induced magic while preserving the logical magic of encoded states under specified correctability conditions.
why_it_matters: The results clarify how coherent errors and error correction redistribute costly non-Clifford resources in fault-tolerant quantum memories.
detailed_summary: The authors quantify coherent-error resources using Robustness of Magic. For a unitary error on a correctable region supporting no stabilizer, the encoded state's robustness equals that of the logical state plus one copy of the error's Choi state; syndrome extraction removes this added contribution. They also derive tests for harmful Clifford errors and find that optimizing the stored-state plane extends low-noise rotated-surface-code lifetimes by about 1.5×.
main_result: Syndrome extraction restores logical robustness after correctable coherent errors, and state-plane selection can extend simulated magic-state lifetimes by about 1.5×.
application_angle: The framework can guide code, state, and recovery choices for preserving non-Clifford resources in fault-tolerant processors.

title: Pulse-Informed Physical Placement for Parallel Two-Qubit Gates in Qubit Arrays
abstract: A parallel two-qubit layer can often be realized with several nonoverlapping sets of physical couplers, but isolated calibrations do not reveal how each realization performs after optimizing its own simultaneous control pulse. We formulate physical placement and pulse synthesis as a coupled decision problem for parallel controlled-$Z$ gates in heterogeneous frequency tunable transmon arrays. The proposed processor-aware structural quantum multi-domain matrix (QMDM) links static processor, edge, incidence, and task information to a dynamic candidate response block. For each candidate placement $P$, QMDM instantiates the active Hamiltonian $H_P$; quantum optimal control (QOCT) generates a placement-specific pulse, direct coupled propagation returns the projected computational subspace overlap $F_{\rm proj}$ and computational survival; and these pulse-conditioned responses are fed back to QMDM to rank and progressively promote physical placements. This placement pulse response feedback defines pulse-informed physical placement. Here, to see the performance of the proposed method on 30 held-out synthetic $3\times3$ processors, the median final $F_{\rm proj}$ is $0.993826$ for pulse-informed placement and $0.984981$ for calibration-based placement. Also, when tested under different system conditions, the proposed pulse-informed approach uses $59.1\%$ fewer candidate QOCT optimizer iterations than the exhaustive finite-budget reference. The QMDM representation and outer search are formulated for arbitrary $L$ simultaneous two-qubit gates. Here, the present global candidate ranking validation is used for $L=2$.
one_liner: Pulse-aware placement improves parallel controlled-Z gates by ranking coupler assignments using placement-specific optimal-control simulations.
why_it_matters: Jointly selecting physical couplers and control pulses addresses crosstalk and heterogeneity that isolated gate calibrations can miss.
detailed_summary: The method couples physical placement with quantum optimal-control synthesis for simultaneous controlled-Z gates in heterogeneous tunable-transmon arrays. A processor-aware QMDM builds each candidate Hamiltonian, incorporates projected computational overlap and survival from direct propagation, and progressively promotes promising placements. On 30 held-out synthetic 3×3 processors with two simultaneous gates, median final projected fidelity rose from 0.984981 to 0.993826 while using 59.1% fewer optimizer iterations than a finite-budget exhaustive reference.
main_result: For synthetic 3×3 processors, pulse-informed placement achieved 0.993826 median projected fidelity and cut optimizer iterations by 59.1%.
application_angle: The workflow could improve parallel-gate scheduling and calibration efficiency in heterogeneous superconducting processors.

title: Quantum Gate Engineering in Superconducting NISQ Platforms: Experimental Methods and Emerging Directions
abstract: This review aims to provide researchers, experimentalists, and quantum engineers with an updated and technically grounded perspective on the implementation of quantum gates in superconducting NISQ devices. The goal is to establish a comprehensive bridge between theoretical quantum circuit synthesis and its practical, experimental implementation, focusing on superconducting quantum technologies. We systematically examine the diverse landscape of superconducting qubits and processor architectures, ranging from conventional transmons to alternative and unconventional designs, evaluating their unique design trade-offs, connectivity constraints, device physics, and materials impact. Moving from theory to actual implementation, we detail how single- and two-qubit operations are synthesized via microwave-driven and flux-activated pulses. We here present our pulse engineering, wave shaping, calibration workflows, demonstrating how to bridge the gap between abstract gate models and real-world hardware limitations in the direction of a hardware-software co-design framework. To validate these operations, we choose benchmarking methodologies with the purpose to get the more efficient metric for the specific evaluation aspect, including truth tables and quantum process tomography. Therefore, we both discuss the theoretical concepts behind the gate synthesis and show experimental implementation of most fundamental gates by proposing a practical workflow.
one_liner: This review connects superconducting-gate theory with pulse engineering, calibration, and experimental validation across NISQ architectures.
why_it_matters: It gives experimentalists a practical bridge from abstract circuit gates to device-specific microwave and flux controls and benchmarking.
detailed_summary: The review surveys conventional transmons and alternative superconducting-qubit architectures, emphasizing device physics, materials, connectivity, and design trade-offs. It explains how microwave-driven and flux-activated pulses realize single- and two-qubit gates, then outlines waveform design and calibration workflows. Truth tables and quantum process tomography are discussed as validation tools for matching metrics to specific experimental questions.
main_result: The article consolidates a practical workflow for synthesizing, calibrating, and validating fundamental gates on superconducting hardware.
application_angle: Its hardware-software co-design perspective can support laboratory gate development and processor-specific control-stack engineering.

title: Hyperentanglement-enabled Quantum Privacy Amplification for Classical-Quantum Coexistence in Fiber Networks
abstract: Integrating quantum communication into existing fiber infrastructures requires coexisting with high-power classical traffic, which generates noise in the quantum channel. Spontaneous Raman Scattering (SpRS) is the dominant noise source, generating a broadband photon background that degrades quantum states and, in Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), can entirely suppress secure key generation. In this work, we implement single-copy entanglement distillation utilizing energy-time and frequency hyperentanglement, and we exploit it to perform Quantum Privacy Amplification (QPA) directly at a physical layer. Strict frequency anti-correlations of spontaneous parametric down-conversion are used to selectively discard uncorrelated Raman photons while preserving genuine entangled pairs, suppressing accidental coincidences by a factor $1/N$, where $N$ is the number of frequency channel pairs. Using passive borosilicate-glass photonic integrated circuits and standard DWDM demultiplexers over a 20~km single-mode fiber testbed, we demonstrate a 4~dB improvement in tolerance to classical laser launch power $P_C$ when QPA is performed, extending the secure key threshold from $P_C=-13.3$ dBm to $P_C=-9.3$ dBm. The result shows that off-the-shelf telecom components can be repurposed as physical-layer quantum privacy amplifiers.
one_liner: Frequency–time hyperentanglement filters Raman noise and raises the classical-power tolerance of entanglement-based QKD over 20 km fiber.
why_it_matters: The experiment shows a passive, telecom-compatible route to stronger quantum–classical coexistence in deployed fiber networks.
detailed_summary: The experiment uses energy-time and frequency hyperentanglement to distill entanglement from a single copy and perform physical-layer quantum privacy amplification. Strict SPDC frequency anticorrelations reject uncorrelated spontaneous-Raman photons, reducing accidental coincidences by 1/N for N frequency-channel pairs. Passive borosilicate photonic circuits and standard DWDM demultiplexers improved classical launch-power tolerance by 4 dB over a 20 km single-mode-fiber testbed.
main_result: Quantum privacy amplification shifted the secure-key cutoff from −13.3 dBm to −9.3 dBm of classical launch power over 20 km.
application_angle: Off-the-shelf telecom filtering and passive integrated optics could enable QKD alongside stronger classical traffic on shared fiber.

title: Probing micron-range fifth forces with cold atoms in optical tweezer arrays
abstract: We propose a new method to search for fifth forces at micron scales, by resonantly exciting the motional state of ground-state-cooled atoms in optical tweezer arrays. We develop a homodyne readout protocol based on sideband thermometry, which can approach the Standard Quantum Limit, and expand the discovery reach for fifth forces by up to four orders of magnitude compared to existing constraints. We show that this level of sensitivity can also probe well-motivated models of extra dimensions beyond the current tabletop state of the art, by leveraging the parametric enhancement of higher-dimensional gravity.
one_liner: Ground-state-cooled atoms in tweezer arrays are proposed as resonant probes of micron-range fifth forces with near-SQL homodyne readout.
why_it_matters: The scheme could expand fifth-force discovery reach by up to four orders of magnitude and test higher-dimensional gravity on a tabletop.
detailed_summary: The proposal resonantly drives the motional state of ground-state-cooled atoms in optical tweezer arrays using a hypothetical micron-range interaction. A homodyne protocol based on sideband thermometry is designed to approach the Standard Quantum Limit. Sensitivity projections indicate up to four orders of magnitude improvement over existing fifth-force constraints and access to extra-dimensional gravity models through parametric enhancement.
main_result: Projected sensitivity improves micron-range fifth-force discovery reach by as much as four orders of magnitude relative to existing bounds.
application_angle: The platform offers a quantum-limited tabletop test of short-range forces and extra-dimensional gravity.

title: Homodyne versus heterodyne detection for classifying families of optical quantum states from finite records of detection events
abstract: Neural networks can identify an optical quantum state from an image of its phase-space function, but a real measurement gives a finite record of $N$ detection events. Heterodyne detection samples the Husimi $Q$ function directly, whereas homodyne detection gives the Wigner function only after a reconstruction from several phases. We ask which scheme better identifies one of seven families of states, including Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states, under loss, dephasing and Gaussian noise. We simulate finite records on identical states for two sets of families, one with equal mean photon number and one built from the code of Ahmed et al. For convolutional networks, heterodyne detection outperforms homodyne detection with filtered back-projection by 14.1 percentage points at $N=100$ events and 20% dephasing in the first set (adjusted $p=0.003$ over $24$ cells across training runs), and it depends on the number of phases and on the reconstruction. At $N=10^3$ and $10^4$ no difference is significant, but the intervals are wide. At $N=100$, a homodyne network without reconstruction does not differ significantly from heterodyne detection in the first set and is nominally worse in the second. Near thermal states we show to leading order that heterodyne detection damps phase-space structure of order $n$ exponentially, whereas homodyne detection shares unit weight among $n+1$ angular components, a local result that does not explain the finite-record differences. Experimental records of a GKP state, photon-subtracted squeezed states and one mode of an Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen source are classified like simulated ones, but these low-power tests probe our counting-noise model, not the seven-class accuracy. A likelihood-ratio observer shows no such gap at $N=100$, so our evidence concerns a reconstruction-based pipeline, not homodyne detection in general.
one_liner: Heterodyne records outperform reconstruction-based homodyne data for neural classification of noisy optical states in a sparse-data regime.
why_it_matters: The study identifies when detector and reconstruction choices materially affect data-driven optical-state recognition with limited measurements.
detailed_summary: Convolutional networks classify seven optical-state families from finite homodyne or heterodyne records under loss, dephasing, and Gaussian noise. At 100 events and 20% dephasing, heterodyne exceeded filtered-back-projection homodyne accuracy by 14.1 percentage points in one controlled family set; no significant gap appeared at 1,000 or 10,000 events. Direct homodyne processing and a likelihood-ratio observer largely removed the gap, showing that the reported advantage belongs to the reconstruction-based pipeline rather than homodyne detection generally.
main_result: With 100 events and 20% dephasing, heterodyne classification beat reconstructed homodyne classification by 14.1 percentage points in one benchmark.
application_angle: The findings inform receiver and inference-pipeline design for low-data optical-state monitoring, including GKP-state experiments.

title: Goldbach Representations in Quantum Optics and Metrology
abstract: We derive a relation between Goldbach representations and photon-number statistics in a quantum-optical setup. Considering an even-number Fock state injected into a stochastic beam splitter with uniformly distributed transmissivity and projections of the two output modes onto prime subspaces, we demonstrate that each successful outcome corresponds to an Goldbach representation and that the averaged detection probability is exactly proportional to the number of Goldbach representations. Then, employing the Hardy--Littlewood asymptotic formula, we demonstrate that the post-measurement state generated by a beam splitter with fixed transmissivity exhibits standard quantum limit scaling of the ultimate precision limit in terms of phase estimation, whereas an equally weighted superposition of Goldbach representations exhibits Heisenberg scaling. These results provide a quantum-optical realization of Goldbach representations and relate their statistics of with quantum metrology.
one_liner: Prime-subspace photon detection maps Goldbach representations onto measurable statistics and links them to phase-estimation scaling.
why_it_matters: It connects a number-theory counting problem to a concrete quantum-optical protocol while identifying states that can attain Heisenberg-limited metrology.
detailed_summary: An even-photon-number Fock state is sent through a beam splitter with uniformly randomized transmissivity, followed by prime-subspace projections on both outputs. Successful detections encode Goldbach decompositions, and their averaged probability is exactly proportional to the number of such representations. For phase estimation, the fixed-transmissivity post-measurement state has standard-quantum-limit scaling, whereas an equal superposition of Goldbach representations reaches Heisenberg scaling.
main_result: The protocol converts Goldbach representation counts into detection probabilities and predicts Heisenberg phase sensitivity for their equal superposition.
application_angle: The construction offers a structured route to preparing and evaluating number-theoretic photonic states for quantum-enhanced phase sensing.

title: Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization for Variable Molecular Geometries
abstract: Quantum and hybrid quantum-classical algorithms have the potential to improve the accuracy and scale of quantum chemistry and impact a broad range of applications such as drug discovery and catalysis. In particular, subspace methods such as sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) can already tackle classically challenging systems. However, practical algorithms that go beyond the computation of electronic ground and excited states are still scarce. Here, we introduce the variable-geometry sample-based quantum diagonalization (VGSQD) algorithm, which extends SQD to variable molecular geometries by reusing quantum samples from a reference geometry at displaced ones, thus significantly reducing quantum computational cost. Using circuits of up to 124 qubits on ibm-quebec, an IBM Heron r2 quantum processor, we determine the equilibrium geometry and energy of the weakly bound, strongly correlated beryllium dimer, as well as the water molecule. Finally, we extend VGSQD to chemical reactions and compute the minimum energy path and energy barrier of a hydrogen exchange reaction. The results are comparable with state-of-the-art classical methods such as CCSD(T) and DMRG. This work broadens the scope of quantum algorithms for chemistry, from energies to geometry optimization and reaction pathways, both essential for practical applications.
one_liner: VGSQD reuses quantum samples across molecular geometries to calculate equilibrium structures and reaction pathways with circuits up to 124 qubits.
why_it_matters: It extends hardware-scale quantum chemistry beyond fixed-geometry energies while reducing repeated quantum sampling during structural and reaction calculations.
detailed_summary: Variable-geometry sample-based quantum diagonalization reuses samples obtained at a reference geometry when solving displaced molecular configurations. Circuits using up to 124 qubits on the IBM Heron r2 processor ibm-quebec were applied to Be2 and H2O equilibrium calculations. The method also recovered a hydrogen-exchange minimum-energy path and barrier, with results comparable to CCSD(T) and DMRG.
main_result: VGSQD demonstrated quantum-hardware calculations of molecular equilibrium geometry and a reaction energy barrier while amortizing sample acquisition across geometries.
application_angle: Reusing samples could lower quantum-resource costs for geometry optimization, catalysis studies, and reaction-path screening.

title: Light and charge yields from nuclear recoils in noble liquids: From sub-keV energies to 1 MeV
abstract: We present a first-principles study of total quanta and charge recombination in noble liquids, based on a solution of Lindhard's integro-differential equation for atomic motion with electronic straggling and detailed modeling of inter-atomic potentials. We introduce the electronic scaling length $ξ_e$ as a fundamental parameter related to a physical observable of the system. We study the energy and electric-field dependence of the exciton-to-ion ratio for nuclear recoils based on the Bates-Griffing process and semiclassical atomic interactions. The resulting light and charge yields are expressed through the recombination probability in the Thomas-Imel box model using the calculated parameter $ξ_e$ and one fitted constant. We compare our model with recent measurements of the electric-field dependence of the box size in LAr and LXe and provide a physical explanation for this behavior. Our model extends to sub-keV energies and provides a consistent description of available data from a few keV to 1 MeV, yielding better overall agreement with existing LAr data than NEST and offering predictions for LXe.
one_liner: A first-principles model predicts nuclear-recoil scintillation and ionization yields in liquid argon and xenon from sub-keV energies to 1 MeV.
why_it_matters: Accurate recoil-yield models directly affect calibration thresholds and signal reconstruction in noble-liquid dark-matter and neutrino detectors.
detailed_summary: The study solves Lindhard's integro-differential equation with electronic straggling and detailed interatomic potentials to model total quanta from nuclear recoils. It introduces an electronic scaling length and calculates the energy- and field-dependent exciton-to-ion ratio before treating recombination with the Thomas-Imel box model. The resulting description spans sub-keV to 1 MeV energies, improves overall agreement with available LAr data relative to NEST, and supplies LXe predictions.
main_result: The model consistently describes field-dependent light and charge production across a broad recoil-energy range using one fitted recombination constant.
application_angle: The predictions support detector calibration, low-threshold event reconstruction, and sensitivity estimates for rare-event searches.

title: Generalized Mean-Field Ising Model as a Benchmark Family with Exact Solutions
abstract: Exactly solvable models provide opportunities to understand complex optimization problems while offering controlled benchmarks for computational methods. However, nontrivial models that combine analytical tractability with challenging optimization structure remain scarce. Here, we introduce the Generalized Mean-Field Ising (GMFI) family, a densely connected and inhomogeneous class of Ising Hamiltonians whose ground states can nevertheless be obtained exactly. This exact solution reveals a hidden low-dimensional structure and enables a complete number-theoretic classification of different system sizes and degenerate ground states. Uniquely, the GMFI family can be used to benchmark both quantum and classical optimization methods over system sizes far beyond exact diagonalization. We investigate the GMFI family using several approaches, including theoretical analysis of quantum annealing, experiments on a D-Wave quantum processor, the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA), imaginary-time evolution (ITE), greedy algorithm, simulated annealing, and a quantum-inspired greedy algorithm. Despite the GMFI model's exact solvability, it exhibits nontrivial algorithmic behavior: although the quantum-annealing gap is expected to decrease with increasing system size, it shows pronounced and unexpected system-size-dependent oscillatory signatures. These results establish GMFI models as a rare bridge between exact many-body theory, number theory, optimization, and quantum hardware, providing a scalable benchmark for identifying and understanding algorithmic limitations in classical and quantum computing.
one_liner: An exactly solvable dense Ising family exposes nontrivial, size-dependent behavior across quantum and classical optimization methods.
why_it_matters: Its exact ground states provide scalable truth data for diagnosing optimization hardware and algorithms beyond sizes accessible to exact diagonalization.
detailed_summary: The generalized mean-field Ising family combines dense, inhomogeneous couplings with a hidden low-dimensional structure that permits exact ground-state solutions. The authors benchmark quantum annealing, QAOA, imaginary-time evolution, simulated annealing, greedy methods, and a D-Wave processor. Despite exact solvability, the family exhibits challenging optimization behavior, including pronounced system-size oscillations in the expected quantum-annealing gap.
main_result: The work establishes a scalable exactly solvable benchmark and identifies unexpected size-dependent signatures in quantum-annealing behavior.
application_angle: The family can reveal hardware and algorithm limitations at problem sizes where brute-force classical validation is unavailable.

title: Key Evaluation of a Relativistic Quantum Key Distribution Over a Turbulent Free-space Optical Channel
abstract: We investigate the performance of relativistic quantum key distribution (RQKD) over turbulent free-space optical channels for both single-photon and coherent-state implementations. A theoretical model is developed to describe the effect of atmospheric turbulence on interferometric visibility and secret-key generation by incorporating turbulence-induced phase fluctuations into the key-rate analysis. Numerical simulations are performed under realistic channel conditions to evaluate the achievable communication distance and secret-key rate. The results show that atmospheric turbulence degrades the protocol performance by reducing interference visibility, with the severity of the degradation determined by the ratio between the interferometer-arm separation $r$ (or temporal separation of signal and reference states $ΔT$) and Fried's parameter. The single-photon protocol remains operational over all investigated turbulence regimes, whereas the coherent-state implementation exhibits a critical dependence on the interferometer geometry (especially on $ΔT$), leading to a threshold beyond which secure key generation is no longer possible. These findings quantify the impact of atmospheric turbulence on relativistic quantum key distribution and provide practical guidelines for the design and optimization of free-space RQKD systems.
one_liner: A turbulence-aware model quantifies visibility and secret-key losses in single-photon and coherent-state relativistic free-space QKD.
why_it_matters: It translates atmospheric coherence and interferometer geometry into concrete design constraints for secure free-space quantum links.
detailed_summary: The analysis incorporates turbulence-induced phase fluctuations into interferometric visibility and secret-key calculations for relativistic QKD. Performance is governed by the ratio of spatial arm separation, or signal-reference delay, to Fried's atmospheric coherence parameter. Simulations indicate that the single-photon protocol operates throughout the investigated regimes, while the coherent-state scheme crosses a geometry-dependent threshold beyond which no secure key is generated.
main_result: The model identifies turbulence- and geometry-dependent key-rate limits, including a critical temporal-separation threshold for coherent-state operation.
application_angle: The results guide interferometer spacing and timing choices for atmospheric quantum communication terminals.

title: Memory-Induced Limits on Entanglement Distribution
abstract: We investigate the operational limits of entanglement distribution through quantum channels reused without reinitialization. Building on an effective repeated-use channel description, we show that residual excitations left in the channel from previous uses act as a memory source that progressively suppresses coherent quantum transmission. To quantify this limitation, we derive an analytical lower bound on the quantum capacity and combine it with the Holevo-Werner semidefinite-programming upper bound. We also provide an analytical criterion to identify entanglement-breaking channels, with thresholds that depend jointly on chain length and reuse. For perfect-state-transfer chains, the resulting capacity window yields tighter estimates than previous bounds, with the relative improvement becoming substantially more pronounced closer to the entanglement-breaking threshold. Moreover, on the second use, our lower bound certifies a maximal relative timing-error tolerance across all chains with internal memory that lies just below 22.63% and is attained by the three-site chain. We further derive a fundamental relative timing-error threshold of 36.41%, above which we analytically guarantee zero unassisted quantum capacity for every chain with internal memory, independent of the number of uses. These results establish a clear benchmark model for repeated entanglement distribution, and identify timing precision, chain length, and memory accumulation as fundamental constraints on scalable quantum-network architectures.
one_liner: Residual channel excitations impose quantitative capacity and timing limits on entanglement distribution through repeatedly used quantum chains.
why_it_matters: It identifies memory accumulation as a fundamental constraint on scalable quantum links and supplies thresholds for timing-control requirements.
detailed_summary: The work models quantum channels that are reused without reinitialization, so residual excitations progressively suppress coherent transfer. Analytical capacity lower bounds are combined with a Holevo-Werner semidefinite-programming upper bound, alongside an entanglement-breaking criterion dependent on reuse and chain length. For the second use, the best certified relative timing-error tolerance is just below 22.63%, while errors above 36.41% guarantee zero unassisted quantum capacity for any chain with internal memory.
main_result: The analysis derives tighter capacity windows and universal timing-error thresholds for memory-affected entanglement transmission.
application_angle: These bounds help specify reset protocols, timing precision, and permissible reuse rates in quantum-network interconnects.

title: The geometry of Floquet states
abstract: This paper studies the moduli space of "good" periodic Hamiltonians, i.e., periodic Hamiltonians with nondegenerate Floquet spectrum. The corresponding Floquet states determine a geometric model for the moduli space of such Hamiltonians. The model is expressed in terms of configuration spaces, flag manifolds, and principal bundles. A corollary of the main result is the complete determination of the rational cohomology ring of the space of good periodic Hamiltonians. The paper also considers the adiabatic driving of a 1-parameter family of good periodic Hamiltonians. We formulate two conjectures describing the resulting asymptotic quantum evolution. These are Floquet analogues of the adiabatic theorem in quantum mechanics.
one_liner: A geometric framework classifies periodic Hamiltonians with nondegenerate Floquet spectra and determines their rational cohomology ring.
why_it_matters: The framework could clarify topological constraints and adiabatic control paths in periodically driven quantum and photonic systems.
detailed_summary: The authors model periodic Hamiltonians with nondegenerate Floquet spectra using configuration spaces, flag manifolds, and principal bundles. This construction yields the complete rational cohomology ring of the corresponding moduli space. They also formulate two conjectures for adiabatic evolution along one-parameter families of such Hamiltonians.
main_result: The work geometrically classifies good periodic Hamiltonians and completely determines the rational cohomology ring of their moduli space.
application_angle: The results provide mathematical tools for designing and analyzing robust control trajectories in Floquet-engineered quantum and photonic devices.

title: Drive-tunable Floquet exchange spectroscopy with Hong--Ou--Mandel interference
abstract: Floquet driving reshapes cavity spectra, but single-photon sideband populations do not reveal how it changes two-photon exchange. Here we show theoretically that delay-resolved Hong--Ou--Mandel (HOM) coincidences can probe this response in a collectively coupled cavity. A frequency-entangled signal photon scatters linearly from the driven cavity while its idler provides a delayed reference. Averaging over an unsynchronized drive phase removes coherence between different net output orders but preserves exchange interference within each order. Fourier transformation of the coincidence trace yields two drive-dependent exchange branches associated with the Floquet-polariton spectrum. As the drive changes, the branches shift and exchange weight; the dominant physical output order also changes, a transfer not reproduced by single-photon sideband populations. We further map the coincidence-trace response over drive frequency and amplitude and connect it to a count-model-dependent Fisher information. Floquet control thus adds a tunable exchange spectrum to HOM interferometry and gives quantitative targets for an experiment.
one_liner: Delay-resolved Hong–Ou–Mandel interference reveals drive-tunable two-photon exchange branches in a Floquet cavity.
why_it_matters: It proposes an experimentally accessible probe of driven cavity dynamics that exposes exchange information absent from single-photon sideband spectra.
detailed_summary: A frequency-entangled signal photon scatters from a collectively coupled driven cavity while its idler serves as a delayed reference. Fourier analysis of the HOM coincidence trace resolves two drive-dependent exchange branches linked to the Floquet-polariton spectrum. The model predicts branch shifts, weight transfer between output orders, and count-model-dependent Fisher information across drive frequency and amplitude.
main_result: The proposed HOM protocol resolves tunable Floquet exchange spectra and output-order transfer not captured by single-photon populations.
application_angle: The protocol supplies concrete drive settings and information metrics for experimental spectroscopy of dynamically controlled cavity systems.

title: Execution bias, repeatability and mitigation cost in parameter-frozen molecular VQE energy evaluation
abstract: A smaller statistical error bar need not mean a more accurate molecular energy. We evaluate noiselessly optimized molecular variational quantum eigensolver states on IBM Aachen and Pittsburgh, two 156-qubit Heron processors (provider-reported revision 3). Only energy evaluation runs on hardware, with parameters, layouts and compiled circuits frozen and dynamical decoupling disabled. A five-molecule pilot, three-molecule isolated cohort in three windows and known-state controls comprise 110 jobs and 28.2 billed quantum processing unit (QPU) minutes; the isolated cohort spans 30.2 h within a 31.7 h campaign. Raw 1024 O2 and BeH2 mean residuals exceed returned uncertainty by factors 12-32. Pittsburgh BeH2 cross-job standard deviation is 5.6 times mean returned uncertainty. The zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE) package reduces O2 absolute residuals by 49.7% on Aachen and 83.5% on Pittsburgh at about fourfold charge. On Pittsburgh, twirled readout error extinction (TREX) removes 80 millihartree (mHa) per Raw 1024 job charge versus 50 mHa for ZNE. Controls reveal qubit-124 preparation or readout errors 5.4-5.6 times calibration; 13 mitigated energy point estimates fall outside the mapped spectrum, with no Raw counterpart. These results support workload checks and repeated measurements before additional sampling.
one_liner: Frozen-circuit VQE tests on two IBM Heron processors expose large execution bias, poor repeatability, and costly mitigation tradeoffs.
why_it_matters: The study shows that reported sampling uncertainties can severely understate hardware error, affecting how molecular VQE results are validated and budgeted.
detailed_summary: The authors evaluated fixed, noiselessly optimized molecular VQE states on two 156-qubit IBM Heron processors across 110 hardware jobs. Raw residuals for O2 and BeH2 exceeded returned uncertainties by factors of 12–32, while cross-job variation also surpassed nominal error bars. ZNE reduced O2 residuals at roughly fourfold charge, whereas TREX offered better error removal per raw-job-equivalent cost in one Pittsburgh comparison; some mitigated estimates became unphysical.
main_result: Hardware energy estimates exhibited systematic bias and variability far beyond returned uncertainties, with mitigation improving bias at substantial cost and sometimes producing unphysical values.
application_angle: The findings motivate workload-specific controls, repeated runs, and cost-aware mitigation checks before trusting quantum-chemistry estimates from current QPUs.

title: Adaptive Local Measurements For Quantum Learning Can Exponentially Outperform Nonadaptive Global Measurements
abstract: Can measurements chosen adaptively, in response to earlier outcomes, be exponentially more informative than measurements fixed in advance? In many quantum settings, adaptivity helps at most polynomially; known exponential advantages require coherent measurements across copies or restricted measurements. We show an exponential advantage measuring one copy at a time, with no quantum memory kept between state copies, even when the nonadaptive learner may perform arbitrary global measurements on each copy. We construct explicit families of multi-qubit states in which a scalar parameter is encoded in one of exponentially many candidate observables, with an auxiliary marker indicating which one. An adaptive protocol identifies the relevant observable and then measures it using only single-qubit measurements and one round of adaptation. At fixed accuracy, it needs logarithmically many copies as the qubit count grows, whereas every nonadaptive protocol needs exponentially many. The same mechanism yields an exponential gap in local asymptotic minimax mean squared error constants, tight up to the exponential base. The states are separable and classical in label-dependent product bases; no entanglement or other nonclassical correlations are required. The gap comes from measurement incompatibility: the candidate observables cannot be measured jointly, so a fixed measurement must divide its information budget among them, while adaptivity selects the informative one. Accordingly, the separation disappears when the candidate observables commute, and cannot occur with fully observed classical samples. Measurement incompatibility thus emerges as a resource for quantum learning, distinct from entanglement and quantum memory, that classical feedback alone can exploit.
one_liner: One-round adaptive local measurements learn a hidden parameter with logarithmic copies where any fixed per-copy measurement needs exponentially many.
why_it_matters: It identifies measurement incompatibility—not entanglement or quantum memory—as a resource that classical feedback can exploit for quantum learning.
detailed_summary: The authors construct separable multi-qubit state families in which a marker identifies one of exponentially many candidate observables carrying a scalar parameter. A one-round adaptive protocol first reads the marker and then selects single-qubit measurements, requiring only logarithmically many copies at fixed accuracy. Every nonadaptive protocol, even with arbitrary global measurements on each copy, requires exponentially many copies; the gap vanishes for commuting observables.
main_result: Adaptive single-copy local measurements achieve an exponential sample-complexity advantage over all nonadaptive per-copy measurement strategies.
application_angle: The result supports feedback-driven measurement architectures for communication receivers, distributed sensing, and low-memory quantum-learning devices.

title: Collective sliding relaxor ferroelectricity across thousand-layer van der Waals superstructures
abstract: Relaxor ferroelectrics are among the most important electromechanical materials owing to their exceptionally large electrostrictive responses. However, conventional relaxor behavior is generally associated with chemical complexity and structural disorder, where local compositional fluctuations generate polar nanoregions, making the microscopic origin of this behavior difficult to control and engineer. Here we report sliding relaxor ferroelectricity (S-RFE), a previously unknown relaxor state in which engineered stacking-phase heterogeneity enables cooperative interlayer sliding to generate collective relaxor behavior. Through stacking-phase engineering in rhombohedral boron nitride, we create sliding domains that act as structural analogues of polar nanoregions and cooperatively align under an electric field through interlayer sliding. This collective state produces reversible electromechanical deformation of up to approximately $-1.6\%$ with negligible hysteresis in approximately 300-nm-thick crystals, corresponding to approximately 1000 atomic layers. The resulting electrostriction coefficient ($Q_{33}$ of approximately $1200\,\mathrm{m}^{4}\mathrm{C}^{-2}$) exceeds those of most crystalline electrostrictors by orders of magnitude. Unlike conventional relaxors, whose electromechanical response is often suppressed by dipolar freezing at low temperatures, S-RFE remains active down to 1.6 K and maintains giant electromechanical functionality. Our results establish sliding relaxor ferroelectricity as a new route to relaxor behavior and reveal how atomic-scale interlayer motion can be amplified into collective mesoscale functionality across approximately one thousand layers, providing a materials-by-design platform for electromechanical, photonic, and quantum technologies based on van der Waals materials.
one_liner: Stacking-engineered rhombohedral boron nitride exhibits giant, low-hysteresis sliding relaxor ferroelectricity across about 1,000 layers.
why_it_matters: Its large cryogenic electrostriction offers a materials-by-design route to compact actuators and tunable components for photonic and quantum platforms.
detailed_summary: Engineered stacking-phase heterogeneity in rhombohedral boron nitride creates sliding domains that cooperatively align under an electric field. Approximately 300-nm-thick crystals show reversible deformation up to about −1.6% with negligible hysteresis and a reported Q33 near 1200 m4 C−2. The response remains active down to 1.6 K, unlike many conventional relaxors limited by low-temperature dipolar freezing.
main_result: The material delivers giant, reversible sliding electrostriction across roughly 1,000 atomic layers while retaining functionality at 1.6 K.
application_angle: Cryogenic, low-hysteresis electromechanical control could enable tunable photonic structures, precision actuators, and components integrated with quantum hardware.

title: Theoretical Study of Classical Dynamics of Electron in Two-Frequency Paul Trap
abstract: We present a theoretical study of trapping an electron in a two-frequency Paul trap, motivated by future hybrid architecture consisting of a doubly charged calcium ion (Ca$^{2+}$) and an electron. By isolating the electron from ionic-electron interactions, we formulate the equations of motion for the electron in the time-dependent trap potentials and cast them in the Hill form. Stability and dynamics are then analysed in terms of the dimensionless q-parameters, which encode the applied voltages, drive frequencies, trap geometry, and the particle's charge-to-mass ratio. Under the combined action of the two radio-frequency fields, the trapped electron's classical motion is shown to be approximated well by a slow secular oscillation modulated by two distinct motion sidebands originating from the low- and high-frequency RF drives. The approximation method presented here enables a quick evaluation of the relation between the device-design q-parameters and the electron motion. It offers a crucial foundation for developing physical models of electron-ion interactions in electron-ion traps.
one_liner: A two-frequency Paul-trap model predicts stable electron motion as a secular oscillation carrying two RF-induced sidebands.
why_it_matters: The analysis links practical trap parameters to electron trajectories, supporting the design of future hybrid electron–ion quantum hardware.
detailed_summary: The study casts the classical electron equations of motion in a two-frequency Paul trap into Hill form and analyzes stability through dimensionless q parameters. Within stable regimes, the trajectory is approximated by slow secular motion modulated by distinct sidebands from the low- and high-frequency drives. The approximation enables rapid mapping from voltages, frequencies, and geometry to expected electron dynamics.
main_result: A compact approximation accurately relates dual-RF trap design parameters to stable electron secular motion and its two drive-induced sidebands.
application_angle: The model provides a design foundation for hybrid traps combining an electron with Ca2+ for future quantum-control and interaction experiments.

title: High bandwidth heterodyne sensing with bulk NV diamond
abstract: Developing high performance portable sensors is of significant importance for both terrestrial and satellite communications, with quantum sensors offering potential advantages in sensitivity and bandwidth. The nitrogen vacancy center in diamond is a popular quantum sensing platform for its relative simplicity and wide range of acceptable operating conditions, but suffers a limited instantaneous bandwidth due to the narrow linewidth of the spin resonance. In this work, we first present a magnetic quantum sensing scheme utilizing heterodyne mixing with strong optical and microwave driving, achieving MHz-scale instantaneous bandwidth with a sensitivity of $548 \; \text{pT/}\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ in an active diamond volume of $ 2.5\times 10^{-4} \; \text{mm}^3$ with $2 \times 10^{11}$ NV centers. We then demonstrate expansion of the sensing bandwidth by employing a strong magnetic gradient and many individually modulated microwave control fields, expanding the single resonance bandwidth to 48 MHz with a peak sensitivity of $8.5 \; \text{nT/}\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$.
one_liner: Bulk-NV heterodyne magnetometry achieves MHz-scale instantaneous bandwidth and extends a single resonance across 48 MHz.
why_it_matters: The approach tackles the narrow-resonance bandwidth bottleneck of NV sensors, supporting broadband magnetic detection for portable and communication systems.
detailed_summary: Strong optical and microwave driving enables heterodyne magnetic sensing with MHz-scale instantaneous bandwidth and 548 pT/√Hz sensitivity. The active diamond volume is 2.5×10^-4 mm³ and contains about 2×10^11 NV centers. A magnetic-field gradient combined with individually modulated microwave fields expands the effective single-resonance bandwidth to 48 MHz, with 8.5 nT/√Hz peak sensitivity.
main_result: The system demonstrates MHz-scale heterodyne sensing and a gradient-multiplexed 48 MHz detection bandwidth.
application_angle: Broadband NV magnetometry could enable compact receivers and sensors for terrestrial or satellite communication environments.

title: Individually Addressed Logical Pauli Measurements by QLDPC Surgery on a Trapped Ion Quantum Computer
abstract: Quantum low-density parity check (QLDPC) codes may lead to order-of-magnitude reductions in the qubit overhead required for fault-tolerant quantum computation. Achieving this improved overhead requires logical operations that selectively address individual logical qubits encoded within multi-qubit code blocks. Recently proposed architectures achieve this through QLDPC surgery, in which non-destructive Pauli measurements are performed using ancillary ''gadget'' systems transiently entangled with the code block, generalising lattice surgery. Here we implement QLDPC surgery on a [[10,2,3]] generalised bicycle code using Quantinuum's H2-2 trapped ion processor. A single-round surgery measurement using seven gadget qubits measures the $\bar{X}_1$ operator with a 0.72 [0.32, 1.41]% (95% credible interval) error rate and agrees with subsequent transversal measurement with 1.03 [0.60, 1.65]% error. Decoding across three rounds of syndrome extraction suppresses the gadget measurement error, reducing the error rate to below 0.26%. The syndrome after surgery confirms return to the code space and the unaddressed ''spectator'' qubit is preserved with error 0.21 [0.04, 0.67]% during the three-round measurement. We further demonstrate composition of conjugate basis gadgets by sequentially measuring $\bar{X}_1$ then $\bar{Z}_2$, reusing the gadget qubits, and obtain a 1.12 [0.60, 1.94]% error in the $\bar{Z}_2$ measurement. These results constitute a hardware validation of the generalised surgery primitive underlying Pauli-based computing for QLDPC architectures.
one_liner: A trapped-ion processor performs individually addressed logical Pauli measurements through QLDPC surgery on a [[10,2,3]] code.
why_it_matters: This hardware demonstration validates a key primitive for operating on selected logical qubits without disturbing spectators in low-overhead QLDPC architectures.
detailed_summary: The experiment implements generalized QLDPC surgery on Quantinuum's H2-2 processor using a [[10,2,3]] bicycle code and seven gadget qubits. Three rounds of syndrome extraction reduce the gadget-measurement error below 0.26%, while the unaddressed logical spectator is preserved with 0.21% error. Sequential X̄1 and Z̄2 measurements further demonstrate conjugate-basis gadget composition and qubit reuse.
main_result: QLDPC surgery selectively measures an encoded Pauli operator, returns the block to code space, and preserves the spectator logical qubit.
application_angle: The primitive supports selectively addressable, Pauli-based fault-tolerant computation with potentially much lower physical-qubit overhead.

title: A rhombic spin-1 interpretation of a room-temperature GaN emitter
abstract: Single defects in GaN show optically detected magnetic resonance at room temperature. In the more abundant class, a minimal $S=3/2$ model leaves a $g\approx 4$ line unexplained. For one defect, this line lies near the sum of the two outer lines, consistent with transitions among three shared levels. A rhombic $S=1$ model reproduces the three line positions with rms errors of 8.1-9.8 MHz. The tested second-order $S=3/2$ fits containing all three transitions and the published minimal model do not reproduce these positions. A ladder fitted to the strong lines remains viable if the $g\approx 4$ line is a separate transition near the sum of the outer two. An unresolved frequency-window shift prevents the existing data from establishing the $S=1$ assignment uniquely. We propose a zero-field sweep that directly tests the isolated $S=1$ assignment.
one_liner: A rhombic spin-1 model explains three room-temperature ODMR lines from a GaN defect better than tested spin-3/2 models.
why_it_matters: Correctly identifying the defect spin Hamiltonian is essential for turning room-temperature GaN emitters into reliable quantum sensors and photonic spin interfaces.
detailed_summary: A rhombic S=1 Hamiltonian reproduces the three observed ODMR line positions with 8.1–9.8 MHz rms error, including the line near g≈4. Tested second-order S=3/2 descriptions containing all three transitions do not reproduce those positions, although a separate-transition interpretation remains viable. Because an unresolved frequency-window shift prevents a unique assignment, the authors propose a discriminating zero-field sweep.
main_result: The measured ODMR spectrum is consistent with a rhombic spin-1 center, but the assignment remains experimentally unconfirmed.
application_angle: A definitive spin assignment would clarify how GaN defects can be controlled and calibrated for nanoscale sensing and integrated quantum photonics.

title: Time-Switching Energy-Harvesting Quantum Relay-Assisted FSO Communication with Displaced Squeezed Signaling
abstract: This paper investigates a quantum relay-assisted free-space optical (FSO) communication system in which a decode-and-forward relay is powered by time-switching optical energy harvesting and forwards the decoded information using displaced squeezed signaling (DSS). To obtain a physically con sistent description of turbulence-induced loss for non-classical signaling, each hop is modeled as a pure-loss bosonic chan nel whose random transmissivity follows a truncated Gamma Gamma law, i.e., the Gamma-Gamma irradiance conditioned on the physically admissible range of a transmittance. Under this channel, coherent states remain pure, whereas squeezed states are mapped to mixed Gaussian states. Under Helstrom-optimal detection, the average error of the coherent hop is derived in exact Laplace-series form. For the DSS hop, we derive the output states, a closed-form Gaussian fidelity with rigorous two sided bounds on the Helstrom error, and prove the existence of a loss-aware optimal photon partition. Furthermore, we prove that optimized squeezing preserves both the turbulence-induced diversity order and the leading asymptotic constant of coherent relaying, so that its benefit is a finite-photon-budget effect, and that an interior throughput-optimal harvesting fraction exists. A covariance-preserving benchmark with an exact series representation yields an analytical upper bound on the achievable throughput whose absolute gap vanishes as the relay photon budget grows. Numerical results based on the exact mixed-state Helstrom error quantify the benefit of squeezing and the regime in which it is useful.
one_liner: A quantum FSO relay combines optical energy harvesting with displaced squeezed signaling under physically bounded turbulent loss.
why_it_matters: The analysis identifies when squeezing improves photon-limited relaying and jointly optimizes nonclassical signaling and the relay's harvesting time.
detailed_summary: Each free-space hop is modeled as a pure-loss bosonic channel with truncated Gamma-Gamma transmissivity, ensuring physically admissible turbulent loss. The work derives exact coherent-hop error expressions, mixed Gaussian output states for displaced squeezed signaling, and rigorous Helstrom-error bounds. It proves an optimal photon partition and an interior throughput-optimal harvesting fraction, while showing that squeezing gives a finite-budget advantage without changing asymptotic diversity.
main_result: Optimized displaced squeezing improves relay performance at finite photon budgets while preserving coherent relaying's turbulence-limited asymptotics.
application_angle: The framework informs power-autonomous optical relays for photon-starved terrestrial, airborne, or satellite quantum communication links.

title: Force Sensing in a Recoverable Bosonic Quantum Memory
abstract: In continuous-variable quantum information, sensing and quantum error correction in the same mode face an intrinsic trade-off: sensors must accumulate weak external displacements, whereas bosonic codes typically suppress such shifts as errors. Here, we establish compatibility by constructing finite-energy bosonic codes that enable a single oscillator to sense an external force while actively protecting an unknown logical qubit. By encoding logical amplitudes across discrete wave-packet sites and capturing the force signal in a shared internal coordinate, we achieve an endpoint probe readout that is independent of the logical state under continuous photon loss $γ$. Crucially, binomial site recovery cancels packet-dependent probe distortions alongside logical errors: for a $(2r+2)$-packet code, memory infidelity is suppressed to $O(γ^{r+1})$ while residual memory-probe correlations scale as $O(γ^{r+2})$. Finally, superconducting quantum circuit benchmarks under competing photon-number dephasing and Kerr nonlinearity identify preferred encoding regimes for hardware implementation.
one_liner: A finite-energy bosonic code lets one oscillator sense force while actively protecting an unknown logical qubit from photon loss.
why_it_matters: It resolves a central conflict between displacement sensing and bosonic error correction, enabling quantum memories that remain useful as sensors.
detailed_summary: Logical amplitudes are distributed across discrete wave-packet sites, while an external-force displacement is accumulated in a shared internal coordinate. Endpoint probe readout is independent of the unknown logical state under continuous photon loss. For a (2r+2)-packet code, binomial recovery suppresses memory infidelity to O(γ^(r+1)) and residual memory-probe correlations to O(γ^(r+2)); circuit benchmarks also include dephasing and Kerr effects.
main_result: The code simultaneously preserves an unknown logical qubit and yields a recoverable force signal under continuous photon loss.
application_angle: The scheme could turn superconducting bosonic memories into protected force or displacement sensors without sacrificing stored quantum information.

title: Dissipation dilution enhances SiV coupling to vdW diamond nanomechanics
