abstract: Solid-state color centers embedded into mechanical resonators, where orbital states mediate interactions between spins and long-lived phonons, are a promising platform for hybrid quantum systems. The negatively charged silicon vacancy center in diamond (SiV-) is particularly favorable for strain-coupling to nanomechanical resonators because of its large spin-strain susceptibility and compatibility with device integration. Tensioned nanomechanical resonators offer an attractive route due to their ultra-long mechanical coherence times enabled by diluting defect-induced dissipation, though it is unclear if the same dilution effect undermines strain-mediated coupling to material defect centers. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a tensioned diamond nanobeam platform that enables enhanced strain coupling to SiV- orbital states. Through monitoring the optical response of the SiVs to the static and dynamical strain of the mechanical resonator, we observe that dynamical strain localizes near the clamps of these resonators under static strain. This allows us to enhance SiV-mechanical coupling and the mechanical coherence simultaneously, and provide a SiV-strain sensitivity with greatly improved accuracy over previous literature values. Thus, our work opens a pathway towards seconds-long coherence hybrid quantum systems utilizing point defects in diamond nanomechanics for quantum information processing.
one_liner: Tension-induced dissipation dilution simultaneously improves SiV strain coupling and coherence in diamond nanobeam resonators.
why_it_matters: The experiment shows that long mechanical coherence need not weaken defect coupling, advancing practical spin-phonon interfaces for hybrid quantum hardware.
detailed_summary: The authors fabricate tensioned diamond nanobeams containing negatively charged SiV centers and monitor their optical response to static and dynamic strain. Static tension localizes dynamic strain near the clamps, allowing enhanced SiV-orbital coupling while retaining dissipation-diluted mechanical coherence. The measurements also provide a more accurate SiV strain-sensitivity estimate than prior values.
main_result: Strain localization near nanobeam clamps enhances SiV-mechanical coupling without forfeiting the coherence benefit of dissipation dilution.
application_angle: The platform offers a route to long-lived spin-phonon nodes for quantum memories, transduction, networking, and mechanically mediated processing.

title: NAKO: A Benchmarking Framework for Evaluating and Diagnosing Neutral-Atom Quantum Compilers
abstract: Reconfigurable neutral-atom processors couple gate scheduling, atom placement, and parallel atom transport, so compiler decisions jointly determine physical execution costs. Evaluating these compilers requires attainable resource references and a way to trace excess costs to their causes. We present NAKO, a benchmarking framework that parameterizes circuits by qubit count, logical depth, and requested one- and two-qubit gate densities, and assigns attainable targets for Rydberg stages, routing intervals, and movement layers. Each benchmark is paired with an executable reference schedule; under the stated execution model, construction guarantees minimum Rydberg-stage and routing-interval counts, and minimum movement among schedules with the minimum Rydberg-stage count. Comparing compiler outputs with these references quantifies resource gaps, while reference mappings and intermediate physical states enable controlled interventions that trace excess costs to specific compiler decisions. In a 648-run evaluation of Enola and OLSQ-DPQA, NAKO identifies distinct bottlenecks. For Enola, placement scoring and cross-stage layout management contribute to excess movement; diagnosis-guided interventions reduce mean movement by 78.9% across five matched circuits. For OLSQ-DPQA, premature candidate selection and limited exploration of preparatory states produce avoidable entangling stages and routing intervals; four fixed-checkpoint continuations each eliminate one Rydberg stage and one routing interval without increasing movement. NAKO thus links resource targets backed by constructive optimality guarantees to controlled diagnosis and validation of compiler-specific resource savings.
one_liner: NAKO benchmarks neutral-atom compilers against executable schedules with constructive resource-optimality guarantees.
why_it_matters: It turns compiler overhead into diagnosable placement, routing, and scheduling decisions, enabling substantial reductions in physical atom movement.
detailed_summary: NAKO generates parameterized circuits with executable reference schedules attaining minimum Rydberg-stage and routing-interval counts under its execution model, plus minimum movement among stage-optimal schedules. Across 648 Enola and OLSQ-DPQA runs, controlled interventions identify compiler-specific placement, layout-management, and search bottlenecks. Diagnosis-guided changes reduce Enola's mean movement by 78.9% on five matched circuits, while fixed-checkpoint continuations remove one Rydberg stage and routing interval from selected OLSQ-DPQA cases.
main_result: NAKO provides attainable resource references and causal diagnostics that expose and validate large compiler-specific execution savings.
application_angle: The framework supports hardware-aware compiler selection and optimization for lower-motion, lower-depth neutral-atom quantum programs.

title: Composable Device-Independent Quantum Digital Signatures
abstract: Extending device-independent (DI) quantum cryptography to composably support all fundamental information security objectives is crucial for secure quantum networks. Achieving this goal requires composable quantum digital signatures (QDSs), which support integrity, authenticity, and nonrepudiation when integrated into quantum networks. Yet existing QDS protocols generally rely on assumptions about the underlying quantum devices, while their security analyses remain largely restricted to stand-alone settings, leaving related-key attacks on the underlying linear feedback shift register (LFSR)-based Toeplitz authentication unaddressed. Here, we establish the first composable security framework for QDS within constructive cryptography, and realize the corresponding ideal QDS resource by developing a DI-QDS protocol employing one-time universal hashing and multi-channel multiplexing. We further derive a related-key security bound for the underlying LFSR-based Toeplitz authentication, thereby establishing unforgeability while extending the forgery boundary considered in previous QDS security analyses. We also demonstrate the practical feasibility of our DI-QDS protocol under realistic quantum network conditions in the finite-size regime, with numerical simulations showing that it enables efficient signing of multibit documents over metropolitan-scale distances. Our results establish QDS as a composable cryptographic primitive and extend DI quantum cryptography to support the full range of information security objectives with composable security guarantees in future quantum networks.
one_liner: A device-independent quantum digital-signature protocol achieves composable security using one-time hashing and multiplexed channels.
why_it_matters: It adds composably secure authenticity, integrity, and nonrepudiation to device-independent metropolitan quantum networks.
detailed_summary: The work defines the first constructive-cryptography framework for composable quantum digital signatures and constructs a device-independent protocol realizing the ideal signature resource. One-time universal hashing and multichannel multiplexing are combined with a new related-key bound for LFSR-based Toeplitz authentication. Finite-size simulations indicate efficient signing of multibit documents under realistic metropolitan-network conditions.
main_result: The protocol establishes composable DI-QDS security, including unforgeability against an expanded class of related-key attacks.
application_angle: It provides a route to trustworthy document signing and authentication within heterogeneous future quantum networks.

title: SeQUeNCe.DQC: Full-stack Simulation of Distributed Quantum Computing
abstract: Distributed quantum computing (DQC) connects multiple quantum processing units to overcome the scale limits of monolithic hardware. We introduce SeQUeNCe$.$DQC a new top-level module within the SeQUeNCe package that compiles monolithic circuits into topology-aware execution plans and coordinates their execution using SeQUeNCe's existing quantum-network modules and protocols. We validate SeQUeNCe$.$DQC by reproducing a two-node trapped-ion Grover experiment in simulation and comparing success probabilities with the reported 71% benchmark. We then evaluate how compiler strategy, topology, and memory capacity jointly govern distributed circuit execution time and success rate. In these experiments, our hybrid compilers successfully identified mixed TeleGate/TeleData execution plans that outperformed pure gate-teleportation strategies. By capturing the physical overhead of distributed quantum primitives, SeQUeNCe$.$DQC provides a rigorous platform for co-designing DQC software and hardware architectures.
one_liner: SeQUeNCe.DQC compiles and simulates topology-aware distributed quantum programs with realistic network-protocol overheads.
why_it_matters: It enables full-stack co-design of distributed compilers, network topologies, quantum memories, and inter-node execution strategies.
detailed_summary: SeQUeNCe.DQC converts monolithic circuits into topology-aware distributed execution plans and runs them through SeQUeNCe's network models and protocols. Validation reproduces a two-node trapped-ion Grover experiment in simulation against its reported 71% success benchmark. Hybrid compilers combining TeleGate and TeleData outperform pure gate-teleportation strategies in the evaluated scenarios, while exposing dependencies on topology and memory capacity.
main_result: The simulator captures physical distributed-operation costs and identifies hybrid TeleGate/TeleData plans that outperform pure gate teleportation.
application_angle: It supports quantitative architecture and compiler trade studies before deploying expensive distributed quantum hardware.

title: Optical clock network tracks tidal variations of the gravity potential
abstract: Gravity affects the passage of time, as described by General Relativity. On Earth, the rate of a clock as seen by a fixed observer changes by about one part in $10^{16}$ per metre in height. Chronometric levelling exploits this effect to directly measure differences in gravity potential by comparing distant clocks. It has been proposed as a complementary approach to established geodetic techniques for linking height reference systems and monitoring the terrestrial gravity potential. Experimental demonstrations have to date focused primarily on static potential differences. Yet, the potentials of the Moon, the Sun and other celestial bodies as well as the Earth's response to their tidal forcing change clock rates by several $10^{-17}$, providing a predictable test signal to demonstrate optical clock networks resolving small variations in relativistic time dilation. Here, we report chronometric observations of time-varying gravity potential differences using a network of optical clocks and phase-stabilized fibre links in Europe. Two distinct geographical configurations, with baselines of about 800 km each, result in different combinations of diurnal and semidiurnal tidal components. One comparison uses a transportable optical clock as a remote sensor. The measured rate shifts track the tidal variations, resolving the predicted signal within 1 d of measurement and agreeing with model predictions. These results extend experimental chronometric levelling from static to dynamic potential differences and highlight the need to account for the time dependence of relativistic time dilation in frequency metrology. They also open the prospect for quantum clock networks with improved stability and availability to move beyond known tides and monitor other gravity potential variations, such as those arising from surface deformation and mass redistribution in geologically or volcanically active regions.
one_liner: A European optical-clock network resolves tidal changes in gravitational potential across two baselines of roughly 800 km.
why_it_matters: It advances chronometric levelling from static height comparisons to dynamic sensing of deformation and mass redistribution.
detailed_summary: Optical clocks connected by phase-stabilized fiber links measured time-dependent relativistic frequency shifts over two approximately 800 km European configurations. The differing baselines sampled distinct diurnal and semidiurnal tidal components, with one comparison using a transportable clock as the remote sensor. The observations resolved the predicted tidal signal within one day and agreed with gravity-potential models.
main_result: The clock network tracks modeled tidal gravity-potential variations at the several-10^-17 fractional-frequency scale within one day.
application_angle: Improved networks could monitor volcanic or geological deformation, hydrological mass shifts, and evolving national height references.

title: Detection and Inhibition of Decoherence Through Collisions: A dynamical approach
abstract: Quantum systems are intrinsically fragile and highly vulnerable to environmental noise, making the preservation of quantum states one of the fundamental challenges in realizing practical quantum technologies. We propose two noise-agnostic quantum state protection protocols based on a collisional model. The first protocol preserves quantum states of qubits without requiring complete prior knowledge of the underlying noise dynamics, and the second even protects a logical qubit under similar circumstances. These protocols provide robust protection for arbitrary single-qubit and entangled states against general noise processes. Furthermore, their capability to safeguard quantum states with an arbitrary number of qubits enhances the reliability, robustness, and scalability of emerging quantum architectures. These results establish the proposed framework as a promising approach for practical quantum information processing.
one_liner: Two collision-model protocols protect physical or logical qubits against general noise without complete knowledge of its dynamics.
why_it_matters: Noise-agnostic state protection could reduce calibration demands when preserving arbitrary and entangled states in evolving hardware.
detailed_summary: The authors propose two dynamical protocols based on repeated system-environment collisions: one protects physical qubit states, while the other protects an encoded logical qubit. The schemes are designed without requiring complete prior characterization of the noise and are claimed to cover general noise processes. Their formulation extends from arbitrary single-qubit states to entangled multiqubit states, although the abstract reports no hardware demonstration.
main_result: The proposed protocols preserve arbitrary physical and logical qubit states under broad, incompletely characterized noise models.
application_angle: The approach could provide adaptable state protection for quantum processors whose environmental noise is difficult to model fully.

title: Error-Corrected Quantum Optimization via Rydberg Atom Array Embeddings
abstract: Rydberg atom quantum optimizers naturally encode the maximum independent set problem on geometric graphs. However, to solve general combinatorial optimization problems on more complex topologies, an embedding is required to overcome the limited-range native interactions. Such embeddings use gadgets, specific arrangements of atoms, which inevitably introduce ancillary atoms. Here, we show that this apparent overhead instead provides an intrinsic resource for error correction. Specifically, we demonstrate that the Parity Architecture-based Rydberg embedding naturally forms a classical error-correcting code, a principle that extends to other Rydberg blockade-based embeddings. Within superatom substructures, exact Rydberg-excitation-number constraints provide local error syndromes at no additional hardware cost and give rise to a strictly nonlinear code. To correct bit-flip errors, we introduce the precisely tailored Cluster decoder, which exploits these local constraints and the underlying gadget structure. Numerically, this approach achieves an error threshold of $p_{\text{th}}\gtrsim26 \%$ across different layout geometries. Experimentally, on the QuEra Aquila QPU, the Cluster decoder recovers exact optimization solutions with an average success rate of $\gtrsim8\%$ for systems of up to 107 atoms, even when bare hardware and standard greedy post-processing find none. A Rydberg atom array embedding is therefore not merely a hardware mapping of an optimization problem, but a co-designed architecture for quantum optimization in which embedding, computation, and error correction emerge from the same physical structure.
one_liner: Rydberg optimization embeddings double as nonlinear error-correcting codes, recovering solutions lost by bare hardware.
why_it_matters: It converts embedding ancillas into zero-extra-hardware error syndromes and demonstrates useful decoding on a 107-atom commercial QPU.
detailed_summary: Parity Architecture-based Rydberg embeddings impose exact local excitation-number constraints within superatoms, creating nonlinear classical codes and hardware-native error syndromes. A tailored Cluster decoder exploits these constraints and gadget connectivity, yielding a numerical bit-flip threshold of at least about 26% across several layouts. On QuEra Aquila, it recovers exact solutions with average success of at least about 8% for instances up to 107 atoms where bare output and greedy post-processing recover none.
main_result: Embedding-aware decoding achieves a numerical error threshold above roughly 26% and experimentally restores exact 107-atom optimization solutions.
application_angle: The co-designed embedding and decoder can improve near-term Rydberg optimization without adding dedicated syndrome hardware.

title: Optimized Dynamical Decoupling for Spin Ensembles with Large Inhomogeneities
abstract: Spin ensembles show increasing promise for highly efficient quantum sensing and quantum technologies. However, protecting their coherent properties remains a significant challenge. Dynamical decoupling (DD) typically employs a sequence of fast pulses that aim to reduce the effect of unwanted system-environment interactions. However, the performance of the DD sequences typically suffers in spin ensembles, e.g., due to amplitude and frequency inhomogeneities and control errors. In this work, we compare the performance of an extensive number of DD protocols for coherence protection and quantum sensing in an ensemble of negatively charged NV centers under ambient conditions. We identify the optimal approach that uses rapid adiabatic passage pulses, which are robust to amplitude and frequency inhomogeneity, in combination with the variation of their phases. We experimentally demonstrate an improved signal contrast and an order-of-magnitude increase in memory time with the optimal sequence compared to the widely used XY8 with standard rectangular pulses. We also apply our approach for improved sensing of a weak oscillating field. While our particular demonstration is with NV centers in diamond, the optimized protocol is generally applicable to other spin ensembles and to systems with high amplitude and/or frequency inhomogeneities.
one_liner: Adiabatic-passage dynamical decoupling extends ambient NV-ensemble memory time by an order of magnitude over rectangular-pulse XY8.
why_it_matters: Robust control against amplitude and frequency inhomogeneity directly improves ensemble coherence, signal contrast, and weak-field sensing.
detailed_summary: The authors experimentally compare many dynamical-decoupling protocols in an ambient negatively charged NV-center ensemble. A sequence combining rapid adiabatic-passage pulses with phase variation remains robust under amplitude and frequency inhomogeneities. It improves contrast, extends memory time by roughly tenfold relative to standard rectangular-pulse XY8, and enhances detection of a weak oscillating field.
main_result: The optimized sequence delivers an order-of-magnitude memory-time increase and improved weak-AC-field sensing compared with conventional XY8.
application_angle: The protocol can strengthen ensemble magnetometers and quantum memories without requiring highly uniform control fields or resonance frequencies.

title: Non-Markovian quantum-emitter dynamics and bound-state formation in an Aubry--André--Harper photonic lattice
abstract: In non-Markovian light-matter interactions, a spectrally structured bath can alter the evolution of a quantum emitter by modifying the vacuum fluctuations experienced by the emitter. This raises the question of how the localization transition and the associated multifractal critical modes induced by a quasiperiodic potential shape the emitter dynamics. We investigate this scenario in the single-excitation sector for a two-level quantum emitter coupled to an Aubry-André-Harper (AAH) photonic lattice. By externally tuning the strength of the quasiperiodic onsite modulation, the lattice is tuned from the extended to the localized regime through a critical point characterized by multifractal modes. Using modal analysis, we show that the quasiperiodic modulation reshapes the local density of states at the coupling site and thereby controls the effective spectral coupling between the emitter and the lattice. The transient dynamics depend strongly on the spatial and spectral overlap between the emitter and the lattice modes: extended modes below the critical modulation generally produce rapid depopulation, whereas critical and localized modes give rise to coherent back-action and persistent Rabi-like oscillations, with particularly pronounced behavior at the critical point. We further identify emitter-photon bound states whose formation is controlled by the quasiperiodic spectral structure of the bath and whose overlap with the initially excited state leads to partial long-time population trapping. These results establish a direct connection between quasiperiodic localization, non-Markovian dynamics, and emitter-photon bound-state formation.
one_liner: A tunable quasiperiodic photonic lattice controls emitter decay, coherent back-action, and emitter-photon bound-state formation.
why_it_matters: It links localization physics to controllable non-Markovian light-matter dynamics, offering a route to engineered decay and excitation trapping.
detailed_summary: The study models a two-level emitter coupled to an Aubry-André-Harper photonic lattice in the single-excitation sector. Varying the quasiperiodic onsite modulation reshapes the local density of states and tunes the bath from extended through multifractal-critical to localized modes. Critical and localized regimes produce coherent back-action, persistent Rabi-like oscillations, and bound states that retain part of the initial emitter population.
platform_or_system: Two-level emitter coupled to an AAH photonic lattice
main_result: Quasiperiodic modulation tunes emitter dynamics from rapid depopulation to persistent oscillations and partial population trapping in emitter-photon bound states.
application_angle: Engineered quasiperiodic reservoirs could provide on-chip control of spontaneous emission, quantum-state storage, and coherent light-matter interfaces.

title: Integrated Circular Polarisation Beam Shaper Based on Tilted Waveguide Bragg Gratings
abstract: Scalable quantum platforms require optical systems that deliver well-defined polarisation without relying on macroscopic bulk optics or manual alignment, motivating chip-integrated approaches capable of shaping both the spatial mode and the polarisation of the emitted field. By developing a full three-dimensional analytical model of the scattering process together with numerical simulations to design and evaluate the emitted field, we show that tilted waveguide Bragg gratings can act as integrated polarisation beam shapers. We find that scattering two co-propagating, orthogonally polarised pumps on a single grating is fundamentally limited: waveguide birefringence and the difference in scattering efficiency prevent full polarisation control. We overcome this with an orthogonal superimposed-grating architecture in which two gratings driven independently by two pumps propagating perpendicular to each other succeed in generating any desired polarisation output apart from directions in a narrow spatial region. The approach provides a scalable, chip-integrated route to polarisation-engineered light delivery for quantum technologies.
one_liner: Orthogonal superimposed tilted Bragg gratings enable chip-scale beam shaping with nearly arbitrary output polarisation.
why_it_matters: The architecture replaces alignment-sensitive bulk polarisation optics with a scalable integrated source interface for quantum photonic systems.
detailed_summary: A three-dimensional analytical scattering model and numerical simulations are used to design tilted waveguide Bragg-grating emitters. A single grating driven by two co-propagating orthogonal modes cannot provide complete polarisation control because of birefringence and unequal scattering efficiencies. Two independently driven, orthogonally superimposed gratings overcome this limitation and generate arbitrary target polarisations except within a narrow spatial region.
main_result: The proposed orthogonal dual-grating architecture provides nearly arbitrary spatially shaped polarisation output from an integrated device.
application_angle: It supports compact, scalable delivery of polarisation-engineered light for quantum emitters, trapped particles, and photonic quantum processors.

title: Cross-Platform Verification of Continuous-Variable Quantum Systems
abstract: Cross-platform verification compares output states of independently operated bosonic and quantum optical systems when classical predictions and joint measurements are unavailable. Continuous-variable distributed inner product estimation (CV-DIPE) provides a local measurement approach, but infinite-dimensional state spaces require rigorous control of truncation error. We develop three CV-DIPE protocols for the natural class of energy-constrained continuous-variable quantum states. One uses coordinated displaced parity, another coordinated Haar measurements, and the third independent homodyne shadows. For arbitrary multimode inputs in this class, including entangled and non-Gaussian states, we establish truncation error bounds and worst-case sample complexity guarantees for the exact inner product. The leading terms of these bounds favor coordinated Haar measurements, whose global implementation is experimentally challenging. These protocols provide certified strategies for cross-platform verification of continuous-variable systems using only local measurement data.
one_liner: Three local-measurement protocols certify inner products between energy-constrained continuous-variable states across independent platforms.
why_it_matters: Rigorous truncation and sample-complexity bounds make cross-platform comparison possible for multimode, entangled, and non-Gaussian optical states.
detailed_summary: The authors formulate three continuous-variable distributed inner-product estimation protocols using coordinated displaced-parity measurements, coordinated Haar measurements, or independent homodyne shadows. For energy-constrained multimode states, they derive truncation-error bounds and worst-case sample complexities for estimating the exact state inner product. Coordinated Haar measurements have the best leading-order bounds, although their global implementation is experimentally demanding.
main_result: The work provides certified local-data protocols for comparing arbitrary energy-constrained bosonic states, including entangled and non-Gaussian inputs.
application_angle: These methods can benchmark independently operated optical processors or networks when joint measurements and reliable classical simulation are unavailable.

title: Simultaneous SI-traceable measurement of the amplitude and the ellipticity of microwave fields with cold Rydberg atoms
abstract: We present a method for the simultaneous measurement of the amplitude and the ellipticity of microwave fields using trap-loss spectroscopy based on Rydberg excitation of a cold ensemble of 87Rb atoms. The measurement consists of probing the energy spectrum of the $61S_{1/2}$ to $61P_{1/2}$ transition in the presence of microwave, which depends on the electric field amplitude $|E|$ and the third Stokes parameter $|S_3|$. We use a millimeter-size magneto-optical trap to perform strongly-localized measurements, which mitigates the effect of microwave field inhomogeneities. This allows us to work with large Rabi frequencies and thus resolve small deviations from linear or circular states of polarization. Taking into account the effect of non-resonant couplings to neighboring Rydberg states, we measure $|E|$ and $|S_3|$ with an accuracy on the order of 1 percent in the Autler-Townes regime where the measurements can be traced to the international system of units. By studying the visibility of the spectral features as a function of the polarization of the excitation laser beams, we extract some information on the angle of arrival of the microwave field onto the atoms, with good agreement between theory and experiment.
one_liner: Cold Rydberg atoms simultaneously measure microwave amplitude and ellipticity with SI traceability and about 1% accuracy.
why_it_matters: A localized atomic probe can characterize microwave strength and polarisation while reducing errors from spatial field inhomogeneity.
detailed_summary: Trap-loss spectroscopy probes the microwave-dressed 61S1/2-to-61P1/2 transition in a millimeter-scale cold 87Rb ensemble. Spectral features jointly encode electric-field magnitude and the third Stokes parameter, with neighboring-state couplings included in the model. In the Autler-Townes regime, both quantities are measured with approximately 1% accuracy, and polarisation-dependent visibility also provides angle-of-arrival information.
main_result: The experiment simultaneously retrieves microwave field amplitude and ellipticity with roughly 1% SI-traceable accuracy.
application_angle: The technique offers localized calibration of microwave fields for antennas, quantum hardware, and precision electromagnetic metrology.

title: Unlimited-Range Absolute Distance Interferometry Outdoors via Tunable Synthetic and Pseudo-Supersynthetic Wavelengths: The TeleYAG-II Interferometer
abstract: Absolute distance interferometry requires an unlimited non-ambiguity range to be truly absolute. Tunable synthetic wavelength interferometry allows for the construction of pseudo-supersynthetic wavelengths using a limited number of optical sources and a standard interferometer setup. This approach facilitates the creation of a series of consecutively deployable synthetic wavelengths, ultimately combining macroscopic unambiguity with microscopic interferometric accuracy. We have implemented and demonstrated this concept in the TeleYAG-II interferometer, designed as an SI-traceable standard for the calibration of geodetic baselines. The system employs two Nd:YAG lasers as optical sources, with their frequency difference controlled by a versatile optical phase-locked loop. Specifically engineered for robustness in field conditions, the heterodyne interferometer was validated through an outdoor measurement campaign. The results demonstrate the efficacy of the method, achieving an expanded measurement uncertainty of 0.13 mm over a distance of 224 m without the need for auxiliary length measurements.
one_liner: TeleYAG-II measures 224 m outdoors with 0.13 mm expanded uncertainty using tunable synthetic interferometric wavelengths.
why_it_matters: It combines macroscopic unambiguous range with microscopic phase sensitivity in a field-ready, SI-traceable distance standard.
detailed_summary: TeleYAG-II uses two Nd:YAG lasers whose frequency difference is controlled by an optical phase-locked loop. Consecutively deployable synthetic wavelengths construct pseudo-supersynthetic wavelengths, extending the non-ambiguity range without auxiliary length measurements. An outdoor campaign demonstrated an expanded uncertainty of 0.13 mm over 224 m.
main_result: The interferometer achieves absolute outdoor distance measurement over 224 m with 0.13 mm expanded uncertainty and no auxiliary ranging system.
application_angle: The field-robust instrument can serve as an SI-traceable standard for calibrating long geodetic baselines and precision surveying systems.

title: Dissipative controller as a hidden source of errors in quantum gates
abstract: Quantum systems are typically controlled by classical devices that necessarily dissipate energy to the surrounding environment. By the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, this implies noise in the control field produced. We investigate the relationship between the resulting errors and the entropy produced by the macroscopic controller, working in the context of a concrete minimal model. In the most experimentally relevant regime of fast control and high fidelity, we find a tradeoff between dissipation and control errors. These findings are exemplified by perturbative calculations of the gate fidelity for simple gate implementations and of the fidelity of state transfer via shortcuts to adiabaticity in the Landau-Zener model. Our results quantitatively demonstrate that suppressing errors in quantum control typically comes at the cost of macroscopic dissipation, which is needed to tame fluctuations in the classical controller.
one_liner: A minimal control model links quantum-gate errors to the entropy production and fluctuations of dissipative classical controllers.
why_it_matters: It identifies controller dissipation as a physical resource for suppressing control noise, exposing a hardware-level fidelity tradeoff often omitted from gate models.
detailed_summary: The authors model a macroscopic dissipative controller whose control-field noise follows from the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. In the fast-control, high-fidelity regime, perturbative calculations reveal a quantitative tradeoff between entropy production and errors. The analysis covers simple quantum gates and shortcut-to-adiabaticity state transfer in a Landau-Zener system.
main_result: Reducing controller-induced errors generally requires increased macroscopic dissipation to suppress control-field fluctuations.
application_angle: The result provides a thermodynamic constraint for designing low-error control electronics and evaluating realistic quantum-gate limits.

title: Distributed Inner-Product Estimation for Continuous-Variable Quantum States
abstract: Distributed inner product estimation (DIPE) is a fundamental task in quantum information, aiming to estimate the inner product between two unknown quantum states prepared on distributed quantum platforms. For multimode continuous-variable (CV) systems, the infinite-dimensional Hilbert space poses an additional challenge. In this work, we develop a CV-DIPE protocol using only local homodyne measurements at shared phase settings and classical communication. Under a known bound on the mean energy per mode, we derive explicit finite-sample guarantees and sufficient copy counts for estimating the full inner product to prescribed accuracy and confidence. The energy constraint yields an inverse-square truncation-bias bound, while Gaussian structure strengthens the tail control to exponential decay and improves the resulting accuracy scaling. Numerical simulations with Gaussian and non-Gaussian states illustrate the balance between truncation bias and statistical error and its dependence on mode number and energy. Our results enable independent CV platforms to benchmark their state preparations against one another, even when neither state admits a tractable classical description.
one_liner: Local homodyne measurements and classical communication estimate inner products between distributed multimode continuous-variable states.
why_it_matters: The protocol enables cross-platform state benchmarking without joint measurements or a tractable classical description of either prepared state.
detailed_summary: The proposed CV-DIPE protocol uses local homodyne measurements performed at shared phase settings, followed by classical communication. Assuming a known mean-energy bound per mode, the authors derive explicit copy requirements for a target accuracy and confidence, with inverse-square truncation bias. Gaussian structure yields exponential tail control and improved accuracy scaling, while simulations test Gaussian and non-Gaussian states across mode number and energy.
main_result: The protocol provides finite-sample inner-product estimates using only local homodyne data under a bounded per-mode energy assumption.
application_angle: Independent photonic processors can compare state-preparation quality without physically transmitting states to a common measurement station.

title: Reversible photorefractive attack in continuous-variable quantum key distribution
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) offers information-theoretic security, but device imperfections introduce implementation vulnerabilities. Experimental evidence of the security consequences of transmitter vulnerabilities in continuous-variable QKD (CV-QKD) remains limited. Here, we experimentally investigate a reversible photorefractive attack in a local-local-oscillator CV-QKD system. Moderate blue-light illumination reduces the modulation variance of a lithium-niobate IQ modulator to a stable value without appreciably increasing estimated excess noise. The variance recovers after illumination is removed. We elucidate the underlying physical mechanisms and develop an attack that exploits recovery to compromise modulation calibration. Receiver measurements confirm that the resulting calibration mismatch leads to overestimated channel transmittance and underestimated excess noise. Key rate calculations based on measured parameters yield a positive estimated rate when the correctly calibrated rate is nonpositive. Recovery can also make the preceding manipulation harder to identify through later inspection. This work provides the first system-level experimental evidence that a reversible photorefractive response can be exploited to compromise modulation calibration in CV-QKD. These findings highlight reversible changes in quantum transmitters as a practical security concern, motivating security analyses and protection strategies that account for both optical perturbations and subsequent recovery.
one_liner: Blue-light exposure reversibly alters a lithium-niobate IQ modulator and corrupts security-parameter estimation in CV-QKD.
why_it_matters: The experiment shows that a recoverable transmitter change can make an insecure CV-QKD link appear to produce a positive secret-key rate.
detailed_summary: In a local-local-oscillator CV-QKD system, moderate blue-light illumination drives the lithium-niobate IQ modulator to a stable lower modulation variance without appreciably raising estimated excess noise. The variance recovers after illumination, enabling an attack on modulation calibration that causes transmittance to be overestimated and excess noise underestimated. Measured parameters can therefore predict a positive key rate even when the correctly calibrated rate is nonpositive.
platform_or_system: Local-LO CV-QKD with LiNbO3 IQ modulation
main_result: A system-level experiment demonstrates a reversible photorefractive calibration attack that produces dangerously optimistic CV-QKD security estimates.
application_angle: The findings motivate optical-perturbation monitoring, calibration safeguards, and security analyses that include reversible transmitter changes.

title: Cubic-Zn(1-x)Mn(x)Te optical modes across the phonon and phonon-polariton regimes
abstract: Alloying offers a convenient route to tune the physical properties of semiconductors, at the price, however, of local lattice/bond distortions needed to accommodate the lattice mismatch. Being nearly lattice-matched and moreover highly resistant to lattice and bond distortions thanks to a largely covalent bonding, cubic Zn(1-x)Mn(x)Te sets a benchmark to test the sensitivity of lattice vibrations to minimum lattice and bond distortions induced by alloying. We explore experimentally the two transverse optical regimes of cubic Zn(1-x)Mn(x)Te (x<0.7), with ab initio calculations in support: (1) the phonon-polariton regime at quasi-infinite (photon-like) wavelengths averaging over the alloy disorder, probed by forward-Raman scattering, and (2) the purely-mechanical phonon regime down to minimum wavelengths nearly matching the lattice constant zooming into the alloy disorder, achieved by inelastic neutron scattering. The short Zn-Te bond is found to exhibit a compact optical duo distinguishing homo from hetero local bond environments (1 bond: 2 mode), as explained by the percolation model. This deviates from the historical Zn(1-x)Mn(x)Te MREI (modified-random-element-isodisplacement) scheme inspired from classical Raman and infrared studies, in which the optical modes are blind to the bond environment (1-bond: 1-mode). So, the test is positive, reinforcing the status of the percolation scheme as a robust decryptor of (even small) lattice distortions induced by alloying through the lattice dynamics.
one_liner: Raman and neutron probes reveal bond-environment-dependent optical modes in cubic ZnMnTe that conventional alloy models miss.
why_it_matters: The measurements validate lattice dynamics as a sensitive probe of even weak local alloy distortions and strengthen the percolation model for semiconductor design.
detailed_summary: Forward-Raman scattering probes the long-wavelength phonon-polariton regime, while inelastic neutron scattering accesses mechanical phonons at wavelengths approaching the lattice constant. Supported by ab initio calculations, the measurements show a compact Zn-Te optical-mode doublet separating homo- and hetero-bond environments. This one-bond/two-mode behavior supports the percolation picture over the historical MREI one-bond/one-mode scheme.
main_result: Zn-Te bonds exhibit two environment-sensitive optical modes across phonon-polariton and short-wavelength phonon regimes.
application_angle: The combined spectroscopy offers a way to diagnose subtle local distortions when engineering alloy-based optical and optoelectronic materials.

title: Detuning-assisted cavity enhancement in spectroscopy
abstract: Cavity-enhanced spectroscopy is a widely used experimental technique. We show that detuning the cavity frequency from the transition of interest can enhance the precision for dipole moment estimation by up to two orders of magnitude beyond the improvement when the cavity is resonant with the transition. We show this for both classical continuous-wave (CW) and pulsed single-photon probes, even in the presence of losses. We trace this enhancement to a detuning-controlled redistribution of information between the light- and matter-like polaritons, with losses determining the optimal branch. We show that this enhancement remains accessible using conventional photodetection and time-correlated single-photon counting.
one_liner: Cavity detuning can improve dipole-moment estimation precision by up to two orders of magnitude over resonant operation.
why_it_matters: The enhancement works with standard photodetection and time-correlated photon counting, making it experimentally accessible for precision spectroscopy.
detailed_summary: The analysis covers classical continuous-wave probes and pulsed single photons in lossy cavity-enhanced spectroscopy. Detuning redistributes parameter information between light-like and matter-like polariton branches, with the loss channels selecting the optimal branch. The predicted precision gain reaches two orders of magnitude relative to resonant cavity operation and remains measurable with conventional detectors.
main_result: Optimized cavity detuning yields up to a 100-fold precision enhancement for dipole-moment estimation compared with resonant enhancement.
application_angle: The method can improve precision spectroscopy and molecular or atomic parameter sensing without requiring exotic detection hardware.

title: High-Fidelity Universal Quantum Gates in a Cryogenic Atom Array
abstract: Neutral atoms in optical tweezer arrays have emerged as a leading platform for quantum information processing. The fidelity of entangling gates mediated by Rydberg interactions has improved rapidly and is increasingly constrained by blackbody-radiation-induced transitions, which shorten Rydberg lifetimes and create contaminant states that can cause correlated errors. Cryogenic environments can suppress these transition rates by more than an order of magnitude. However, realizing a universal gate set in such an environment has remained an outstanding challenge. Here, we demonstrate a universal quantum gate set in a cryogenic $^{133}$Cs atom array, with a single-qubit gate fidelity of 99.970(2)% and a raw two-qubit entangling-gate fidelity of 99.76(8)%, within the range of leading room-temperature implementations. The entangling gate uses direct single-photon coupling between the electronic ground state and a Rydberg $P$ state, avoiding scattering and light shifts associated with two-photon coupling. The gate operates at a modest Rabi frequency of $2π\times4.3$ MHz. The measured fidelity agrees with our error model dominated by atomic motion, indicating a straightforward route to higher fidelity through improved cooling, while the fundamental error contribution from Rydberg decay is below $3\times10^{-4}$. These results establish a path to entangling-gate fidelities substantially beyond the current state of the art through cryogenic suppression of Rydberg decay, reducing the overhead for fault-tolerant computation.
one_liner: A cryogenic cesium tweezer array demonstrates universal gates with 99.970% single-qubit and 99.76% raw two-qubit fidelity.
why_it_matters: Cryogenic suppression of blackbody-driven Rydberg decay offers a credible route beyond current neutral-atom gate fidelities and toward lower fault-tolerance overhead.
detailed_summary: The experiment realizes a universal gate set in a cryogenic 133Cs optical-tweezer array. Direct single-photon coupling from the ground state to a Rydberg P state avoids scattering and light shifts from two-photon excitation, while operating at a 2π×4.3 MHz Rabi frequency. The measured two-qubit error agrees with a model dominated by atomic motion, and the fundamental Rydberg-decay contribution is below 3×10^-4.
main_result: The platform achieves 99.970(2)% single-qubit fidelity and 99.76(8)% raw Rydberg-mediated two-qubit fidelity.
application_angle: Improved atomic cooling combined with cryogenic lifetime enhancement could reduce error-correction overhead in scalable neutral-atom quantum computers.

title: Quantum communication: a discrimination approach
abstract: We develop a state discrimination approach to unassisted quantum communication through a noisy quantum channel. Starting from the operational duality between entanglement recovery and state discrimination, we construct entanglement-generation codes with explicit decoders constructed from Petz recovery maps. The resulting error bounds hold for every number of channel uses and are expressed in terms of Petz-Rényi coherent information. For product sources, they yield exponential error decay at rates below coherent information.
one_liner: A state-discrimination framework yields explicit Petz-map decoders and finite-blocklength guarantees for noisy quantum communication.
why_it_matters: The approach connects operational decoding to computable coherent-information bounds, supporting rigorous code design at finite channel uses.
detailed_summary: The work converts an operational duality between entanglement recovery and state discrimination into entanglement-generation codes for noisy quantum channels. It supplies explicit decoders based on Petz recovery maps and error bounds valid for every number of channel uses. For product sources, the error decays exponentially at communication rates below the coherent information.
platform_or_system: Noisy quantum channels with Petz-map decoding
main_result: Explicit entanglement-generation codes achieve finite-use error bounds and exponential error decay below coherent-information rates for product sources.
application_angle: The framework offers analytically controlled decoder constructions for future quantum-network links operating over noisy channels.

title: Ionization and Dissociation Energies of Molecular Hydrogen
abstract: Molecular hydrogen (H$_2$) is the simplest neutral molecule and its ionization and dissociation energies are key benchmarks for testing first-principles calculations of nonadiabatic, relativistic, quantum-electrodynamic and finite-nuclear-size effects in molecules. To obtain improved H$_2$ ionization and dissociation energies, we performed precision measurements of 15 transition frequencies in para-H$_2$. They connect the X $^1Σ_g^+(v=0,N=0)$ ground state, the long-lived EF $^1Σ_g^+(v=0,N=0)$ excited state, and several high members of the $n$p and $n$d Rydberg series with principal quantum number $n$ in the range between 48 and 70. The new data by itself leads to a five times more accurate value of the ionization energy of the ground state of para-H$_2$, equivalent to a relative frequency accuracy of $5\times 10^{-11}$. Combined with a global network analysis of 45 energy intervals in para- and ortho-H$_2$ that have been measured in the past three decades, we obtain new statistically robust values for the ionization energy [$E_{\rm I}(0,0)/(hc)= 124\,417.491\,1573(58)$~cm$^{-1}$] and the dissociation energy [$D_0^{N=0}=36\,118.069\,6646(58)$~cm$^{-1}$] of H$_2$. These values have an unprecedented accuracy equivalent to 175 kHz. The network analysis also leads to improved term values and dissociation energies of the excited states involved in the analysis. By comparing the results with first-principles calculations of the level structures of H$_2$ and H$_2^+$ , a significantly reduced upper bound of 540 kHz is derived for putative beyond-the-standard-model contributions to the energy difference between para- and ortho-H$_2$.
one_liner: Precision spectroscopy and global network analysis determine H2 ionization and dissociation energies with 175 kHz-equivalent accuracy.
why_it_matters: These molecular benchmarks sharpen tests of nonadiabatic, relativistic, QED, finite-size, and possible beyond-standard-model effects.
detailed_summary: Fifteen transition frequencies connect the para-H2 ground and long-lived EF states to np and nd Rydberg states with principal quantum numbers 48–70. The new measurements improve the ground-state ionization energy fivefold, while a network analysis of 45 para- and ortho-H2 intervals yields ionization and dissociation energies with 175 kHz-equivalent accuracy. Comparison with first-principles calculations limits beyond-standard-model contributions to the para–ortho energy difference to 540 kHz.
main_result: The study determines H2 ionization and dissociation energies with unprecedented 175 kHz-equivalent accuracy.
application_angle: The measurements provide stringent calibration benchmarks for molecular theory and sensitive searches for physics beyond the standard model.

title: Fault-Tolerant Heisenberg-Limited Quantum Metrology with Bosonic Probes
abstract: Quantum sensors have been shown to enable more precise measurements than classical sensors. By using entanglement and coherent evolution, the estimation error can be made to scale better in interrogation time, photon count, and other resources, achieving Heisenberg-limited scaling. However, environmental noise and hardware errors typically destroy the coherence of the sensitive quantum states. This motivates the use of fault-tolerant techniques to create more robust quantum sensing protocols. Such fault-tolerant quantum sensing approaches have been shown to enhance sensitivity for qubit systems, but many practical sensors require bosonic probes. In this paper, we propose a fault-tolerant protocol using bosons to estimate displacements in the presence of dephasing noise. We construct an optimal error-correcting code under a mean photon-number constraint. Controlled displacements couple the probe to a repetition-encoded qubit register, while repeated boson-parity measurements and resets remove probe noise without erasing the stored logical phase. Under circuit-level bit-flip noise, a distance-$d$ code suppresses logical failures to order $p^{(d+1)/2}$. We show that, for a decay rate $γ_A$, a total sensing time $T$ and a mean photon number budget $N$, and for sufficiently small residual signals, the Fisher information scales as $NT^2$ over interrogation times of order $γ_A^{-(d+1)/2}$. This is a significant improvement over the non-fault-tolerant approach that achieves Heisenberg scaling only for a total time $\mathcal O(γ_A^{-1})$.
one_liner: A bosonic error-corrected sensing protocol preserves Heisenberg scaling under dephasing and circuit-level bit-flip noise.
why_it_matters: It extends fault-tolerant metrology to practical bosonic probes while lengthening the useful coherent interrogation regime.
detailed_summary: The protocol estimates bosonic displacements under dephasing using an optimal code constrained by mean photon number. Controlled displacements transfer phase information to a repetition-encoded qubit register, while repeated parity measurements and resets remove probe noise without erasing that phase. A distance-d code suppresses circuit-level logical failures to order p^((d+1)/2), and the Fisher information scales as NT² over parametrically extended interrogation times.
platform_or_system: Bosonic probe coupled to a repetition-coded qubit register
main_result: The protocol sustains Fisher-information scaling of NT² for interrogation times of order γ_A^(-(d+1)/2).
application_angle: The architecture could improve displacement, force, and field sensors built from cavities or oscillator-like quantum probes.

title: Nonlinear Jackiw-Rebbi exciton-polaritons at van der Waals topological interfaces
abstract: Topological photonic structures provide a powerful means of confining and directing light through interface states formed between photonic phases with distinct topological properties. Van der Waals (vdW) materials offer complementary opportunities for nanophotonics: their optical properties can be selected from a wide family of layered crystals, while their atomically smooth surfaces and lack of lattice-matching constraints enable complex photonic heterostructures to be assembled layer by layer. This flexibility allows topological photonic confinement and strong excitonic coupling to be engineered separately within the same structure. Here, patterned low-loss dielectric hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) defines the photonic modes, while an encapsulated WSe2 monolayer provides the excitonic resonance that couples directly to the confined optical field. We use this approach to realise Jackiw-Rebbi exciton-polaritons in a one-dimensional hBN double-grating heterostructure. Strong coupling between the WSe2 exciton and a photonic Jackiw-Rebbi state localised at the interface between two topologically distinct gratings produces upper and lower Jackiw-Rebbi polariton branches. By varying the temperature from 4.7 to 300 K, we tune the exciton across the photonic bandgap and trace the evolution and anticrossing of these branches using angle-resolved reflectance and photoluminescence spectroscopy. Power-dependent photoluminescence further reveals a pronounced nonlinear response of the confined Jackiw-Rebbi polariton, including a blueshift of up to 5 meV and correlated changes in its intensity scaling and linewidth. These results establish vdW photonic heterostructures as a versatile platform for engineering tunable and nonlinear polaritons localised at topological interfaces.
one_liner: An hBN–WSe2 heterostructure realizes tunable Jackiw-Rebbi polaritons with a nonlinear blueshift reaching 5 meV.
why_it_matters: It combines topological optical confinement, strong exciton coupling, room-temperature tunability, and useful polariton nonlinearity in one vdW device.
detailed_summary: A patterned hBN double grating supplies a photonic Jackiw-Rebbi interface state, while an encapsulated WSe2 monolayer provides the excitonic resonance. Angle-resolved reflectance and photoluminescence from 4.7 to 300 K resolve upper and lower polariton branches and their anticrossing. Power-dependent emission shows a blueshift up to 5 meV together with correlated intensity-scaling and linewidth changes.
platform_or_system: hBN double grating with encapsulated monolayer WSe2
main_result: Strong coupling produces localized Jackiw-Rebbi polariton branches with temperature tunability and a power-dependent blueshift up to 5 meV.
application_angle: The platform supports compact nonlinear and tunable topological photonic elements for switching, routing, and polaritonic circuitry.

title: Fast and accurate neural triage decoding of ultra-high-rate quantum LDPC codes
abstract: Quantum error correction is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing. High-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes have emerged as a promising approach to reducing the substantial physical qubit overhead of quantum error correction, enabling encoding rates exceeding $1/2$ in blocks of approximately one thousand physical data qubits. However, their practical implementation requires decoders that combine high accuracy with low latency to keep pace with quantum hardware. Existing decoders of high-rate qLDPC codes can achieve high accuracy but often incur substantial computational latency, whereas neural network decoders have yet to be demonstrated for high-rate qLDPC codes. Here, we introduce \emph{neural triage decoding}, a framework that uses syndrome consistency to adaptively allocate neural computation. A local neural message-passing network rapidly predicts error corrections, additional iterations reduce residual syndrome violations, and a rarely invoked diversification stage searches for consistent corrections to the remaining shots. We demonstrate that the \texttt{Triage} decoder can decode ultra-high-rate qLDPC codes encoding a few hundred logical qubits, including lifted-product and Kasai codes, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy comparable to the near optimal algorithmic decoders while reducing decoding latency by approximately one to two orders of magnitude. Our framework is inspired by a rigorous analysis of the exact bitwise marginal decoder, revealing a distance-independent syndrome-inconsistent error floor. In addition, we show the robustness of neural network decoders to mismatched error priors. Our results establish adaptive neural decoding as a promising route towards fast, accurate, and scalable quantum error correction in the near term.
one_liner: Neural triage decoding matches leading qLDPC accuracy while cutting latency by roughly one to two orders of magnitude.
why_it_matters: Low-latency decoding of codes carrying hundreds of logical qubits addresses a key control bottleneck for scalable fault-tolerant hardware.
detailed_summary: Triage uses syndrome consistency to adaptively allocate neural computation across decoding instances. A local message-passing network proposes corrections, extra iterations address residual violations, and a rarely used diversification stage searches for consistent solutions. On lifted-product and Kasai codes encoding hundreds of logical qubits, it approaches near-optimal decoder accuracy with approximately 10–100× lower latency and remains robust to mismatched error priors.
platform_or_system: High-rate lifted-product and Kasai qLDPC codes
main_result: Adaptive neural decoding achieves state-of-the-art qLDPC accuracy while reducing decoding latency by about one to two orders of magnitude.
application_angle: The method could enable real-time error correction for high-rate quantum processors with substantially reduced classical-control overhead.

title: Using domain walls to benchmark fast quantum anneals
abstract: We consider the distribution of domain walls arising in ground states of frustrated 1-dimensional Ising spin chains with anti-parallel boundary spins. For ideal chains, a sine-squared particle-in-a-box distribution of domain walls is expected in the quantum setting, and a uniform distribution expected classically. However, for chains with random imperfections, prior work [Chancellor et al., npj Quantum Inf. 8, 73, 2022] found that the distribution in a physical implementation corresponded to neither. Instead, the domain wall distribution forms a U-shaped profile arising from a classical model with random fields, where the combination of averaging over these fields and thermal averaging produces the characteristic U-shape. With D-Wave's newer fast anneal feature, we access anneal times shorter than the coherence time and observe the expected coherent quantum behavior in the form of a sine-squared distribution. For the shortest available anneal time, the dynamics have not yet reached the sine-squared shape and instead display a different U-shape in the middle of the chains. This motivates using the extent of the domain wall distribution tail in this regime as a platform independent metric that provides a signature of both coherence time and noise levels.
one_liner: Fast D-Wave anneals reveal the sine-squared domain-wall profile expected from coherent quantum dynamics.
why_it_matters: A simple domain-wall statistic offers a platform-independent benchmark sensitive to both coherence time and hardware noise.
detailed_summary: The experiment studies domain-wall positions in frustrated one-dimensional Ising chains with antiparallel boundary spins. Anneals shorter than the hardware coherence time recover the sine-squared distribution predicted for coherent quantum evolution, unlike the disorder-induced classical profile seen previously. At the shortest anneal, a distinct central U-shape motivates using distribution-tail extent as a joint indicator of coherence and noise.
main_result: Sub-coherence-time anneals produce the predicted coherent sine-squared domain-wall distribution and motivate a tail-based hardware metric.
application_angle: The protocol provides a compact benchmark for comparing fast-annealing coherence and noise across quantum-annealing platforms.

title: On the gauge-invariant orbital angular momentum of vector optical vortices in the paraxial approximation and beyond
abstract: In this paper we present a gauge-invariant formalism for describing the spin and orbital angular momenta of scalar and vector optical vortices. The correction term, arising from consistent incorporation of the transverse vector potential's nonlocality, restores gauge invariance and makes it possible to separate the total angular momentum into spin and orbital components. We propose a method for calculating the orbital and spin angular momenta of multimode vector vortex fields and show that the orbital angular momentum of such beams contains two qualitatively different components. The polarization-independent contribution to the orbital angular momentum is related to the topological charge that determines the order of the phase singularity, while the polarization-dependent one is proportional to the helical topological charge that determines the spatial inhomogeneity of the polarization. We also discuss the quantization procedure for fields with spatially inhomogeneous polarization in terms of modes with a helical topological charge, and examine the limits of applicability of the proposed formalism.
one_liner: A gauge-invariant framework separates spin and orbital angular momentum in scalar and vector optical vortices beyond simple paraxial treatments.
why_it_matters: It enables physically consistent analysis and quantization of structured light with spatially varying polarization, relevant to optical manipulation and information encoding.
detailed_summary: The work incorporates a correction arising from the nonlocal transverse vector potential to obtain a gauge-invariant separation of optical spin and orbital angular momentum. For multimode vector-vortex fields, it identifies a polarization-independent orbital term set by phase-singularity charge and a polarization-dependent term set by helical polarization charge. It also formulates quantization using modes carrying helical topological charge and discusses the formalism's validity limits.
main_result: The authors derive a gauge-invariant spin-orbital decomposition in which optical orbital angular momentum contains distinct phase- and polarization-dependent components.
application_angle: The framework can improve the design and interpretation of structured-light systems for optical trapping, mode multiplexing, and photonic quantum-state encoding.

title: Grow, Compress, and Perturb: A Hybrid Quantum-Classical Pathway to Scalable Quantum Chemistry on Quantum Computers
abstract: While Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) variants are among the leading candidates for electronic structure calculations on quantum computers, gradient-based operator selection limits their scalability. To solve this, we introduce the Hamiltonian-gradient-free VULCAN (Variational Upbuilding, Layered Compression, Adaptive N-body perturbation) layered VQE framework. Our method dynamically generates ansatz operators using Variational Double Bracket Flow (VDBF) equations. Combined with a linearly scaling minimal complete pool, it creates a pool 4-12 times smaller than QEB (Qubit-Excitation-Based) pools. By appending entire layers simultaneously, Hamiltonian gradient measurements are completely eliminated. Circuit depth is managed via a grow-then-compress scheme using efficient state-overlap measurements, and qubit requirements are reduced by projecting the Hamiltonian onto a dominant-determinant subspace. Using high-performance emulation up to 32 logical qubits, we achieve chemical accuracy at just 5-20% of the measurement cost of batched ADAPT-VQE for hydrogen chains, BeH2 and H2O. For the 32-qubit C3H6, where batched ADAPT-VQE does not reach chemical accuracy, a single VULCAN layer combined with a GPU-accelerated stochastic Epstein-Nesbet (ENPT2) correction does. This stochastic ENPT2 post-processing step enables early termination at chemical accuracy.
one_liner: VULCAN combines gradient-free ansatz growth, circuit compression, subspace projection, and perturbative correction for scalable quantum chemistry.
why_it_matters: The method cuts measurement cost and logical-qubit demand while retaining chemical accuracy, directly addressing major bottlenecks in quantum chemistry workflows.
detailed_summary: VULCAN generates complete ansatz layers through variational double-bracket-flow equations, avoiding Hamiltonian-gradient measurements and using a minimal operator pool 4–12 times smaller than qubit-excitation pools. A grow-then-compress procedure controls depth, while dominant-determinant subspace projection reduces qubit requirements. Emulations through 32 logical qubits reach chemical accuracy at 5–20% of batched ADAPT-VQE's measurement cost on several molecules; stochastic ENPT2 enables chemical accuracy for 32-qubit C3H6.
platform_or_system: Layered VQE on up to 32 logical qubits
main_result: VULCAN achieves chemical accuracy with substantially fewer measurements and succeeds on a 32-qubit C3H6 case where batched ADAPT-VQE does not.
application_angle: The workflow offers a lower-overhead route to useful electronic-structure calculations on resource-constrained quantum processors.

title: Algebraic strong-to-weak symmetry breaking and partial decodability in the surface code
abstract: Coherent noise can give rise to unconventional regimes of quantum information recovery and mixed-state order. We study these phenomena in two settings related by Wegner duality: the triangular-lattice surface code subject to single-qubit Pauli-$Z$ rotations followed by syndrome measurements, and a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ paramagnet subject to strongly symmetric decoherence. Increasing the rotation angle drives a transition from a decodable phase to a \emph{partially decodable} critical phase in the code, and from a strongly symmetric phase to a phase with \emph{algebraic} $\mathbb{Z}_2$ strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (SWSSB) in the dual paramagnet. We develop a common description of these phenomena in terms of a weakly coupled $\mathrm{SO}(n)$ nonlinear sigma model in the replica limit $n\to1$. Taking this replica limit analytically, we derive universal signatures of the critical phase: an optimal Pauli decoding fidelity that approaches a universal function of the system's aspect ratio in the thermodynamic limit, and a dual fidelity correlator that decays as a universal power law. These observables relate to correlations of twist operators in the sigma model description. Large-scale numerical simulations confirm these analytical predictions. We also argue that the algebraic SWSSB phase cannot be realized by any Pauli dephasing channel acting on the $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ paramagnet. We probe this "non-classical" character through the output state's sensitivity to well-separated $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ fluxes inserted in the initial state, which reveals persistent coherence between distinct $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ charge trajectories at long distances.
one_liner: Coherent rotations drive a surface code into a critical phase where quantum information remains only partially decodable.
why_it_matters: The results expose a nonclassical recovery regime under coherent noise and provide universal benchmarks for assessing realistic quantum-error-correction hardware.
detailed_summary: The authors study a triangular-lattice surface code under coherent single-qubit Z rotations followed by syndrome measurements and connect it by Wegner duality to a decohered Z2 paramagnet. Beyond a transition, the code enters a partially decodable critical phase corresponding to algebraic strong-to-weak symmetry breaking in the dual model. Replica-limit sigma-model analysis predicts universal aspect-ratio-dependent decoding fidelity and power-law fidelity correlations, which large-scale simulations confirm.
platform_or_system: Triangular-lattice surface code under coherent Z noise
main_result: The study identifies and characterizes a universal partially decodable critical phase that cannot be reproduced by a conventional Pauli dephasing channel.
application_angle: Its fidelity signatures can guide decoder evaluation and coherent-noise diagnosis in surface-code experiments.

title: Probing fluctuations in photon emission statistics of spin injected quantum dots with time dependent electronic excitation
abstract: Electrically spin-injected ensembles of InGaAs/GaAs quantum dots emit circularly polarized single photons, with the emission helicity determined by the spin polarization of the injected electrons. A ferromagnetic CoFeB spin-injection layer with perpendicular magnetic anisotropy, combined with an MgO tunnel barrier, enables spin-polarized electron injection into the quantum-dot active region, resulting in circularly polarized photon emission at zero applied magnetic field. These devices realize direct spin-charge-photon conversion in an electrically driven, microelectronics-compatible quantum light source that operates without an external pump laser. Using an extended Hanbury Brown-Twiss interferometer with four detectors and time-tagged readout, we measure time-resolved photon-number statistics that resolve up to $|2\rangle$ Fock states within a single excitation cycle. While single-photon ($n=|1\rangle$) emission tracks the electrical excitation pulse as expected, the two-photon ($n=|2\rangle$) statistics exhibit pronounced fluctuations at multiple temporal positions within the pulse. These fluctuations vanish upon demagnetization of the spin-injection layer, establishing a direct link between the multi-photon emission dynamics and the spin polarization of the injected carriers. The observations indicate that spin injection controls not only the helicity of the emitted photons but also higher-order temporal correlations of the emission. The behavior is phenomenologically captured by inserting both a variable excitation mechanism and a set of multi-emitter collapse operators within a stochastic wave function evolution. The platform thus opens a route to electrically driven, spin-controlled single and multi-photon Fock-state sources and provides a testbed for spin-conditioned multi-emitter dynamics in solid-state quantum light sources.
one_liner: Time-resolved measurements link spin injection to fluctuating two-photon emission in electrically driven InGaAs/GaAs quantum dots.
why_it_matters: The device combines zero-field spin control, electrical excitation, and resolved Fock-state statistics in a microelectronics-compatible quantum-light platform.
detailed_summary: A CoFeB/MgO injector supplies spin-polarized electrons to InGaAs/GaAs quantum-dot ensembles, producing circularly polarized photons at zero applied magnetic field without optical pumping. A four-detector, time-tagged Hanbury Brown-Twiss setup resolves one- and two-photon components within individual electrical excitation cycles. Pronounced temporal fluctuations in the two-photon statistics disappear after demagnetizing the injector, tying higher-order emission correlations directly to carrier spin polarization.
main_result: The experiment resolves up to two-photon Fock components and shows that spin polarization controls their higher-order temporal emission statistics.
application_angle: The platform could support electrically driven, spin-programmable single- and multiphoton sources for integrated quantum photonics.

title: Left-Handed Transmission Lines for the Dynamical Casimir Effect
abstract: Left-handed (LH) superconducting transmission lines, built with series capacitors and shunt inductors instead of the series inductors and shunt capacitors of a conventional right-handed (RH) line, have a spectrum with a nonzero lower band edge and modes that become sparse at high frequencies. We study the dynamical Casimir effect in a LH line terminated by a flux-modulated SQUID and compare it with an RH line built from the same elements and with a long coplanar waveguide terminated by the same SQUID. We derive the quantum Hamiltonian and show that the coupling between two modes factorizes into their amplitudes at the SQUID. Together, the LH spectrum and the mode dependence of this coupling determine which modes are populated and how fast. With equal elements, the LH coupling grows with frequency and exceeds the RH one above a crossover pump frequency set by the cell inductance and capacitance, and only the LH line has resonances above the RH band edge. Pumping two modes at once lets a weakly coupled mode borrow coupling from a strongly coupled one, while crossings of resonance lines populate three or four modes without increasing the growth rate. Compared with the coplanar waveguide, the LH line has a similar coupling but keeps the created particles in the target mode, whereas the nearly equidistant waveguide spreads them over many pairs and needs more pump energy.
one_liner: A SQUID-terminated left-handed superconducting line offers selective, high-frequency dynamical Casimir photon generation.
why_it_matters: Its engineered spectrum can concentrate generated microwave photons into chosen modes while accessing resonances unavailable to conventional transmission lines.
detailed_summary: The paper derives the quantum Hamiltonian of a left-handed superconducting transmission line terminated by a flux-modulated SQUID and compares it with right-handed and coplanar-waveguide designs. The coupling factorizes into the participating modes' SQUID amplitudes and, in the left-handed line, grows with frequency and supports resonances above the right-handed band edge. Multimode pumping can transfer strong coupling to weaker modes, while the sparse spectrum suppresses unwanted pair generation.
main_result: The analysis predicts stronger high-frequency coupling and more selective dynamical Casimir photon generation than comparable right-handed or coplanar-waveguide systems.
application_angle: The architecture could provide controllable microwave-photon and correlated-pair sources for superconducting quantum circuits.

title: Entanglement diagnostics of stochastic-resetting steady states: theory and measurement on superconducting qubits
abstract: Stochastic resetting drives quantum systems into nonequilibrium stationary states unreachable under uninterrupted unitary evolution, and their entanglement depends on whether the reset history is resolved or averaged over. We study this interplay in the transverse-field Ising chain, deriving closed-form results for two qubits and evaluating chains of up to 12 qubits exactly. In the two-qubit system, these closed-form results show that phase matching between energy eigenstates produces resonances, and their visibility in the stationary state is determined by the symmetry of the reset state. Measurements on an IBM superconducting processor show the entropies evaluated before and after the reset average closely following noiseless predictions with no fitted parameter, while concurrence lies below prediction across most of the hardware measurements. The two diagnostics respond differently because they read different components of the same reconstructed state, and a depolarizing model captures the concurrence suppression with one fitted parameter. The difference between the two entropies, i. e., the Jensen gap of entanglement entropy, equals the Holevo information that a subsystem retains about the time since the last reset. With a Bell-state reset, this information grows with chain length across a half-chain cut over the sizes studied, without visible saturation at the smaller reset probabilities. Since reset times are sampled and recorded classically, the trajectory-averaged entropy, and with it the Jensen gap, is obtained without postselection, in contrast to monitored circuits, where trajectory-resolved entanglement requires sampling exponentially rare measurement records.
one_liner: IBM superconducting-qubit measurements test entanglement and retained timing information in stochastic-reset nonequilibrium steady states.
why_it_matters: The protocol makes trajectory-averaged entanglement information experimentally accessible without exponentially costly postselection.
detailed_summary: The study derives two-qubit closed-form results and exact calculations through 12-site transverse-field Ising chains subject to stochastic resetting. IBM processor measurements reproduce predicted pre- and post-reset entropies without fitted parameters, although concurrence is suppressed and is captured by a one-parameter depolarizing model. The entropy Jensen gap equals the Holevo information retained by a subsystem about time since reset and grows across studied half-chain cuts for Bell-state resets.
