main_result: Hardware measurements validate entropy diagnostics of stochastic-reset steady states and extract trajectory information without postselection.
application_angle: Recorded reset histories provide a practical route to probing nonequilibrium entanglement and memory effects on programmable quantum processors.

title: Comparison of entangling strategies for unitary synthesis
abstract: Trapped-ion quantum computers are promising as a platform for realizing quantum computational advantage. They promise long coherence times, near all-to-all connectivity, and potential multiqubit gates as distinguishing advantages compared to competing platforms. Regarding these advantages, it is crucial to understand the trade-offs between increasing engineering complexity and actual improvements in running quantum algorithms with a more flexible gate set. In this work, we investigate this question and develop a versatile toolset to evaluate the performance of gate sets composed of native Mølmer--Sørensen multiqubit gates. To this end, we employ unitary synthesis as an application-agnostic benchmark target and identify specific hardware requirements for multiqubit gates to be advantageous.
one_liner: A unitary-synthesis benchmark identifies when native multiqubit Mølmer–Sørensen gates outperform simpler trapped-ion entangling strategies.
why_it_matters: The framework connects added gate-control complexity to measurable algorithm-level benefits, helping trapped-ion designers prioritize useful multiqubit capabilities.
detailed_summary: The authors develop an application-agnostic framework for comparing trapped-ion gate sets built from native multiqubit Mølmer–Sørensen interactions. Using unitary synthesis as the benchmark, they evaluate trade-offs between flexible entangling operations and their additional engineering burden. The analysis identifies hardware requirements under which multiqubit gates provide a genuine synthesis advantage.
main_result: The study establishes specific hardware conditions required for native multiqubit Mølmer–Sørensen gates to improve unitary synthesis.
application_angle: The results can guide gate-set selection and control-stack investment for trapped-ion processors targeting lower compilation overhead.

title: Renormalization for Robust Memory without Synchronization
abstract: Local error correction can preserve classical information against noise, but protection under synchronized updates need not survive when sites evolve at independent random times. Establishing stability is particularly challenging when protection relies on the collective action of competing local rules. Here we develop a spacetime renormalization framework that reveals how independently acting local updates can collectively stabilize memory. We identify sufficient conditions under which the geometry of stable interfaces and suppression of defect propagation produce reliable erosion at large scales. Applying this framework, we prove stability of the asynchronous \textsf{R} squeezing code and introduce robust processes in two and three dimensions. In these systems, both encoded phases persist under sufficiently weak noise, even when the noise favors one phase. Our results provide a criterion for designing autonomous memories sustained by competing local stochastic dynamics.
one_liner: A spacetime-renormalization framework proves that autonomous local dynamics can preserve encoded memory without synchronized updates.
why_it_matters: It supplies design criteria for robust autonomous memories whose components update asynchronously, as real distributed hardware often must.
detailed_summary: The work develops a spacetime-renormalization method for memories governed by independently timed local updates. Stable interfaces and suppressed defect propagation are shown to yield reliable large-scale erosion of errors. The framework proves stability of the asynchronous R squeezing code and supports robust two- and three-dimensional processes, even under weak phase-biased noise.
main_result: Both encoded phases remain stable under sufficiently weak noise without requiring synchronized local updates.
application_angle: The criteria offer a route to designing autonomous error-correcting hardware that tolerates timing disorder and biased noise.

title: Gapless and Non-Equilibrium Topology in Blockaded Ladders
abstract: We propose a multi-leg PXYP model as a minimal setting to explore constraint-induced intertwinement between itinerant and internal degrees of freedom. We argue that the Rydberg-like blockade induces correlations in squeezed space, providing a unified mechanism for nontrivial string order both in and out of equilibrium. In a two-leg geometry, this leads to an intrinsically gapless topological ground state, which can terminate at a supersymmetric multicritical point. This mechanism also leads to the preservation of string order for parametrically long times after a quench, which we verify using tensor network simulations and a classical stochastic approximation to the dynamics. In a three-leg geometry, the blockade leads to an additional emergent $U(1)$ symmetry, resulting in a multicomponent Luttinger liquid where both itinerant and internal degrees of freedom are critical. This family of models arises naturally in a range of quantum simulator platforms such as Rydberg tweezer arrays and dipolar atoms in optical lattices.
one_liner: Blockade-constrained ladder models host gapless topology, long-lived post-quench string order, and emergent multicomponent criticality.
why_it_matters: The predicted phases and dynamics arise naturally in programmable Rydberg and dipolar-atom simulators, offering accessible targets for topology experiments.
detailed_summary: A multi-leg PXYP model is introduced to study how blockade constraints intertwine itinerant and internal degrees of freedom. Two-leg ladders exhibit an intrinsically gapless topological ground state and parametrically long-lived string order after a quench, supported by tensor-network and stochastic simulations. Three-leg ladders acquire an emergent U(1) symmetry and form a multicomponent Luttinger liquid.
main_result: Blockade constraints generate gapless topological order, persistent nonequilibrium string order, and multicomponent criticality in ladder geometries.
application_angle: The model provides experimentally programmable protocols for probing constrained topology and long-lived order in neutral-atom quantum simulators.

title: Singlet-Triplet Transition of Rotating Moiré Atoms in a Magnetic Field
abstract: Moiré superlattices can bind several electrons to each potential minimum, forming few-electron "moiré atoms." Using neural quantum states that obey magnetic periodic boundary conditions, include full Landau-level mixing, and treat both spin sectors, we map the ground state of two-electron moiré atoms in a superlattice as a function of moiré depth and magnetic field strength. At strong field each atom is a spin-triplet maximum-density droplet with canonical angular momentum $\langle L_z\rangle=-1$ and a persistent circulating current: the rotating counterpart of the "Wigner molecular crystal" recently imaged in moiré superlattices. Deepening the wells drives a singlet-triplet transition to non-rotating spin-singlet atoms whose only current is a weak diamagnetic counter-circulation. The transition moves to deeper wells as the field grows, so depth and field together open a window for the formation of rotors. This is the collective analog of the singlet-triplet transition of two-electron quantum dots. At the transition, the orbital magnetic moments of the atoms reverse sign as their spin polarization switches, a joint signature accessible to magnetometry. If the atoms are instead polarized by other means, such as magnetic proximity coupling, the rotors lock at weak field into a spontaneously ordered crystal of dimers in a pinwheel pattern.
one_liner: Two-electron moiré atoms switch between rotating triplet droplets and nonrotating singlets, reversing their orbital magnetic moments.
why_it_matters: The predicted magnetic-moment reversal gives magnetometry a direct signature of spin and orbital transitions in moiré quantum matter.
detailed_summary: Neural quantum states with magnetic periodic boundaries and full Landau-level mixing are used to map two-electron moiré atoms versus well depth and magnetic field. Strong fields favor spin-triplet maximum-density droplets with angular momentum −1 and persistent circulating current, while deeper wells produce nonrotating spin singlets. At the transition, spin polarization changes and the orbital magnetic moment reverses sign; proximity-polarized rotors may also form a pinwheel dimer crystal.
main_result: The calculations predict a field- and depth-controlled singlet–triplet transition accompanied by reversal of circulating current and orbital magnetic moment.
application_angle: Local magnetometry could detect the transition and characterize correlated spin-orbital states in moiré materials.

title: Relating approaches to interacting quantum clocks and systems
abstract: The problem of describing the dynamics of quantum systems relative to quantum clocks with which they interact is relevant to the physics of quantum reference frames and quantum gravity alike. There have been different approaches that derive a relational time-dependent Schrödinger equation for the system relative to the clock from a time-independent Hamiltonian constraint. We show that some of these approaches, due to Smith and Ahmadi, Gemsheim and Rost, as well as the so-called Born-Oppenheimer approach, can be unified in a single framework for describing conditional quantum states. In particular, the Born-Oppenheimer approach to quantum cosmology is seen to correspond to a type of interacting Page-Wootters formalism. We discuss the issue of unitarity and linearity, or lack thereof, in the relational dynamics, and we conclude with a brief outlook to further developments.
one_liner: Several formalisms for quantum systems interacting with quantum clocks are unified through conditional quantum states.
why_it_matters: The unified treatment clarifies when relational dynamics is linear and unitary, foundational requirements for operational quantum-clock protocols.
detailed_summary: The paper places the Smith–Ahmadi, Gemsheim–Rost, and Born–Oppenheimer approaches within one conditional-state framework. It shows that the Born–Oppenheimer treatment of quantum cosmology can be interpreted as an interacting Page–Wootters construction. The analysis highlights conditions under which the resulting relational Schrödinger dynamics loses linearity or unitarity.
main_result: Distinct relational-time approaches are shown to be instances of a common conditional-state formalism, with their unitarity and linearity properties exposed.
application_angle: The framework can support consistent modeling of interacting quantum clocks and reference systems used in precision timing and foundational tests.

title: Fock-space delocalization and its control in scarred-vs-ergodic dynamics
abstract: Quantum many-body scarred dynamics in Rydberg-atom arrays is characterized by revivals, in which the system repeatedly returns to its initial state despite its many-body complexity. But how extensively does the wave function explore the space of allowed configurations between revivals? We address this question by quantifying the fraction of configurations occupied during PXP dynamics initialized from the paradigmatic polarized and Néel states, which respectively exhibit thermalizing and scarred dynamics. Despite their striking revivals, dynamics from the Néel state spreads over exponentially many configurations, yet occupies a vanishing fraction of the full space in the thermodynamic limit. Dynamics from the polarized state, by contrast, occupies a finite fraction of the configuration space, close to anticoncentration and random-state statistics, although chiral symmetry limits this fraction to one third. A weak quasiperiodic field enables the polarized state to occupy half of the configuration space by lifting the constraint imposed by chiral symmetry. The Néel state, however, requires a stronger field to reach a comparable anticoncentrated regime. As the field increases further, the occupied fraction decreases for both initial states, revealing a nonmonotonic dependence of Fock-space delocalization on field strength without necessarily implying localization.
one_liner: Rydberg-array scarred and thermalizing states show sharply different, field-tunable exploration of constrained Fock space.
why_it_matters: Fock-space occupancy provides a hardware-accessible diagnostic for separating scarred, ergodic, symmetry-limited, and field-controlled dynamics.
detailed_summary: The study quantifies the fraction of allowed configurations explored by PXP dynamics from polarized and Néel initial states. Scarred Néel dynamics reaches exponentially many configurations but a vanishing fraction of Fock space, whereas polarized dynamics approaches random-state statistics over a finite fraction limited to one third by chiral symmetry. A weak quasiperiodic field lifts that constraint to one half for the polarized state, while stronger fields are needed for the Néel state and eventually reduce occupancy for both.
platform_or_system: Rydberg-atom array implementing the PXP model
main_result: Initial state and quasiperiodic-field strength jointly control whether constrained dynamics remains sparse, symmetry-limited, or anticoncentrated in Fock space.
application_angle: The diagnostic can help benchmark controllable ergodicity, scar dynamics, and state-space coverage in programmable neutral-atom processors.

title: Benchmarking One-Dimensional Quantum Lattice Boltzmann Methods on Quantum Hardware
abstract: Classical computational fluid dynamics (CFD) methods encounter significant computational bottlenecks in large systems and at high Reynolds number flows due to the rapid increase in degrees of freedom, even on flagship supercomputers. As quantum computers emerge, the Quantum Lattice Boltzmann Method (QLBM) has been proposed as a quantum-native alternative for solving fluid dynamics problems. However, until recently, nearly all studies have relied on classical quantum simulators rather than real quantum hardware. This study presents a benchmark of a one-dimensional QLBM implementation executed on three different IBM Quantum hardware. We design and test a quantum circuit for the advection-diffusion equation using amplitude encoding, a Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook (BGK)-type collision operator, and a streaming step with periodic boundary conditions. Our numerical experiments evaluate transpiled two-qubit gate count, total circuit depth, runtime, and accuracy metrics including maximum absolute error ($L_\infty$ norm) and root-mean-square error (RMSE). We find that the present collision and streaming operators dominate the overall cost and become the primary scalability bottleneck on current hardware. To mitigate the prohibitive cost of full quantum state tomography on hardware-based benchmarking exercises, we introduce a sampler-based measurement strategy that reconstructs macroscopic density fields directly from computational-basis measurements. This approach substantially reduces measurement overhead while preserving the expected advection-diffusion dynamics on hardware. These results provide a quantitative assessment of QLBM performance in the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) regime and identify the principal algorithmic and experimental limitations that must be addressed for QLBM to become viable for fluid dynamics.
one_liner: A one-dimensional quantum lattice Boltzmann solver is benchmarked across three IBM quantum processors for advection-diffusion dynamics.
why_it_matters: The hardware data expose collision and streaming circuits as key scaling bottlenecks while demonstrating a lower-overhead alternative to full state tomography.
detailed_summary: The authors implement a one-dimensional quantum lattice Boltzmann circuit with amplitude encoding, a BGK-type collision operator, periodic streaming, and execution on three IBM quantum processors. They quantify two-qubit gates, circuit depth, runtime, maximum error, and RMSE, finding that collision and streaming dominate resource costs. A sampler-based readout reconstructs macroscopic density fields from computational-basis measurements without full state tomography.
main_result: Real-hardware QLBM runs reproduce expected advection-diffusion behavior while identifying collision and streaming as the dominant NISQ bottlenecks.
application_angle: The benchmark clarifies which circuit and measurement improvements are needed before quantum fluid-dynamics solvers can become practically competitive.

title: Colloquium: Quantum information processing with ensembles of identical particles
abstract: Identical particles underpin most quantum technologies, but the role of indistinguishability in these processes extends far beyond the symmetrization of many-particle states. This Colloquium presents a unified operational perspective on how particle identity, indistinguishability, exchange statistics, and many-particle interference can instead be harnessed as resources for quantum information processing. We first clarify the notions of entanglement and indistinguishability for identical particles, emphasizing their dependence on the accessible measurements and information. We then review how spatial overlap, multiparticle interference, and path identity enable the generation, extraction, protection, and distillation of coherence and entanglement. Their applications to quantum metrology and imaging, state discrimination, teleportation, entanglement swapping, and quantum cloning are examined. Finally, we discuss the thermodynamic role of indistinguishability, from the Gibbs paradox to quantum thermal machines and statistics-driven engines. Across these settings, indistinguishability emerges as a controllable, task-dependent resource whose benefits are determined by state preparation, exchange statistics, interference, and measurement constraints.
one_liner: This Colloquium frames particle indistinguishability and exchange statistics as controllable resources for quantum information tasks.
why_it_matters: It unifies how identical-particle interference can support metrology, imaging, state discrimination, teleportation, and entanglement processing.
detailed_summary: The review develops an operational account of identity, indistinguishability, exchange statistics, and entanglement under realistic measurement constraints. It surveys spatial overlap, path identity, and multiparticle interference as tools for generating, protecting, extracting, and distilling coherence and entanglement. Applications span quantum metrology and imaging, state discrimination, teleportation, entanglement swapping, cloning, and quantum thermodynamics.
main_result: The article establishes a unified task-dependent framework for exploiting indistinguishability across quantum information processing, sensing, and thermodynamics.
application_angle: The framework helps experimentalists identify when particle overlap and accessible measurements can improve sensing or communication protocols.

title: Clifford synthesis is NP-complete
abstract: We show that the problem of synthesizing a quantum circuit for a given Clifford operator using at most a specified amount of resources is NP-complete for several resource models of practical interest. Specifically, we study synthesis of a given Clifford operator using single-qubit Clifford gates and two-qubit Clifford gates, with full qubit connectivity and no additional ancilla qubits. With single-qubit gates free and CNOT as the only two-qubit gate, we show that deciding whether a given target admits an implementation using at most a specified number of CNOT gates is NP-complete, and we show that the problem remains NP-complete when any two-qubit Clifford gate is allowed and the budget counts all such gates. Moreover, we show that both results continue to hold when SWAP gates may be inserted for free, and when single-qubit gates are also considered part of the budget. In each case, we build on recent work by Li and Guan and show that there are polynomial-time reductions from Hamiltonian path in grid graphs to these decision problems, using a number of qubits quadratic in the number of grid vertices.
one_liner: Resource-bounded synthesis of Clifford circuits is proved NP-complete under several practically relevant gate-cost models.
why_it_matters: The result establishes fundamental limits on exact gate-count optimization even with full connectivity and free single-qubit or SWAP operations.
detailed_summary: The paper proves NP-completeness of deciding whether a target Clifford operator can be synthesized within a specified CNOT or two-qubit Clifford gate budget. The results assume full connectivity and no ancillary qubits and remain valid when SWAP gates are free or single-qubit gates count toward the budget. The reductions originate from Hamiltonian paths in grid graphs and use a quadratic number of qubits.
main_result: Exact resource-optimal Clifford synthesis is NP-complete across multiple gate models relevant to quantum compilation.
application_angle: Compiler and hardware teams should expect scalable exact optimization to require restricted instances, approximations, or heuristic synthesis methods.

title: Metadevices that compute: mathematical foundations and experimental implementations for neuromorphic nanophotonics
abstract: Wave-based analog computing has re-emerged as a compelling alternative to digital electronics for specific linear-algebraic and machine-learning workloads, promising massively parallel, high-bandwidth, and energy-efficient information processing. Metamaterials, metasurfaces, and integrated metastructures (collectively, metadevices) now perform mathematical operations, solve integral and differential equations, multiply matrices, and implement trainable photonic neural networks directly in the wave domain. This focused review consolidates the mathematical foundations that underpin such devices, i.e., the mapping between linear operators and wave scattering, the feedback architectures that realize equation inversion, and the inverse-design and scientific machine-learning toolchains that make their synthesis and training tractable, and connects them to the rapidly growing body of experimental demonstrations, from free-space diffractive processors to reconfigurable guided-wave metastructures. We conclude with open problems and opportunities for this emerging neuromorphic nanophotonics ecosystem.
one_liner: A focused review connects wave-scattering mathematics and inverse design to experimentally realized neuromorphic photonic metadevices.
why_it_matters: It consolidates architectures for high-bandwidth, energy-efficient analog computation from free-space processors to reconfigurable integrated metastructures.
detailed_summary: The review maps linear operators, matrix operations, and equation solving onto wave scattering in metamaterials, metasurfaces, and integrated metastructures. It explains feedback architectures for equation inversion and design workflows based on inverse methods and scientific machine learning. Experimental implementations range from free-space diffractive processors to trainable and reconfigurable guided-wave systems.
main_result: The article provides a unified mathematical and experimental foundation for metadevices that execute analog linear algebra and neuromorphic workloads.
application_angle: These architectures could accelerate specialized signal-processing and machine-learning tasks with massive optical parallelism and reduced energy consumption.

title: Optical Quantum Memory Processing for Quantum Hashing
abstract: Sender authentication is an important requirement for secure quantum communication networks. We propose programmable photon-echo quantum memory processing of a multi-time-bin photonic qudit for implementing a quantum-hash-based verification protocol. In this approach, using QM, sender (Alice) generates a quantum hash state by transforming a single stored photonic wave packet into the programmable photonic qudit. Bob's memory coherently maps the received time-bin photonic qudit into a single output mode according to phase encoding. Our scheme relies on a time-resolved coherent detection method introduced here, in which the coherent responses from individual time-bins are sequentially accumulated within Bob's spin coherence prior to the final sender verification. The key advantage of this coherent detection for quantum hashing is shown, and its potential applications are also discussed. The performed analysis demonstrates that experimentally verified parameters of contemporary optical quantum memories enable a proof of principle realization of the proposed architecture. These results reveal an additional role for quantum memories, serving not only as synchronization and repeater resources for long-distance quantum communication, but also as active elements for quantum hashing in conventional quantum key distribution systems.
one_liner: Programmable photon-echo memories are proposed as active processors for quantum-hash authentication using multi-time-bin photonic qudits.
why_it_matters: The scheme extends quantum memories beyond storage and synchronization by using coherent time-bin accumulation for sender verification in quantum networks.
detailed_summary: Alice's programmable photon-echo memory transforms a stored single-photon wave packet into a multi-time-bin quantum hash state. Bob's memory coherently accumulates phase-dependent responses from successive time bins in a spin coherence before mapping them to one output mode for verification. Analysis using experimentally demonstrated memory parameters indicates that a proof-of-principle implementation is feasible.
main_result: The proposed memory-processing architecture enables coherent quantum-hash verification of multi-time-bin photonic qudits with contemporary device parameters.
application_angle: Active memory-based authentication could be integrated into QKD and future repeater networks without requiring a separate photonic processing stage.

title: Characteristics of VHF and UHF band detection using Stark shifting in Rydberg-atom sensors
abstract: We present a characterization of the sensitivity of broadband electric field measurements in the Very High Frequency (VHF) and Ultra High Frequency (UHF) bands using AC stark shifting of Rydberg states. The dependence of the sensitivity and dynamic range of the field measurements using nD5/2 states of cesium for principal quantum numbers n= 60, 70, 80, 90 and 100 is presented, detailing the intricacies involved. The frequencies considered for the measurement range from 50 MHz to 900 MHz for which a transverse electromagnetic (TEM) cell is used to excite the Rydberg atoms with the RF fields. The corresponding sensitivities achieved are in the $(μV/m)/\sqrt{Hz}$ range. A general trend of better sensitivity for higher principal quantum numbers is observed. This work paves the way for a better understanding of the AC Stark dependent field measurements using Rydberg sensors.
one_liner: Cesium Rydberg sensors achieve broadband VHF-to-UHF electric-field detection through AC Stark shifts of high-lying nD states.
why_it_matters: The measurements quantify sensitivity and dynamic-range tradeoffs from 50 to 900 MHz, reaching microvolt-per-meter-per-root-hertz sensitivity.
detailed_summary: The experiment probes cesium nD5/2 Rydberg states with principal quantum numbers from 60 to 100 inside a TEM cell driven between 50 and 900 MHz. AC Stark shifts provide broadband electric-field measurements with sensitivities in the microvolt-per-meter-per-root-hertz range. Higher principal quantum numbers generally improve sensitivity, while the study also characterizes associated dynamic-range behavior.
main_result: AC-Stark-based Rydberg electrometry delivers broadband 50–900 MHz detection with microvolt-per-meter-per-root-hertz sensitivity and improved response at higher n.
application_angle: The approach supports atom-based calibration and sensitive broadband RF detection across communication, spectrum-monitoring, and electromagnetic-measurement bands.

title: Comparison of melanin subtypes using pump-probe microscopy
abstract: Pump-probe microscopy (PPM) is used to probe excited state dynamics of endogenous chromophores to generate contrast that is unavailable in traditional forms of microscopy. Here we apply PPM to characterize melanin, a pigment central to photoprotection, skin and eye pigmentation, and melanoma pathogenesis. Melanin is notoriously difficult to analyze due to its structural and chemical complexity. We imaged melanin from six different lesion categories: cutaneous nevi, lentigo, cutaneous malignant melanoma, conjunctival melanocytic lesions, vulvar melanocytic lesions, and a murine melanoma model, across 21 independent biological samples and 109 regions of interest. Using model fitting, adapted phasor analysis, and support vector machine classification, we characterize and quantify excited-state dynamics as a surrogate for chemical and structural heterogeneity. Heterogeneity of melanin separates cutaneous from non-cutaneous lesions, but is not correlated with malignancy. Benign lentigo is the most heterogeneous population in the dataset, exceeding cutaneous malignant melanoma, while conjunctival lesions are the most homogeneous despite receiving direct solar exposure. Classification on full transient absorption curves separates most subtypes well above the six-class chance level. These findings demonstrate the ability of PPM to reveal subtle differences in melanin photophysics across diverse tissue environments, with implications for optical tissue classification and the understanding of melanoma pathogenesis.
one_liner: Pump-probe microscopy distinguishes melanin photophysics across six lesion categories using transient dynamics and machine learning.
why_it_matters: Label-free excited-state contrast could support optical tissue classification while revealing that melanin heterogeneity tracks tissue environment rather than malignancy.
detailed_summary: The study analyzes 21 biological samples and 109 regions of interest spanning six melanocytic lesion categories. Model fitting, adapted phasor analysis, and support vector machines quantify and classify melanin excited-state dynamics from full transient-absorption curves. Melanin heterogeneity separates cutaneous from non-cutaneous tissue but does not correlate with malignancy in this dataset.
main_result: Transient-absorption signatures classified most melanin subtypes above six-class chance and exposed tissue-dependent photophysical heterogeneity.
application_angle: The method offers label-free contrast for tissue classification and mechanistic studies of melanin in melanoma pathogenesis.

title: Microscopic Theory of Spin-Orbit Interactions of Light
abstract: Optical spin-orbit interactions (SOI), demonstrated experimentally in optical cavities, enable the polarization degrees of freedom of light to be described and controlled as an effective pseudospin, providing a foundation for spintronic-like control of light and the development of next-generation optical technologies. However, prior works describe this emergent effect using phenomenological models that fail to uncover its microscopic quantum origins, and as a result, a rigorous connection between material electronic structure and the optical SOI remains elusive. In this work, we address this fundamental challenge by developing a microscopic quantum theory starting from the non-relativistic quantum electrodynamical (QED) description of light-matter interactions. We show that this effect arises from virtual interactions between confined photons and material excitations. Crucially, our theoretical framework provides microscopic material-design principles for tuning the distinct components of optical SOI, which include the optical birefringence, photonic self-energies, TE-TM splitting, and optical Zeeman splitting, enabling precise engineering of effective magnetic fields, diabolical points, and pseudospin textures. We anticipate that the predictive capability of our microscopic theory will enable systematic screening and design of material systems for photonic spintronics and optical technologies.
one_liner: A microscopic QED theory links optical spin-orbit interactions in cavities to virtual photon–material-excitation processes.
why_it_matters: The framework converts material electronic structure into actionable design rules for photonic pseudospins, effective fields, and spintronic-like optical devices.
detailed_summary: Starting from non-relativistic QED, the authors derive optical spin-orbit interactions from virtual coupling between confined photons and material excitations. The theory resolves microscopic contributions to birefringence, photonic self-energies, TE-TM splitting, and optical Zeeman splitting. It also provides material-level parameters for engineering effective magnetic fields, diabolical points, and pseudospin textures.
main_result: The work derives optical spin-orbit coupling microscopically and establishes design principles connecting electronic structure to photonic pseudospin Hamiltonians.
application_angle: The theory can guide material screening and cavity design for polarization control, photonic spintronics, and pseudospin-based optical sensing.

title: Preparation of a Laughlin-like fractional Chern insulator on a superconducting quantum processor
abstract: Fractional Chern insulators (FCIs) are lattice analogues of fractional quantum Hall states, hosting topological order and fractionalized anyonic excitations. Their realization poses a demanding target for quantum simulation. Here, we realize a bosonic FCI on an IBM Nighthawk superconducting quantum processor using classically optimized variational circuits. We target a Laughlin-like state that is an exact zero-energy ground state of a long-range parent Hamiltonian on a torus, eliminating physical edges and providing a favorable geometry for accessing fractional quantum Hall physics in a small system. On a $4\times4$ qubit lattice, we prepare both the four-boson FCI ground state and a three-boson state hosting two quasiholes. Measurements of particle densities and correlations reproduce the characteristic structure of the target states, while reconstructed chiral magnetization currents resolve the circulating current pattern associated with the quasiholes. The preparation of these strongly correlated topological states with shallow circuits establishes a route toward the digital simulation and manipulation of fractionalized excitations, including measurements of topological invariants and anyonic braiding.
one_liner: A 4×4 superconducting-qubit processor prepares a Laughlin-like fractional Chern insulator and a two-quasihole state.
why_it_matters: The experiment brings fractionalized topological states and quasihole-current observables within reach of shallow-circuit digital quantum simulation.
detailed_summary: Classically optimized variational circuits prepare a four-boson FCI ground state on a 4×4 IBM Nighthawk qubit lattice with toroidal geometry. The processor also prepares a three-boson state containing two quasiholes. Density and correlation measurements reproduce target-state structure, while reconstructed chiral magnetization currents reveal circulation associated with the quasiholes.
main_result: Shallow circuits prepared Laughlin-like FCI and quasihole states whose correlations and reconstructed chiral currents matched their expected topological structure.
application_angle: The approach supports future digital studies of topological invariants, fractionalized excitations, and anyonic manipulation or braiding.

title: Vacuum amplification across a programmable bosonic Bogoliubov stability boundary in a trapped-ion chain
abstract: A quantum oscillator always carries vacuum fluctuations, and modulating its parameters converts them into correlated pairs of real quanta. This vacuum amplification underlies squeezed light and Hawking radiation. In a closed quadratic system, pair creation competes with the energy splitting of the modes, and growth turns exponential only once pairing overcomes the splitting. Here we realize this competition in two motional modes of a trapped-ion chain. A two-mode-squeezing drive creates the pairs, and a beam-splitter coupling splits the motion into two coupled modes at different frequencies. The two rates are tuned and calibrated independently. Starting near the motional ground state, we cross the stability boundary in two ways. First, with the drive at the sum of the two bare-mode frequencies, the phonon number stays bounded until the pairing rate exceeds the splitting and grows exponentially beyond it. Second, tuning the drive into resonance with one coupled mode lowers the threshold to zero, and only that mode is amplified into a squeezed vacuum. Separate control of the two interactions makes the threshold for vacuum amplification programmable. This control can be used to simulate particle creation and quantum phase transitions, and to operate parametrically driven bosonic devices close to their stability limit.
one_liner: A trapped-ion chain crosses a programmable bosonic stability boundary and amplifies motional vacuum fluctuations into phonon pairs.
why_it_matters: Independent control of squeezing and mode splitting enables tunable studies of particle creation, critical dynamics, and near-threshold bosonic devices.
detailed_summary: Two motional modes in a trapped-ion chain are coupled through independently calibrated two-mode-squeezing and beam-splitter interactions. At the bare-mode sum frequency, phonon occupation remains bounded until pairing exceeds the mode splitting, after which it grows exponentially. Resonating with one coupled mode reduces the threshold to zero and selectively generates a squeezed vacuum in that mode.
main_result: The experiment programmably shifted and crossed the Bogoliubov stability threshold, demonstrating bounded dynamics, exponential pair growth, and mode-selective squeezing.
application_angle: This controllable bosonic simulator can probe particle-creation analogues and quantum phase transitions or benchmark parametric devices near instability.

title: Quantum Advantage in Beam-Displacement Estimation for Inter-Satellite Quantum-Secure Time Transfer
abstract: In this work, we investigate the practical feasibility of achieving a quantum advantage, in the context of inter-satellite quantum communication, of satellite position estimation. The investigation focuses on a quantum-enhanced scheme in which squeezing is added to the derivative mode of a Gaussian probe beam as a means of estimating photon-beam displacement. The performance of the scheme is compared against the standard quantum limit achieved by an optimal classical beam-displacement estimation scheme under a fair same-total-energy constraint. We find that although the benefit provided by squeezing rapidly diminishes as the inter-satellite distance increases due to diffraction-induced beam spreading and subsequent truncation by the finite receiver aperture, a quantum advantage can still be expected over inter-satellite distances up to approximately 100 km under practical satellite configurations. This distance scale between satellites is anticipated for Starlink-type satellite constellations.
one_liner: Derivative-mode squeezing can improve satellite beam-displacement estimation beyond the classical limit over links approaching 100 km.
why_it_matters: It identifies a practical operating range where quantum-enhanced pointing estimation could strengthen inter-satellite secure time-transfer systems.
detailed_summary: The proposed scheme adds squeezing to the derivative spatial mode of a Gaussian probe and estimates transverse beam displacement under a fixed total-energy constraint. It is compared with an optimal classical estimator at the standard quantum limit. Modeling diffraction, beam spreading, and finite-aperture truncation predicts a diminishing but persistent quantum advantage out to approximately 100 km for practical configurations.
main_result: The analysis predicts quantum-enhanced beam-displacement estimation over inter-satellite separations of up to roughly 100 km despite diffraction and aperture loss.
application_angle: Improved relative-position sensing could aid beam pointing and quantum-secure clock synchronization in satellite constellations.

title: Intensity-Domain Demultiplexing of Orbital Angular Momentum Channels for Optical Communication
abstract: Orbital angular momentum (OAM) multiplexing has been limited in practice by the complexity and optical loss of the elements that separate the channels at the receiver side. Here we adopt the azimuthal harmonics of OAM petal patterns as the demultiplexing basis, which makes the receiver the optical counterpart of the circular antenna arrays used in radio OAM links: the petal pattern of topological charge $\ell$ carries a single azimuthal harmonic of order $2\ell$, so one Fourier transform of the azimuthal intensity profile returns every channel, without gratings or mode sorters. The petals are formed by projecting a vector vortex beam from a single q-plate onto a linear polarization. A two-channel system at 515 nm with a 16-position circular photoreceiver array reaches 5.2 Gb/s below the forward error correction threshold, 2.6 Gb/s per channel from a 1.4 GHz photoreceiver.
one_liner: Azimuthal intensity Fourier analysis demultiplexes OAM channels without gratings or conventional spatial-mode sorters.
why_it_matters: A simple, low-loss receiver architecture delivers multi-gigabit OAM communication using a circular detector array and intensity-only processing.
detailed_summary: A q-plate produces vector vortex beams whose linear-polarization projection forms petal patterns carrying an azimuthal harmonic of order 2ℓ. A single Fourier transform of intensity samples from a 16-position circular photoreceiver array separates the multiplexed channels without gratings or mode sorters. The two-channel 515 nm link achieves 5.2 Gb/s, or 2.6 Gb/s per channel, below the forward-error-correction threshold.
main_result: The intensity-domain receiver demultiplexed two OAM channels at an aggregate 5.2 Gb/s below the forward-error-correction threshold.
application_angle: The architecture could reduce receiver loss and complexity in free-space OAM links while remaining compatible with compact detector arrays.

title: Testing hardware quantum machine learning claims with a null circuit: fill prediction on Binance futures with 129 qubits of an IBM Heron processor
abstract: Quantum processors are now used as feature generators for classical models on tabular data. A circuit encodes each record, the device returns expectation values, and a classical model learns from them. A recent report claimed large gains from such features, gains that appeared only on noisy hardware. These claims are hard to check, because a quantum device is not a static function. Its state changes from job to job and from one calibration to the next, and that drift can leak information about the outcome into the features. We propose a five-step protocol for testing claims of this kind. It runs a circuit that carries no data in the same jobs as the real one. It checks whether the hardware leaves a recognizable mark on each job. It compares random and natural assignments of records to jobs, replays the null results under other submission orders, and closes the leak with a job-purged backtest. We apply it, pre-registered, to the HSBC and IBM study of fill probabilities in bond trading, which reported a large hardware-only gain. We use a public analog task and run the study's circuit on a 129-qubit chain of an IBM Heron processor. Under controlled assignment the hardware features give no gain over classical features, and the device reproduces the ideal features about as well as shot noise allows. Yet every job carries a distinct fingerprint. A circuit with no data at all predicts fills well above chance when records are batched by outcome and the same job sits on both sides of the train/test split. Removing that overlap removes the effect. The protocol costs under an hour of processor time and is designed for any hardware feature or kernel pipeline on tabular data.
one_liner: A null-circuit audit reveals job-dependent leakage that can create spurious quantum machine-learning gains on a 129-qubit IBM Heron processor.
why_it_matters: The protocol offers a low-cost way to distinguish genuine hardware-enabled learning from calibration drift and train-test leakage in quantum feature pipelines.
detailed_summary: The authors pre-register and apply a five-step validation protocol to an analog of a reported hardware-only advantage in fill prediction. Controlled record assignment yields no improvement from quantum features, while null circuits expose distinct job fingerprints that predict labels when outcome-correlated jobs overlap training and test sets. Job-purged backtesting removes the apparent advantage, and the complete audit uses under one hour of processor time.
main_result: The study shows that job-dependent hardware fingerprints, rather than useful quantum features, can produce apparent predictive gains that vanish under job-purged evaluation.
application_angle: The audit can be incorporated into tabular-data quantum kernel and feature-generation experiments before operational or financial value is claimed.

title: Dual-rate optical frequency comb based on a cylindrical microresonator with a nanoscale radius variation
abstract: We theoretically find that a cylindrical microresonator with nanoscale radius variation can be a source of coherent microcombs with two repetition rates, independently controlled by the device geometry. This phenomenon arises from the formation of two-dimensional axial-azimuthal dissipative Kerr solitons (2D DKS), which we discovered through numerical simulations of the nonlinearly coupled Lugiato-Lefever equations with realistic microresonator device parameters. We demonstrate that, despite the variation in the dispersion characteristics of azimuthal modes at different axial numbers, the spontaneous synchronization mechanism leads to a unified soliton repetition rate. We consider near-parabolic variations in the radius of a cylindrical resonator, compatible with the surface nanoscale axial photonics (SNAP) platform. In our example, we generate 2D DKS with an azimuthal rate of approximately 329 GHz and an axial rate of 6 GHz, which can be adjusted on demand by selecting the appropriate resonator geometry, thereby promising compact sources of frequency combs operating simultaneously across different frequency scales.
one_liner: A SNAP-compatible cylindrical microresonator is predicted to generate coherent Kerr microcombs with independently engineered axial and azimuthal repetition rates.
why_it_matters: Dual-rate comb generation in one compact resonator could connect widely separated frequency scales without requiring multiple synchronized comb sources.
detailed_summary: Numerical solutions of coupled Lugiato-Lefever equations predict two-dimensional axial-azimuthal dissipative Kerr solitons in a cylindrical resonator with nanoscale radius variation. Spontaneous synchronization produces a common soliton rate despite axial-mode-dependent azimuthal dispersion. A representative geometry gives approximately 329 GHz azimuthal and 6 GHz axial repetition rates, both selectable through resonator design.
main_result: Simulations demonstrate geometry-controlled, coherent dual-rate microcombs with representative repetition rates of about 329 GHz and 6 GHz.
application_angle: The approach could provide compact multi-scale comb sources for spectroscopy, frequency synthesis, communications, and photonic signal processing.

title: Time-Domain Multiplexing for Resource-Efficient Heralded GKP State Preparation
abstract: Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states are key resources for fault-tolerant photonic quantum computing, but their conditional preparation via Gaussian boson sampling involves a trade-off between source count and photon-number resolution. Distributing heralding photons across more measured modes reduces the resolution required per mode, yet increases the number of simultaneously operated squeezed sources in fully squeezed spatial architectures. Here, we show that time-domain multiplexing (TDM) can reduce these physical source requirements while preserving GKP state quality. Using an end-to-end differentiable Bargmann framework, we find that TDM circuits reusing one or two squeezed sources achieve fidelities comparable to fully squeezed spatial circuits across several configurations. Selected nine-mode configurations retain fidelities above 0.95 with one photon heralded in each measured mode, mitigating detector resolution demands without a proportional increase in source count. Loss-aware reoptimization further shows that, under the investigated spatial loss models, two-mode TDM maintains fidelities near 0.80 at 1.0 dB per channel, whereas the corresponding spatial benchmarks fall below 0.60. These results demonstrate that temporal reuse provides an effective architectural route for balancing source overhead, detection demands, and state preparation performance in the presence of optical loss.
one_liner: Time-domain multiplexing reuses one or two squeezed sources to prepare high-fidelity heralded GKP states with reduced source and detector demands.
why_it_matters: Temporal reuse offers a practical route to photonic GKP resources while balancing squeezed-source count, photon-number resolution, and optical-loss tolerance.
detailed_summary: An end-to-end differentiable Bargmann model optimizes time-multiplexed GKP preparation circuits that reuse one or two squeezed sources. Selected nine-mode designs exceed 0.95 fidelity while heralding one photon in every measured mode, easing photon-number-resolution requirements. After loss-aware reoptimization at 1.0 dB per channel, two-mode TDM retains fidelity near 0.80, compared with below 0.60 for the studied spatial benchmarks.
main_result: One- and two-source TDM circuits match spatial-circuit state quality, with selected designs exceeding 0.95 fidelity and showing improved resilience to modeled loss.
application_angle: The architecture can lower the hardware overhead of producing bosonic resource states for fault-tolerant photonic quantum computers.

title: Loss-aware optimization of realistic GKP gid states
abstract: Realistic preparation of Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states, the prime candidates for quantum computation with bosonic systems, is inevitably burdened by photon loss. We show how taking this loss into account can lead to more robust quantum states, thereby diminishing its negative influence. Using GKP squeezing as an operational figure of merit, we formulate a loss-aware optimization procedure based on the ground state representation of GKP states. Numerical simulations for square, hexagonal, and asymmetric GKP states show that the optimal preparation generally requires a different initial grid spacing than that of the desired ideal code state. For symmetric and hexagonal lattices, the optimal parameters asymptotically follow the simple scaling relation. The optimized states exhibit better GKP squeezing and greater resilience to losses. These results provide a simple and experimentally relevant strategy for improving realistic photonic GKP state preparation in the presence of known photon loss.
one_liner: Loss-aware tuning of the initial grid spacing produces photonic GKP states with stronger effective squeezing and improved photon-loss resilience.
why_it_matters: The method supplies a simple preparation adjustment that can improve realistic bosonic-code resources when an experiment's optical loss is known.
detailed_summary: The work optimizes realistic GKP states using operational GKP squeezing rather than fidelity alone. Simulations cover square, hexagonal, and asymmetric lattices and show that the best input grid spacing generally differs from that of the target ideal code state. For symmetric and hexagonal lattices, the optimized parameters approach a simple asymptotic scaling relation and yield states more robust to photon loss.
main_result: Numerical optimization shows that deliberately shifting the prepared grid spacing improves GKP squeezing and loss resilience across several lattice geometries.
application_angle: Known channel or component loss can be incorporated directly into state-preparation settings without changing the target bosonic code.

title: Helper-assisted quantum sensing with low dressed-state leakage
abstract: We study a two-qubit sensing protocol in which only a helper qubit is read out. Calibrated loading and unloading encode a transverse signal in the helper's phase, keep leakage out of a selected dressed-state band small, and return the sensor close to its idle ground state. We derive an information bound for a single sensor whose excitation stays below a prescribed budget, and simulate repeated operation with an uncertain coupling and finite-duration resets in a driven open-system model. At the tested settings, finite measurement records support estimation with infrequent resets. A helper flip at zero coupling, combined with a reversal of the coupling sign, suppresses a static helper offset shared across a record while retaining the signal, at a cost of about 27% of the no-offset information of a plain sequence of equal duration. Under slowly varying noise, averaging each cycle's likelihood over the correct noise law removes most of the added bias, and a wrong noise law can worsen the estimate. A selected directly read sensor with ideal controls and repeated nondemolition verification has the higher information rate. Any practical benefit of avoiding direct readout therefore requires a device-specific disturbance model.
one_liner: A helper-only two-qubit sensing protocol encodes transverse signals with low dressed-state leakage and suppresses record-wide static offsets.
why_it_matters: It clarifies when indirect readout can protect a sensor from measurement disturbance and quantifies the information cost of offset cancellation and resets.
detailed_summary: Calibrated loading and unloading map a transverse signal onto a helper qubit's phase while limiting leakage and returning the sensor near its ground state. A helper flip plus coupling-sign reversal cancels a static helper offset across a record while retaining about 73% of the plain sequence's information. Correct likelihood averaging suppresses bias from slow noise, but direct sensor readout remains faster under ideal controls and nondemolition verification.
main_result: The protocol enables helper-only signal estimation with low leakage and static-offset rejection, although its advantage depends on device-specific direct-readout disturbance.
application_angle: It could support sensors in which direct measurement disrupts the sensing qubit, provided the avoided disturbance outweighs the indirect protocol's information penalty.

title: Real-time BP decoding of a high-rate QEC code
abstract: We present a real-time FPGA decoder for a high-rate $[[512,174,8]]$ 3D product qLDPC code. We construct a circuit-level detector-error model for a compact syndrome-extraction schedule and propose a small parallel ensemble of row-wise serial min-sum decoders with cumulative memory. The decoder matches $\text{BP+OSD-CS}_\text{10}$ accuracy with one core and Relay-BP accuracy with three cores. The FPGA implementation meets the latency budget of neutral-atom and trapped-ion systems. An ASIC implementation would improve the latency, enabling real time decoding even for superconducting systems. At a physical error rate of $p=10^{-3}$, three FPGA devices decode 174 logical qubits with a logical error rate of $5\times10^{-7}$ and effective distance 6. For $p=10^{-4}$, and assuming the number of BP iterations is capped to 30, the decoder's average latency is $5.1\,$\textmu s and its worst-case latency is $97.9\,$\textmu s.
one_liner: An FPGA belief-propagation decoder performs real-time circuit-level decoding for a high-rate [[512,174,8]] 3D product qLDPC code.
why_it_matters: The design combines 174 encoded qubits, competitive decoding accuracy, and hardware latency compatible with neutral-atom and trapped-ion control cycles.
detailed_summary: The decoder uses a compact syndrome-extraction model and a parallel ensemble of row-wise serial min-sum cores with cumulative memory. One core matches BP+OSD-CS10 accuracy, while three cores match Relay-BP performance. At a physical error rate of 10^-3, three FPGAs decode 174 logical qubits at a logical error rate of 5×10^-7; at 10^-4, capped decoding averages 5.1 µs with a 97.9 µs worst case.
platform_or_system: FPGA decoder for a 3D product qLDPC code
main_result: The implementation achieves real-time decoding for neutral-atom and trapped-ion timing budgets while maintaining competitive logical-error performance.
application_angle: It provides a concrete classical-control path for high-rate fault-tolerant processors, with an ASIC version projected to meet superconducting-qubit latency needs.

title: oracq: A Modular Framework for Implementing and Analyzing Quantum Scientific Computing Algorithms
abstract: Quantum algorithms for scientific computing are specified against access models such as block-encodings, sparse oracles, state preparations, and quantum random-access memories. Their concrete realization is deliberately left open, yet it is a research variable that changes both the numerical behavior and the resource cost of the program, so every reported conclusion is attributable to one realization. In this paper, we present oracq, a Python framework that makes this choice a managed and checkable decision. Our claim is linguistic rather than infrastructural. Algorithms are stored as persistent register-level programs whose oracle slots are declared and typed but unimplemented. A separate binding pass links compatible realizations, so one stored algorithm can be re-bound to a gate network, a QRAM-backed table, or compiled reversible arithmetic and compared across them. Typed QRAM resources, a compiler from pure Python numerical formulas to reversible fixed-point circuits, and block-encoding algebra with qubitization and QSVT-style kernels supply the constructions. Two end-to-end workflows exercise the framework, a quantum finite-volume pipeline for the compressible Euler equations and a quantum homotopy-analysis pipeline that lifts nonlinear PDEs to composable linear input models. The verification methodology separates implementation error from method error, and logical resource accounts cover programs before and after binding. The framework is openly available at https://github.com/IAI-USTC-Quantum/oracq.
one_liner: oracq separates quantum algorithms from typed oracle implementations, enabling systematic comparison of gate, QRAM, and reversible-arithmetic realizations.
why_it_matters: The framework makes implementation-dependent accuracy and logical-resource costs explicit for quantum scientific-computing workflows.
detailed_summary: oracq stores algorithms as persistent register-level programs with typed but initially unimplemented oracle slots. A binding pass connects those slots to gate networks, QRAM-backed tables, or compiled reversible fixed-point arithmetic while separately tracking implementation and method errors. End-to-end examples cover finite-volume simulation of compressible Euler equations and homotopy-based treatment of nonlinear PDEs.
main_result: The framework enables one quantum algorithm specification to be verified and resource-accounted across multiple concrete oracle realizations.
application_angle: It supports more credible implementation planning and cross-platform resource comparison for future quantum scientific-computing systems.

title: Ultraviolet Raman spectroscopy using multimode aluminum oxide waveguides
abstract: Waveguide-based Raman spectroscopy offers a route toward compact and integrated photonic sensors. While most waveguide Raman platforms operate in the near-infrared, extending excitation toward the visible and ultraviolet is attractive because shorter excitation wavelengths can provide substantially stronger Raman scattering and access to resonance-enhanced molecular responses. This transition, however, places greater demands on the photonic material because of optical loss, absorption and waveguide-generated spectral background. Here, we investigate aluminum oxide ($Al_2O_3$) waveguides as a low-background platform for Raman spectroscopy at 532 nm and 325 nm using a back-collected excitation and detection geometry. At 532 nm, after normalization to the incident excitation power-time product, the measured $Al_2O_3$ background was more than two orders of magnitude lower than that of $Si_3N_4$. Under 325 nm excitation, the waveguides maintained a weak and reproducible spectral background across the investigated widths. Using immersion oil as a model analyte deposited over the waveguide surface, we demonstrate that analyte-specific Raman fingerprints can be recovered above the waveguide background at both wavelengths. Signal-to-background ratio and spectral contrast were used to quantify analyte visibility relative to the waveguide background, and both metrics consistently confirmed clear detection of the analyte bands. These results demonstrate that $Al_2O_3$ combines low measured spectral background with operation from the visible into the ultraviolet, providing a promising route toward integrated Raman spectroscopy at shorter excitation wavelengths.
one_liner: Multimode aluminum-oxide waveguides enable low-background Raman sensing at visible and ultraviolet excitation wavelengths.
why_it_matters: Low waveguide background at 325 and 532 nm could bring stronger, resonance-sensitive Raman measurements into compact integrated sensors.
detailed_summary: The study characterizes multimode Al2O3 waveguides in a back-collected Raman geometry at 532 and 325 nm. At 532 nm, their normalized spectral background is over two orders of magnitude lower than that measured from Si3N4, while the ultraviolet background remains weak and reproducible across waveguide widths. Immersion-oil fingerprints are recovered above the device background at both wavelengths using signal-to-background and spectral-contrast metrics.
main_result: Analyte-specific Raman bands were clearly detected on Al2O3 waveguides under both 532 nm and 325 nm excitation.
application_angle: The platform offers a path toward compact visible-to-UV Raman chips for chemical and resonance-enhanced molecular sensing.

title: eCAS: An Orbital Embedding Method for Quantum Computing
abstract: Future fault-tolerant quantum computers will allow us to calculate electronic structures of atomistic systems. However, these systems will be intrinsically limited in size, requiring embedding theories for many systems because of the unfavorable scaling of the number of terms describing the electron-electron interaction in the second-quantized electronic Hamiltonian. Quantum embedding theories address this challenge by partitioning a quantum system into a region of interest, the impurity, and its (larger) complement, the environment. However, currently available quantum embedding methods place restrictive demands on near-future quantum computers, such as the need to measure reduced density matrices or the need for repeated evaluations. Here, we introduce the new orbital embedding method eCAS that steers clear of these pitfalls by constructing a multi-CAS problem, the active spaces of which are localized and can be solved independently of each other with any quantum algorithm. This also allows for the development of comparatively simple gradient expressions. eCAS leverages the Schmidt decomposition to construct initial impurity and bath orbitals and augments them with localized environment orbitals, based on a mutual correlation criterion. The mutual correlation criterion makes eCAS systematically improvable without the need for any iteratively determined quantities.
one_liner: eCAS partitions electronic-structure problems into localized active spaces that quantum processors can solve independently.
why_it_matters: It may reduce qubit and measurement demands for quantum chemistry without iterative embedding or reduced-density-matrix measurements.
detailed_summary: eCAS constructs impurity and bath orbitals through a Schmidt decomposition, then adds localized environment orbitals selected by mutual correlation. The resulting multi-CAS problem contains localized active spaces that can be solved independently with arbitrary quantum algorithms. Its correlation criterion permits systematic improvement without iteratively fitted quantities and yields comparatively simple gradient expressions.
main_result: The method converts a large electronic-structure calculation into independently solvable localized active-space problems without repeated embedding evaluations.
application_angle: eCAS could make chemically relevant atomistic simulations fit within the constrained qubit and measurement budgets of early fault-tolerant machines.

title: High-efficiency photonic GHZ measurements with linear optics
abstract: Probabilistic and destructive Bell-measurements, also known as fusions, constitute a fundamental primitive for photonic quantum technologies. These operations rely only on pairwise photonic interference, whereas the computational power of photonic quantum systems originates from many-body interference. Here, we introduce a family of high-efficiency linear-optical GHZ measurements based on four-mode interferometers and show that incorporating many-body interference into this ubiquitous primitive leads to more efficient entangling operations. For the four-photon case, the success probability is $9/32$, and adaptive variants ensure that unsuccessful events project onto useful stabilizer states. We further show that the approach naturally generalizes to larger GHZ measurements, yielding an exponentially higher success probability than previous linear-optical schemes. Finally, we demonstrate practical advantages for graph-state resource generation, entanglement distribution between remote spin-photon interfaces, and fusion-based quantum computing. Our results establish high-efficiency many-body measurements as a new primitive for scalable photonic quantum information processing.
one_liner: Four-mode linear-optical interferometers perform photonic GHZ measurements with many-body interference and improved success probabilities.
why_it_matters: More efficient GHZ projections can lower resource overheads in photonic networking, graph-state generation, and fusion-based quantum computing.
detailed_summary: The authors introduce a family of linear-optical GHZ measurements built from four-mode interferometers rather than only pairwise photonic interference. The four-photon protocol succeeds with probability 9/32, and adaptive failure events still produce useful stabilizer states. Generalized schemes achieve an exponentially higher success probability than prior linear-optical approaches and are analyzed for graph-state production and remote spin-photon entanglement.
main_result: The proposed four-photon GHZ measurement reaches 9/32 success probability and generalizes with an exponential advantage over previous linear-optical schemes.
application_angle: The primitive can improve entanglement distribution and reduce overhead in scalable photonic and fusion-based quantum architectures.

title: FaultScope: A software package for fast error attribution in quantum error correction
abstract: We introduce FaultScope, a classical simulator for quantum error correction circuits, implemented in Rust with a Python interface. FaultScope estimates logical error rates and their derivatives with respect to component error rates from the same sampled and decoded shots, without modifying or differentiating through the decoder. These derivatives enable error attribution to individual noisy components, helping identify noise hotspots for targeted noise reduction. FaultScope supports forward simulation of error propagation through circuits and direct sampling of detector and logical observable outcomes from detector error models. In our noiseless and noisy benchmarks, FaultScope has the lowest runtime among the tested simulators at every size. Computing all derivatives adds only 0.33--0.97\% to the runtime of logical error rate estimation across five repetition code sizes with 7--2047 error locations. FaultScope can be used to benchmark large-scale quantum error correction schemes and guide targeted noise reduction efficiently, thereby facilitating the design and optimization of fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures.
one_liner: FaultScope rapidly attributes logical quantum-error rates to individual noisy circuit components using shared simulation samples.
why_it_matters: Near-zero-overhead error derivatives expose hardware noise hotspots and help prioritize improvements in fault-tolerant architectures.
detailed_summary: FaultScope is a Rust simulator with a Python interface that propagates circuit faults or samples detector error models. From the same sampled and decoded shots, it estimates logical error rates and derivatives with respect to component error rates without differentiating through the decoder. Across repetition codes containing 7 to 2047 error locations, computing all derivatives adds only 0.33–0.97% to estimation runtime.
main_result: FaultScope delivered the lowest benchmark runtime while adding under 1% overhead for component-level logical-error derivatives.
application_angle: Its attribution data can direct calibration and engineering effort toward the components that most strongly limit logical performance.

title: Symmetries and model reduction in a $\cos 2\varphi$ transmon qubit
abstract: Engineered symmetries in superconducting circuits can protect quantum information; much like selection rules in atomic physics, they forbid transitions between the qubit states. Protected circuits, however, combine several loops and islands and host multiple nonlinearly coupled modes, calling for reduced low-energy models that inherit the circuit symmetries and make the protection manifest. We develop such a reduction for the $\cos 2\varphi$ transmon qubit, recently realized experimentally with a two-Cooper-pair interferometer, whose circuit hosts three coupled modes. Exploiting the separation of energy scales between the heavy transmon mode and the light internal modes of the interferometer, we derive an effective single-band Born-Oppenheimer model, including its geometric correction, and extend it to several bands. We identify the symmetries of the full and reduced Hamiltonians and derive exact selection rules. Finally, we identify a parameter regime beyond the single-band description that suppresses flux-noise dephasing without degrading charge-noise protection.
one_liner: A symmetry-preserving reduction captures the low-energy physics and exact selection rules of a three-mode cos(2φ) transmon.
why_it_matters: The model identifies operating regimes that suppress flux dephasing while retaining symmetry-based protection from charge noise.
detailed_summary: The work reduces a three-mode cos(2φ) transmon containing a two-Cooper-pair interferometer by exploiting the energy-scale separation between its heavy transmon mode and light internal modes. It derives single- and multiband Born-Oppenheimer descriptions, including a geometric correction, while retaining the symmetries of the complete circuit. Those symmetries yield exact transition-selection rules and reveal a multiband regime with reduced flux-noise dephasing.
main_result: The reduced model preserves exact circuit symmetries and identifies a regime with suppressed flux-noise dephasing and maintained charge-noise protection.
application_angle: The analysis provides concrete guidance for biasing and designing symmetry-protected superconducting qubits with improved coherence.

title: Simulating two-Dimensional decaying vortex structure with the Carleman-Lattice-Boltzmann method
abstract: We perform a numerical study of the free decay of two-dimensional nonlinear vortex structures using the second-order-truncated Carleman-Lattice Boltzmann method (CLB2). To this purpose, we simulate the nonlinear vortex system on a $128\times128$ grid at two initial Reynolds numbers, $Re\approx15$ and $Re\approx46$, by resorting to a highly-tuned multi-GPU implementation of the CLB2 code. At $Re \approx 15$, CLB2 shows significant accuracy all along the decay process, up to six diffusive times (corresponding to $950$ time steps), with structure-preserving errors below 10\% in amplitude, where by structure-preserving we imply that such errors can be almost entirely reabsorbed by a global time-dependent rescaling factor. At $Re \approx 46$, the evolution is carried out over $2850$ time steps, also corresponding to six diffusive times. In this scenario, however, the errors grow in time well above 10\% in amplitude with a still relatively modest but appreciable effect on the spatial structure of the flow. These results indicate that CLB2 is capable of preserving the nonlinear evolution of coherent structures over sufficiently long time spans to reach an effective zero steady-state. However CLB2 shows a constant sub-dissipative trend (more energy than the corresponding Lattice Boltzmann configurations) with a deteriorating accuracy at increasing time and Reynolds number. The present results shed hope that further developments, such as suitable closures instead of truncation and/or various forms of regularization, may lead to a significant improvement of the CLB2 accuracy, prior or even without escalating to expensive higher-order truncations.
one_liner: A multi-GPU Carleman–Lattice-Boltzmann solver tracks decaying 2D vortices for six diffusive times, with accuracy degrading at higher Reynolds number.
why_it_matters: The benchmarks expose the accuracy and dissipation limits that must be addressed before truncated Carleman formulations become useful for quantum fluid simulation.
detailed_summary: The authors simulate free decay on a 128×128 grid using a second-order-truncated Carleman–Lattice-Boltzmann implementation optimized for multiple GPUs. At Re≈15, amplitude errors remain below 10% and are largely removable by global time-dependent rescaling through 950 steps. At Re≈46, errors exceed 10% over 2,850 steps and begin altering spatial structure, while a persistent sub-dissipative bias leaves excess energy relative to standard lattice-Boltzmann results.
main_result: CLB2 preserves coherent vortex evolution through six diffusive times at modest Reynolds number but loses accuracy and under-dissipates as Reynolds number and time increase.
application_angle: The study supplies concrete targets for closures and regularization needed in future quantum-compatible Carleman fluid solvers, though it does not demonstrate sensing hardware or a quantum processor.

title: A Highly Nondegenerate Photon-Pair Source for Detector-Matched Quantum Key Distribution
abstract: In a commercial entanglement-distribution system over telecom fibre, the single-photon detectors are the largest part of the hardware cost. In entanglement-based quantum key distribution (QKD), both photons of each pair must be detected. With two telecom photons, each arm needs either an InGaAs single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) of low efficiency or a superconducting nanowire single-photon detector (SNSPD) with its own cryostat. We study a highly nondegenerate photon-pair source that needs a telecom detector on one arm only. Two periodically poled KTiOPO$_4$ (ppKTP) crystals pumped at 405~nm emit pairs at 548 and 1550~nm. A Si-SPAD with 82\% efficiency detects the 548~nm photon at the source node, and only the 1550~nm photon travels through fibre. A first, unoptimised module in a polarisation-correlated configuration generates about $1.5\times10^6$ pairs/s per mW of pump power. It collects 13\% of the pairs on the 548~nm arm and 23\% on the 1550~nm arm. In an asymptotic BBM92 model, we compare its links with generic $2\times1550$~nm links that use a bright published source at the same pump power. At 50~km, our link with one SNSPD costs about 25\% more per secret bit than the generic link with one SNSPD. With optimistic target values of 52\% collection and twice the brightness, it costs about 40\% as much as the generic link with two SNSPDs. Our link without a cryostat then costs about 70\% less than the generic link with one SNSPD. If every link runs at its own best pump power, the two-SNSPD link is again the cheapest. The source can also serve clock synchronisation and detector calibration, which need only time-correlated pairs. All key rates assume the entangled configuration of the source, which is under development.
one_liner: A 405-nm-pumped ppKTP source produces 548/1550-nm photon pairs so only the fiber arm requires an expensive telecom detector.
why_it_matters: Matching each photon to a low-cost Si-SPAD or fiber-compatible telecom detector could substantially reduce entanglement-based QKD receiver cost.
detailed_summary: Two ppKTP crystals pumped at 405 nm generate polarization-correlated pairs at 548 and 1550 nm, allowing an 82%-efficient Si-SPAD to detect the local photon while its partner traverses telecom fiber. The unoptimized module produces about 1.5×10^6 pairs s⁻¹ mW⁻¹, with collection efficiencies of 13% and 23% on the visible and telecom arms. BBM92 cost modeling indicates strong savings under improved brightness and collection, but the entangled source configuration assumed for key-rate estimates remains under development.
main_result: The prototype demonstrates high-rate, highly nondegenerate correlated-pair generation and models detector-cost advantages for asymmetric entanglement-based QKD links.
application_angle: The architecture can lower QKD hardware costs by reserving cryogenic or InGaAs detection for one arm and can also support clock synchronization and detector calibration.

title: Dipolar Exciton Polarons in a van der Waals Homobilayer
abstract: Fermi polarons exemplify how many-body interactions give rise to emergent quasiparticles, providing a fundamental framework for understanding interacting quantum matter. In electron-doped two-dimensional semiconductors, exciton polarons offer optical access to Fermi-polaron physics and electrical tunability, yet achieving stronger and more controllable exciton-electron interactions remains a key challenge. Here, we realize dipolar exciton polarons in an electrically tunable van der Waals homobilayer, where interlayer excitons with spatially separated electrons and holes act as quantum impurities carrying permanent electric dipole moments. These dipolar polarons exhibit substantially enhanced exciton-electron interactions, with binding energies more than four times those of conventional intralayer exciton polarons. We further demonstrate that Fermi-sea layer polarization provides an additional degree of freedom for controlling many-body interactions.
